item.title: [1.8] Immunotherapy response in TLS-positive solid tumors treated with regorafenib plus avelumab: the prospective, multicenter, open-label, phase 2 REGOMUNE trial
item.description:
Tertiary lymphoid structures organize local immune responses, but their presence does not ensure benefit from immune checkpoint blockade. Here we report the mature tertiary lymphoid structure-positive cohort of REGOMUNE, a prospective, multicenter, open-label, single-arm phase 2 trial of regorafenib plus the anti-programmed death-ligand 1 antibody avelumab in advanced solid tumors. The primary endpoint was the 6-month progression-free rate; secondary endpoints included best overall response, objective response rate, progression-free and overall survival, growth modulation index and safety. Among 132 patients screened, 38 were treated and 34 were assessable for efficacy. The prespecified primary endpoint was met: 10 of the first 29 eligible and assessable patients were progression free at 6 months, exceeding the success boundary of 8. In all 34 assessable patients, the 6-month progression-free rate was 35.3% (95% confidence interval, 19.8–53.5%), and the objective response rate was 26.5%. The median progression-free and overall survival were 3.6 and 8.6 months, respectively. Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 23 of 38 patients; no treatment-related deaths occurred. Exploratory tumor and blood profiling associated benefit with antigen-presentation programs, TCF1-7-positive T-cell niches and early systemic immune remodeling. These functional immune features warrant independent prospective validation. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03475953 . In this REGOMUNE phase 2 trial, Italiano and colleagues evaluated the efficacy of avelumab in combination with regorafenib in patients with advanced solid tumors exhibiting TLSs.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] CCT6A confers chemoresistance in esophageal adenocarcinoma by stabilizing YBX1 against TRIM21-mediated degradation
item.description:
Esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) has a poor prognosis, primarily due to chemoresistance, yet its mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Although the chaperonin subunit CCT6A promotes tumor progression in other malignancies, its role in EAC is unclear. Here, we performed high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA) on single-cell RNA sequencing data from EAC patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy, identifying CCT6A as a hub gene associated with chemoresistance. Public database analyses confirmed CCT6A upregulation in EAC tissues and its association with poor prognosis, which was further validated in clinical samples. Functionally, CCT6A knockdown sensitized EAC cells to oxaliplatin. Mechanistically, CCT6A directly binds and stabilizes YBX1 protein by interfering with TRIM21-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Structural modeling and molecular dynamics simulations suggested that CCT6A binds a shared recognition interface within the YBX1 C-terminal domain, restricting TRIM21 recognition and providing a structural basis for YBX1 stabilization. Stabilized YBX1 promotes chemoresistance by activating DNA damage repair, particularly BRCA1-mediated homologous recombination repair, while simultaneously inducing an immunosuppressive microenvironment through PD-L1 upregulation and CD8⁺ T cell suppression. Rescue experiments demonstrated that YBX1 mediates CCT6A-driven DNA damage repair and immunosuppression. Our study identifies the CCT6A–YBX1 axis as a promising therapeutic target for overcoming chemoresistance and immunosuppression in EAC.

item.title: [1.7] Targeting chemotherapy-induced CD200 via a nucleoside-enhanced nanocarrier for cancer immunochemotherapy
item.description:
Immune checkpoint blockade has transformed cancer therapy, yet its efficacy is frequently undermined by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. In addition, the immune-related toxicities restrict combination therapy targeting several immune checkpoints. Here, we identify chemotherapy-induced CD200 upregulation as a stress-adaptive resistance mechanism that reinforces tumor immune evasion under treatment pressure. Leveraging a tumor-restricted, nucleoside-enhanced nanocarrier, we achieve spatially selective silencing of tumor-intrinsic CD200, thereby reprogramming the tumor immune microenvironment, enhancing antitumor efficacy, and enabling effective combination with PD-1 blockade. Importantly, this strategy minimizes the colitis exacerbation associated with systemic CD200/PD-1 dual blockade in a DSS-induced susceptibility model, suggesting its potential to preserve immune homeostasis while reducing immune-related toxicity. Together, our findings establish CD200 as a context-dependent immune resistance node and demonstrate a nanotechnology-based framework for precise and safe immune checkpoint modulation. The efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade therapy is limited by the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Here this group identifies the chemotherapy-induced CD200 upregulation as a resistance mechanism then develops a nanotechnology-based framework for spatially selective CD200 silencing, thereby reprogramming TME and enhancing antitumor efficacy.

item.title: [1.7] NNMT/EBF1 axis in cancer-associated fibroblasts drives CCL2/CCR2-mediated M2 polarization of macrophages to promote HNSCC progression
item.description:
Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are abundant in the tumor microenvironment of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) and exert pivotal pro-tumorigenic functions, including extracellular matrix remodeling, angiogenesis, and immunosuppression. In this study, we investigated the molecular mechanisms by which CAFs orchestrate the recruitment and functional polarization of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) to drive HNSCC progression. Nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT), a key regulator of CAFs, exhibited a markedly positive correlation with CD163+ macrophage infiltration in human HNSCC tissues. Functional validation demonstrated that NNMT mediated CAF-driven recruitment and M2 polarization of TAMs in HNSCC in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, NNMT upregulated CCL2 secretion in CAFs, facilitating CCR2-dependent TAM recruitment and M2 polarization in HNSCC. Moreover, NNMT activated the PI3K/Akt pathway, leading to upregulation of the EBF transcription factor 1 (EBF1), which directly regulates CCL2 transcription in CAFs. Furthermore, the combination of NNMT inhibitors and anti-PD-1 antibodies synergistically suppressed tumor growth and modulated anti-tumor immunity in a syngeneic mouse model. In conclusion, these findings reveal that the NNMT/PI3K/Akt/EBF1 signaling axis contributes to CAF-mediated TAM recruitment and M2 polarization in HNSCC through the CCL2/CCR2 axis. Our study sheds new light on CAF-macrophage crosstalk in HNSCC and provides potential therapeutic strategies for patients. Background/Aims: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are abundant in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) and exert pivotal pro-tumorigenic functions. Understanding how CAFs regulate tumor immunity may lead to new immunotherapies for HNSCC. Methods: First, we determined the correlation between nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT) and M2 macrophage infiltration in HNSCC tissues using public transcriptomic databases. Next, we investigated how NNMT mediates CAF-driven recruitment and polarization of macrophages using cell experiments and mouse models. Finally, we evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of combining an NNMT inhibitor with anti-PD-1 antibodies in tumor-bearing mice. Results: NNMT positively correlated with M2 macrophage infiltration in HNSCC tissues and drove CAF-mediated recruitment and M2 polarization of macrophages via the CCL2/CCR2 axis. The combination of an NNMT inhibitor with anti-PD-1 antibodies significantly suppressed tumor growth and improved anti-tumor immunity in mice. Conclusions: Our study provides novel insights into the mechanisms underlying CAF-macrophage crosstalk in HNSCC and offers potential therapeutic strategies for patients.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] Therapeutic antibodies targeting PD-1 or PD-L1 impact the circulation time of soluble checkpoint receptor/ligand targets
item.description:
Using OLINK PEA and Meso Scale Discovery, MSD, we quantified soluble PD-1 (sPD-1) and PD-L1 (sPD-L1) in lung cancer patients receiving pembrolizumab, nivolumab or atezolizumab monotherapy. Elevated sPD-1 and sPD-L1 levels were significantly therapy-dependent; pembrolizumab and nivolumab increased sPD-1, while atezolizumab increased sPD-L1. Thus, elevated levels may reflect therapeutic antibody-mediated half-life extension via antibody-soluble target complex formation, rather than solely biologically induced target shedding or production.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.2] Nuclear factor I connects H3K27M to a targetable purine dependency in diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma
item.description:
Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma is a lethal pediatric brainstem cancer with few effective treatments. Here, we integrate metabolomic, transcriptomic, chromatin, genetic and in vivo analyses to identify a purine-metabolic dependency associated with the H3K27M histone mutation. The histone H3 lysine 27-to-methionine substitution increases Nuclear Factor I transcriptional activity, which promotes coordinated expression of enzymes involved in purine biosynthesis and degradation, including 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide formyltransferase/inosine monophosphate cyclohydrolase and purine nucleoside phosphorylase. Sustained purine degradation limits feedback inhibition of purine synthesis, enabling continued purine production, utilization and catabolism. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of the terminal de novo purine biosynthesis enzyme reduces tumor-cell fitness, slows orthotopic tumor progression and extends survival in mice. These results connect histone-mutation-associated chromatin remodeling to a Nuclear Factor I-regulated, therapeutically targetable purine dependency in diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma. Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma is an aggressive childhood cancer commonly driven by H3K27M with few treatment options. This study links H3K27M-driven chromatin remodelling to NFI-dependent purine metabolism, causing ATIC/PNP-mediated metabolic rewiring and ATIC-targetable tumour dependence.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.0] Choline kinase α promotes glycolysis and tumor growth by phosphorylating and activating enolase 1
item.description:
Tumor cells exhibit aberrantly upregulated glycolysis, in which glycolytic enzyme enolase 1 (ENO1) plays a critical role. However, how ENO1 activity is dynamically regulated in tumor cells remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate that hypoxic stimulation promotes the binding of p38 MAP kinase to choline kinase α (CHKα). p38 phosphorylates CHKα at S114, subsequently leading to CHKα to interact with ENO1. Importantly, CHKα functions as a protein kinase and phosphorylates ENO1 Y44 thereby enhancing the metabolic activity of ENO1 to increase glycolysis. Knock-in expression of CHKα S114A or ENO1 Y44F inhibits brain tumor cell glycolysis and proliferation, blunts brain tumor growth in mice with inhibited lactate production, and prolongs mouse survival. In addition, CHKα S114 and ENO1 Y44 phosphorylation levels are positively correlated with each other and associated with poor prognosis in glioblastoma patients. These findings highlight the critical regulation of glycolysis by the noncanonical function of CHKα and underscore the potential to target the moonlighting function of CHKα for cancer treatment. Tumor cells rely on increased glycolysis for growth. Here, authors show that choline kinase α activates enolase 1 through phosphorylation, promoting glycolysis and tumor progression in glioblastoma.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] Artificial intelligence in DNA repair: from mechanism to medicine
item.description:
DNA repair pathways safeguard genome integrity yet are frequently dysregulated in cancer and other human diseases. In tumors, DNA repair defects drive tumor evolution while creating therapeutic vulnerabilities exploitable by chemotherapy, DNA damage-response inhibitors, and immunotherapy. Although pathway-focused studies have elucidated key repair mechanisms, they lack the scale needed to interpret the high-dimensional genomic, transcriptomic, imaging, structural, and clinical datasets generated by modern precision oncology. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning help address this gap by offering new ways to measure DNA repair activity, predict repair outcomes, and connect diverse biological data. Here we organize AI applications in DNA repair into a biology-driven three-wave framework: mutational footprint-based repair-state inference; lesion-level repair outcome prediction; and multimodal repair-state inference for biomarker discovery, therapy response prediction, synthetic lethality, and structure-guided drug discovery. We go beyond cataloging AI applications by evaluating their strengths, limitations, and appropriate use. We also clarify how AI findings should be interpreted from predictive correlations to experimentally supported mechanisms. Finally, we discuss challenges in model transparency, dataset bias, imperfect labels, overfitting, validation, and clinical translation, and outline principles for developing biologically grounded AI frameworks that advance mechanistic discovery and precision oncology. DNA repair pathways are crucial for maintaining genome stability by correcting DNA damage from various sources. This study highlights the dynamic nature of DNA repair, emphasizing that dysfunction in these pathways can lead to genomic instability and cancer, creating therapeutic opportunities. The authors propose a framework using artificial intelligence (AI) to integrate diverse molecular and clinical data, aiming to infer DNA repair states and generate biologically informed hypotheses. They describe three waves of AI application: inferring repair deficiencies from mutational footprints, predicting repair outcomes at DNA lesions, and integrating multimodal data for context-aware repair-state inference. Key findings include AI’s ability to predict repair deficiencies and therapeutic vulnerabilities, offering insights into repair pathway choices and outcomes. This study advances the understanding of DNA repair mechanisms and suggests future directions for AI in precision oncology. This summary was initially drafted using artificial intelligence, then revised and fact-checked by the author.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.7] Discovery of novel drug combinations for oral squamous cell carcinoma through integrated analysis of single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets
item.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is associated with high morbidity and mortality, yet treatment options remain limited and resistance driven by intratumoral heterogeneity (ITH) is frequent. To characterize ITH and identify strategies to overcome it, we integrated twelve public single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets into an unprecedentedly large dataset and combined it with spatial transcriptomics. A novel, pathway-based clustering approach revealed seven highly recurrent and distinct tumor cell clusters, each defined by divergent cell-cell interactions, distinct positions along the cell trajectory tree, and spatially defined localization within tumors. To overcome ITH therapeutically, we sought to identify drug targets that were overexpressed in the vast majority of these highly diverse tumor cells, which was reasonably achieved only through pairwise target combinations. Pharmacological inhibition of LGALS1 plus CTSC, and LGALS1 plus TYMP, suppressed growth of OSCC spheroids, with further enhancement by cisplatin. Additional anti-tumor activity is expected in vivo through known effects of these inhibitors on the tumor microenvironment. Our work characterizes ITH in OSCC and reveals strategies to overcome it by broadly targeting malignant and microenvironmental drivers of OSCC, providing a basis for the rational design of novel combination therapies.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.9] A cholesterol addiction creates an Achilles' heel in APC-truncated colorectal cancer
item.description:
Cholesterol auxotrophy, dependence on exogenous cholesterol, is an emerging metabolic vulnerability of cancer that remains poorly understood. Here, we show that APC-truncated CRC cell lines displayed cholesterol auxotrophy, whereas CTNNB1-mutant cells were cholesterol-independent. The endolysosomal Niemann Pick type C2 (NPC2) protein is a key transporter of cholesterol from lysosomes to cellular membranes. NPC2 knockdown (KD) in auxotrophic APC-mutant cells depleted plasma-membrane cholesterol, disorganized lipid-raft scaffolding and signaling, and inhibited stemness, xenograft growth and metastasis. In contrast, NPC2 KD CTNNB1-mutant cells retained tumorigenic and metastatic capacity. Genome-wide transcriptional responses to NPC2 loss were nearly uncorrelated between APC and CTNNB1 mutant cell lines revealing genotype-dependent adaptation and opposite cell signaling pathways alterations. NPC2 KD auxotrophs showed abortive compensatory cholesterol synthesis with no alternative egress route, whereas CTNNB1-mutant cells restored lysosomal cholesterol egress by inducing NPC1 and sustaining Wnt/stemness identity, AP-1/YAP/TAZ signaling and a pro-invasive secretome. Lipidomics confirmed the signaling divergences: sphingomyelin collapse, membrane-fluidity remodeling exclusive to the auxotrophs, and opposite-direction diacylglycerol signaling in CTNNB1 mutants. Notably, APC-truncated cells phenocopied selected Niemann Pick type C hallmarks, linking lysosomal cholesterol export to tumor fitness. Thus, NPC2 constitutes a synthetic-lethal vulnerability specific to cholesterol-auxotrophic APC-mutant CRCs, providing a mechanistic rationale for targeting the secreted and recaptured NPC2 pool in this molecular subset of patients.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.0] PI3Kβ inhibition creates a ferroptosis vulnerability in PTEN-deficient cancers
item.description:
PTEN loss represents one of the most frequent oncogenic events across human cancers, with PI3K{beta} emerging as a dominant driver of tumor progression and therapy resistance in PTEN-deficient tumors. Although genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PI3K{beta} suppresses tumor growth, actionable synthetic lethal vulnerabilities associated with PI3K{beta} inhibition remain poorly defined. Here, through integrative analysis of gene expression, CRISPR dependency, and drug sensitivity datasets from the Cancer Dependency Map, we uncover ferroptosis resistance as a hallmark of PTEN-deficient cancers. Using genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs)-derived breast cancer cells and systematic cell death screens, we show that Pik3cb deletion selectively sensitizes Pten-deficient tumors to ferroptosis. Mechanistically, PI3K{beta} promotes lipid metabolic reprogramming primarily through activation of the SREBP1-dependent de novo lipogenesis, lipid droplet formation, and sequestration of ferroptosis-sensitive polyunsaturated fatty acids, thereby limiting lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic cell death. Therapeutically, combined PI3K{beta} inhibition and ferroptosis induction synergistically suppress tumor growth and prolong survival across GEMMs, human cancer cell line-derived xenografts, and patient-derived xenografts. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized role of PI3K{beta} in ferroptosis resistance and establish a mechanistically informed combination strategy for PTEN-deficient cancers.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] Generation of tumor organoids and cancer-associated fibroblasts from minimal pancreatic cancer biopsies enables investigation of tumor-stroma interactions
item.description:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains among the deadliest forms of cancer, accounting for the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in North America. A critical factor in this poor outcome is the inability to effectively treat patients not eligible for surgery. The development of patient-derived organoids (PDOs) from tumors has shown promise as a personalized approach for treating PDAC. In the case of PDAC, PDOs need to be generated immediately upon diagnosis due to the rapid mortality observed in these patients. In addition, the tumor microenvironment, a significant factor in PDAC, needs to be considered. To address these two issues, we developed an approach to isolate both cancer and non-cancer-cells of PDAC tumors through endoscopic ultrasound at the time of initial diagnosis. PDOs and cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) cultures retain patient-specific heterogeneity related to the in vivo tumor phenotype with PDOs showing two distinct and stable phenotypic and molecular profiles. These subtypes were affected by introducing conditioned media from primary CAF cultures, which promoted transcriptomic and epigenetic changes in PDOs reflective of a more resistant phenotype. This study identifies approaches for rapid establishment of multiple tumor compartments ex vivo and highlights the importance in considering the tumor microenvironment when assessing the effects of chemotherapeutic responses in patients.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.4] Combined BRAF and RAS inhibition overcomes acquired resistance in BRAF-mutated colorectal cancer
item.description:
BRAFV600E-mutated colorectal cancer is aggressive and associated with poor patient prognosis. Combined BRAF and EGFR inhibition improves patient outcomes but acquired resistance limits treatment efficacy. We integrated molecular profiling and functional drug screening of BRAF-mutated cell lines (n = 17) and patient-derived organoids (n = 17) to identify and target mechanisms of intrinsic and acquired resistance. Acquired resistance to dual BRAF and EGFR inhibition was associated with RAS activation, including emerging NRAS hotspot mutations, KRAS amplification and transcriptomic MAPK signaling. Intrinsic and acquired resistance shared transcriptomic features including IGF1R, PI3K, inflammatory, and proteasome-associated signaling. Screening of 28 drug combinations revealed context-dependent sensitivity to co-inhibition of BRAF with IGF1R, MEK and SRC. Notably, RAS inhibitors daraxonrasib and RMC-7977 showed pronounced synergy with encorafenib in models with acquired RAS alterations, restoring treatment sensitivity and suppressing ERK1/2 phosphorylation. These findings identify acquired resistance associated with RAS reactivation as a therapeutic vulnerability and provide a preclinical rationale for combined BRAF and RAS inhibition in BRAF-mutated colorectal cancer.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.5] Dissecting the Tumor Microenvironment at Single-Cell Resolution to Prioritize Candidate Tumor Antigens Across Multiple Cancer Types
item.description:
Cancer immunotherapy has emerged as a revolutionary therapeutic approach, advancing the treatment of several cancer types. However, the identification of candidate tumor antigens remains challenging, as multiple lines of evidence are required to establish malignant-cell enrichment and therapeutic suitability. This study aimed to characterize and prioritize candidate tumor antigen genes based on their enrichment in malignant cells through the integration of single-cell transcriptomic data with complementary immunological and clinical evidence from the literature and public databases. An integrated pan-cancer dataset comprising 355,941 cells across 10 tumor types and 21 cell populations was analyzed using enrichment categories adapted from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA). Candidates were characterized according to antigen classification, gene expression in healthy tissues, presence of reported epitopes, recurrence across tumor types, and associations between gene expression and overall survival. Among the 22,779 genes evaluated, 30 candidates were retained after the prioritization process. CLDN6, MAGEC2, and PLAC1 stood out due to previous investigations in recent clinical immunotherapy research. Additionally, 16 of these 30 candidates showed significant associations between gene expression and overall survival across distinct cancer types, potentially supporting their prioritization for further investigation as immunotherapy targets. In contrast, some cancer-testis antigens (CTAs), previously regarded as promising therapeutic targets, were found to have limited suitability due to their enriched, enhanced, or group-enriched expression in non-malignant cells. Most of these steps can be independently reproduced using the publicly available Nextflow pipeline developed for this study.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] XPC restrains cancer stemness by modulating STAT1-SOX2 signaling in non-small cell lung cancer
item.description:
Cancer stem cells (CSCs) drive tumor initiation, therapeutic resistance, and disease relapse, yet the molecular mechanisms sustaining CSC maintenance remain incompletely defined. Xeroderma pigmentosum complementation group C (XPC) is a core DNA damage recognition factor in nucleotide excision repair, and its loss is linked to cancer predisposition. Beyond its canonical role in genome maintenance, XPC has emerged as a transcriptional co-regulator capable of modulating gene expression. Here, we identify XPC as a critical suppressor of CSC phenotypes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Genetic depletion of XPC enhances CSC self-renewal and tumor-initiating capacity, whereas inducible XPC expression restricts the CSC population. Transcriptomic and functional analyses reveal that XPC negatively regulates the stemness factor SOX2. Mechanistically, XPC selectively suppresses STAT1 activation by inhibiting phosphorylation at Tyr701, physically associates with STAT1 in the nucleus, and limits STAT1 recruitment to the SOX2 promoter. Loss of XPC results in elevated STAT1 signaling, increased SOX2 transcription, and CSC expansion. Notably, STAT1 signaling is highly activated in CSC-enriched populations and is required for CSC self-renewal. Collectively, these findings uncover a DNA repair-independent function of XPC mediated through a previously unrecognized XPC-STAT1-SOX2 axis, redefining XPC as a regulator of tumor cell plasticity and highlighting STAT1 signaling as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in XPC-deficient tumors.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] Dual HSP90/HDAC6 inhibition remodels the tumor microenvironment to enhance cancer immunotherapy
item.description:
Tumor microenvironment (TME) arises from dynamic and reciprocal interactions between cancer cells and stromal components such as immune cells, fibroblasts, and tumor vasculature, thereby generating extensive intratumoral heterogeneity that underlies resistance to many anticancer therapies. Addressing this complexity requires strategies that move beyond single-target interventions to engage hub proteins coordinating multiple malignant pathways at integrated regulatory nodes. Here, we developed PSY-3-11, a rationally designed dual inhibitor of heat shock protein 90 and histone deacetylase 6, and validated its coordinated antitumor activities. PSY-3-11 induced multifaceted remodeling across TME compartments by suppressing pathological angiogenesis, promoting vascular normalization, reducing epithelial–mesenchymal transition and PD-L1 expression, and reprogramming immunosuppressive myeloid populations toward an M1-like phenotype. In syngeneic tumor models, it markedly enhanced CD8⁺ T cell infiltration, activation, and cytotoxic readiness. Moreover, when combined with CTLA-4 blockade, PSY-3-11 produced robust and durable antitumor responses without increasing systemic toxicity, including in immunologically “cold” tumors that typically fail to respond to checkpoint inhibitors. Collectively, PSY-3-11 represents a promising immunomodulatory therapeutic candidate capable of reconditioning the heterogeneous TME and overcoming intrinsic resistance to immunotherapy. Its mechanism and favorable safety profile support its use as a combination-ready adjuvant to potentiate a range of cancer immunotherapies, including checkpoint inhibitors and adoptive cell therapies. The study explores the potential of PSY-3-11, a dual inhibitor targeting heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) and histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), to remodel the tumor microenvironment and enhance cancer immunotherapy. PSY-3-11 addresses the challenge of immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments in solid tumors by simultaneously inhibiting HSP90 and HDAC6, which are overexpressed in cancer cells and contribute to tumor progression. The authors designed PSY-3-11 to bind the catalytic domain of HDAC6 and the ATP-binding pocket of HSP90, effectively disrupting tumor-promoting pathways. In vivo and in vitro experiments demonstrated that PSY-3-11 suppresses tumor growth, normalizes vasculature, and enhances T cell-mediated immunity by reducing PD-L1 expression and promoting M1-like macrophage polarization. These findings suggest that PSY-3-11 can convert “cold” tumors into “hot” ones, making them more responsive to immune checkpoint inhibitors. This summary was initially drafted using artificial intelligence, then revised and fact-checked by the author.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] Reassessment of RNF43 function reveals no impact on endogenous EGFR or BRAF protein stability
item.description:
RNF43 is best known for removing the Wnt-receptor complex from the cell surface, thereby maintaining Wnt-signaling at minimal essential levels. Recent studies reported that RNF43-mutant colorectal cancers carrying the common BRAFV600E mutation, respond more effectively to combined BRAF/EGFR inhibition. To determine whether RNF43 directly regulates EGFR or BRAF protein abundance, multiple pancreatic and colorectal cancer cell line models were generated in which RNF43 was knocked out, repaired, or stably overexpressed. Total and cell surface EGFR levels, as well as endogenous BRAF expression, were quantified. Across all models, no consistent evidence emerges that RNF43 modulates endogenous EGFR or BRAF levels. R-spondins likewise fail to alter EGFR levels or internalization. Notably, elevated EGFR expression observed in a subset of RNF43 knockout clones is induced by unintended CRISPR/Cas9 vector integration rather than the absence of RNF43 itself, highlighting a previously underappreciated artifact that can confound interpretations of EGFR regulation in genome edited lines. Overall, the data argue against a direct and general role for RNF43 in controlling EGFR or BRAF protein abundance, contradicting recent reports that propose degradation of these targets. Further studies are required to resolve these discrepancies and clarify the mechanistic basis underlying these conflicting observations. Colorectal cancers with mutations in a gene called RNF43 have been reported to respond better to combined treatment targeting the cancer-related proteins EGFR and BRAF. One proposed explanation is that loss of RNF43 increases the amount of EGFR or BRAF in cancer cells. We tested this possibility using several pancreatic and colorectal cancer cell models in which RNF43 was removed, restored, or increased. We also examined whether R-spondins, proteins that regulate RNF43 activity, affected EGFR. Across these different models, we found no consistent evidence that RNF43 controls the amount of EGFR or BRAF. We also found that increased EGFR levels in some gene-edited cells were associated with unintended integration of the CRISPR/Cas9 editing vector rather than loss of RNF43. These findings do not support direct regulation of EGFR or BRAF by RNF43 and highlight the importance of carefully validating gene-edited cell models.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.6] Harnessing interconnected regulated cell death programs to prime antitumor immunity for immune checkpoint blockade
item.description:
Immune checkpoint inhibitors are unlikely to rescue tumors in which treatment-induced injury fails to generate a tumor-reactive immune substrate. Regulated cell death (RCD) offers a route to address this upstream limitation, but apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis and cuproptosis create distinct immune states. This Review compares these programs as context-dependent routes of immune priming rather than interchangeable mechanisms of tumor killing. Apoptosis is temporally controlled but may be erased by efferocytosis; necroptosis and pyroptosis increase immune visibility through membrane disruption but risk chronic or systemic inflammation; ferroptosis couples tumor redox vulnerability to T-cell pressure but may damage dendritic and lymphoid compartments; and cuproptosis remains an emerging mitochondrial stress program with limited clinical validation. Across these programs, immunotherapy efficacy is shaped by antigen availability, inflammatory signal emission, myeloid antigen-presenting competence and lymphoid receptiveness. These variables support a three-module therapeutic logic: tumor-restricted RCD for priming, checkpoint blockade to consolidate a tumor-reactive lymphoid state, and barrier control only when vascular, stromal, myeloid or metabolic restraints prevent effector entry, persistence or function. We translate this framework into compartment-resolved, time-dependent readouts of death execution, type I interferon activity, dendritic cell activation and functional licensing, cross-presentation, tumor-reactive lymphoid states, tissue barriers and collateral immune injury. Evidence from positive, negative and inconclusive combination trials is used to distinguish pathway engagement from immune-state conversion. The objective is not to maximize death or inflammation but to route tumor injury into durable antitumor immunity while preserving the immune compartments required for the checkpoint response.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] A pincer attack to take down cancer
item.description:
In this issue of Cell, Qiang et al. explore a new combination therapy that attacks pancreatic cancer from two angles. The therapy uses a KRAS inhibitor to target cancer cells, along with an AI-designed interleukin-21 mimetic to amplify an antitumor immune response mediated by effector CD4 T cells.
— Source: Cell

item.title: [2.2] Beyond canonical: Hidden phosphoregulatory control in RAS signaling reveals context-dependent rewiring in Y1 tumor cells
item.description:
Cell signaling pathways are not static. Regulatory mechanisms finely control the signal across complex networks to promote signal propagation. Among them, phosphorylation is one of the most important regulatory mechanisms, in which signal cascades propagate signals to the nucleus, enabling responses. Phosphorylation events can be regulated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) to coordinate the activation state of small G-proteins. In the Y1 cell derived from the adrenal gland of a mouse, the tumor phenotype is driven by constitutive overexpression of non-mutated KRAS with high SOS (Son of Sevenless)-mediated KRAS-GTP levels, activating downstream ERK signaling. Our previous finding showed that SOS is not a sole GEF in KRAS activation, pointing that much of the GEF and GAP regulatory system remains unknown. This motivated the generation of a comprehensive time-resolved proteome (DIA) and TMT phosphoproteome (DDA) under FGF2 stimulation combined or not with the SOS inhibitor BI-3406 (SOSi) to investigate adaptive signaling dynamics. Our findings revealed ERK feedback relief through parallel pathway activation and differential phosphorylation dynamics consequent of SOS inhibition, revealing novel layers of phospho-signaling rewiring beyond canonical RAS activation.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.3] Targeting ATR-CHK1-WEE1 signaling enhances IMPDH inhibitor efficacy in mTORC1-driven tumor cells
item.description:
Uncontrolled activation of the master metabolic regulator Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (mTORC1) in tumors confers strong dependence on the guanylate nucleotide synthesis enzyme inosine-5'-monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) for tumor cell growth and viability. Clinically approved IMPDH inhibitors reduce the guanylate nucleotide pool available for DNA synthesis in mTORC1-driven tumor cells, resulting in prolonged DNA replication stress and accumulation of DNA damage that culminates in apoptosis. These early molecular events are accompanied by activation of adaptive DNA replication stress response (RSR) and DNA damage response (DDR) pathways. We hypothesized that targeting these adaptive responses could enhance IMPDH inhibitor efficacy. We find that combining IMPDH inhibition with inhibition of the ATR-CHK1-WEE1 signaling axis increases the efficacy and durability of response in cell models, and in a syngeneic xenograft tumor model of the mTORC1-driven genetic tumor syndrome Tuberous Sclerosis Complex. Mechanistically, abrogating ATR-CHK1-WEE1 signaling during prolonged IMPDH inhibition causes aberrant cell cycle progression, increased DNA double-strand breaks, and formation of micronuclei. Together these findings uncover adaptive mechanisms that restrict IMPDH inhibitor efficacy, informing a combination strategy to improve treatment efficacy, while maintaining selectivity for targeting tumor cells that are driven by uncontrolled mTORC1 activation.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.5] Fishing for new immunotherapy compounds to boost innate tumor rejection
item.description:
Despite significant advances in cancer immunotherapy, tackling immunosuppression remains critical to achieve more effective responses. While developing the zebrafish xenograft model, we found that some human tumors engraft very efficiently ("progressors"), while others are cleared by the host ("regressors"). We showed that this was dependent on innate immunity, which recognizes and eliminates some cancer cells, while others are able to evade and suppress it. This opened an opportunity to perform an in vivo phenotypic drug screen to find compounds that induce clearance by boosting innate-tumor rejection. Zebrafish xenografts of human colorectal (CRC) and breast cancer (BC) that show a high engraftment/low clearance phenotype were used to screen over 500 FDA-approved small-molecule compounds, with tumor clearance serving as the phenotypic readout. The screen identified 23 hit compounds, of which six were effective across both cancer models. Mechanism-of-action enrichment analysis revealed a significant overrepresentation of autonomic nervous system-targeting drugs among the hits, particularly cholinergic ones. Immune profiling in myeloid reporter lines showed that the lead hit, Tiotropium bromide, a muscarinic receptor antagonist, reprograms tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory, anti-tumoral state. Tiotropium significantly increased macrophage phagocytosis, and macrophage depletion completely abolished its pro-clearance activity, establishing these myeloid cells as essential effectors. In a syngeneic CT26 colorectal mouse model, Tiotropium synergized with anti-PD-1 to control tumor growth and improve survival, outperforming all monotherapy arms. This effect was immune-dependent, as it was lost in immunodeficient NSG mice. Together, these findings demonstrate that in vivo phenotypic screening of FDA-approved compounds in zebrafish xenografts is a productive strategy for innate immune drug discovery in cancer. The identification of Tiotropium as a myeloid-reprogramming innate immune primer, together with the unbiased recovery of the neuro-immune axis as a druggable target, opens new avenues for overcoming immunotherapy resistance.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.5] Beyond IgG: Oral Secretory IgA as a new efficient modality for cancer immunotherapy
item.description:
Monoclonal antibody therapies have revolutionized cancer treatment but are almost exclusively based on intravenously administered IgG antibodies. Here, we developed and evaluated the first orally delivered anti-CEACAM5 secretory IgA (SIgA) for colorectal cancer. The pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, antitumor efficacy and immune effects of oral anti-CEACAM5 SIgA (ABC-101) were evaluated in an orthotopic metastatic human colorectal cancer model. Its therapeutic activity was compared with cetuximab, as monotherapy and in combination with irinotecan- or FOLFIRI-based chemotherapy along with that of an anti-CEACAM5 IgG1 sharing the same antigen-binding domain. Tumor-associated FcRI (CD89)-expressing myeloid populations were characterized at primary and metastatic sites. ABC-101 activity was evaluated on a second human cancer cell line, in vivo in an orthotopic human gastric cancer model. Oral anti-CEACAM5 SIgA (ABC-101) exhibited a unique pharmacokinetic profile, selectively accumulating in CEACAM5-positive primary tumors and metastases while maintaining minimal systemic exposure. Compared with the anti-CEACAM5 IgG1 and cetuximab, oral SIgA achieved superior inhibition of primary tumor growth and metastatic dissemination. It also enhanced the efficacy of irinotecan- and FOLFIRI-based chemotherapy, outperforming the FOLFIRI/cetuximab standard-of-care comparator. Mechanistically, ABC-101 remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment by promoting the recruitment of FcRI (CD89)-expressing neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells at both primary and metastatic sites, consistent with enhanced innate antitumor activity. Oral ABC-101 shows targeted activity against CEAhigh MKN-45 cells, reducing markers of cell proliferation and migration. These findings establish therapeutic SIgA as a first-in-class oral antibody immunotherapy combining selective tumor targeting, innate immune activation, and enhanced chemotherapy efficacy. More broadly, this work establishes mucosal immunity as a promising therapeutic frontier, demonstrating that orally delivered antibodies can enable systemic control of metastatic digestive cancers.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.8] Locoregional administration of bispecific CAR-T cells targeting CD44 and CD133 in recurrent high-grade glioma: a first-in-human investigator-initiated trial
item.description:
Grade IV glioma remains highly lethal, and effective therapies for recurrent disease remain limited. Glioma stem cells (GSCs) contribute to therapeutic resistance and tumor recurrence, providing a rationale for GSC-targeted immunotherapy. We conducted a single-center, single-arm investigator-initiated trial evaluating locoregional administration of CD44/CD133 bispecific chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells incorporating a truncated interleukin-7 receptor α (IL-7Rα) intracellular domain in ten adults with recurrent grade IV glioma. Treatment was well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities or Grade ≥2 cytokine release syndrome. Adverse events were predominantly mild and transient, and no patient required IL-6 or IL-1 blockade. CAR-T cell leakage into peripheral blood remained minimal, whereas cerebrospinal fluid cytokine elevations were modest following infusion. Three patients achieved partial responses. The median overall survival after the first CAR-T cell infusion was 465 days. Exploratory single-cell RNA sequencing and proteomic analyses suggested patient stratification in macrophage-associated signatures, particularly in interferon signaling and antigen-presentation programs, which were associated with distinct clinical outcomes independently of IDH mutation status in this cohort. These findings demonstrate the feasibility and safety of repeated locoregional administration of GSC-targeting IL-7Rα-armored bispecific CAR-T cells. Exploratory immune profiling further identified inter-patient heterogeneity in macrophage-associated immune programs, which warrants validation in larger prospective studies. (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05577091, NMPA No. CXSL2500032).
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.0] PD-L1 glycoforms regulate therapeutic antibody binding and response to anti-PD-L1 therapy
item.description:
Immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1/PD-L1 have transformed the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer, yet their clinical benefit remains limited even among patients with PD-L1-positive tumours, highlighting the need for improved predictive biomarkers. Although PD-L1 is heavily N-glycosylated, whether site-specific glycoform heterogeneity regulates therapeutic antibody binding and contributes to clinical outcome remains unclear. We applied a site-resolved glycoproteomic platform to characterise PD-L1 N-glycan heterogeneity in lung cancer cell lines and archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumours from patients treated with atezolizumab monotherapy. Structural modelling, functional assays, and tumour analyses were used to assess the mechanistic and clinical relevance of defined glycoforms. We identified poly-N-acetyllactosamine (poly-LacNAc) elongation at Asn200 of PD-L1 as a glycoform feature associated with reduced atezolizumab binding. Structural modelling indicated that extended N200 glycans can approach and partially occlude the antibody-binding interface, supporting a steric basis for impaired binding. Clinically, PD-L1 immunohistochemistry alone had limited value for progression-free survival stratification, whereas stratification based on PD-L1-associated poly-LacNAc revealed significant outcome differences. Patients with poly-LacNAc-positive PD-L1 had markedly shorter progression-free survival than those without this feature. Site-specific PD-L1 glycosylation determines therapeutic antibody binding and represents a clinically relevant layer of immune checkpoint regulation in lung cancer.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.6] Synthesis and anticancer evaluation of a novel bromobiphenyl–imidazole chalcone: DFT, in vitro, docking, MD, MM/GBSA, and FEL studies
item.description:
Cancer remains a major global health burden, highlighting the need to develop novel anticancer agents with improved efficacy and selectivity. In this study, a novel bromobiphenyl–imidazole chalcone (compound 3) was synthesized via base-catalyzed Claisen–Schmidt condensation and characterized using 1H-NMR, 13C-NMR, IR, UV, and ESI-MS spectroscopy. Compound 3 exhibited concentration-dependent cytotoxicity against A549 lung carcinoma cells, with an IC50 of 58.75 µM. In the human fetal osteoblast cell line, approximately 25% inhibition was observed at the highest tested concentration, and the IC₅₀ was not reached within the tested range; therefore, cancer cell selectivity has not yet been established. Treatment with compound 3 increased intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and was associated with apoptosis-like changes in nuclear morphology. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations performed at the B3LYP/6-311 + + G(d, p) level yielded a HOMO–LUMO energy gap of 1.63 eV, indicating moderate chemical reactivity and electronic stability. Furthermore, comprehensive in silico studies were performed to investigate the potential molecular interactions, binding stability, and energetic characteristics of compound 3. Molecular docking analysis predicted a favorable interaction between compound 3 and GNAI3, with a docking score of − 7.13 kcal/mol. A 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulation further supported the stability of the predicted compound 3-GNAI3 complex, with an average RMSD of approximately 2.21 Å and persistent protein–ligand interactions throughout the simulation. MM/GBSA calculations provided additional insights into the binding energetics, and free-energy landscape analysis characterized the conformational stability and energetic states of the complex. In silico ADMET profiling further characterized the physicochemical, pharmacokinetic, and toxicity properties of compound 3, including its predicted intestinal absorption, blood–brain barrier permeability, and potential toxicity liabilities. The combined experimental and computational findings provide preliminary evidence of the in vitro cytotoxic activity of compound 3 against A549 lung carcinoma cells and support its further investigation as a chalcone-based candidate scaffold. However, cancer cell selectivity, the mechanism underlying the observed cellular effects, and the proposed involvement of GNAI3 have not been experimentally established. Further studies involving additional cancer and normal cell models, target validation experiments, and in vivo evaluation are required to clarify its biological activity and therapeutic potential.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] Autosomal dosage compensation in aneuploidy and cancer involves transcriptional burst regulation
item.description:
Aneuploidy, resulting from whole-chromosome or segmental gains and losses, is generally detrimental to organismal fitness and is strongly associated with tumorigenesis. While sex chromosome aneuploidies are relatively well tolerated due to dedicated allelic dosage compensation mechanisms, the existence of comparable regulatory processes for autosomes remains debated. Here, we investigate transcriptional responses to autosomal aneuploidy and identify widespread dosage compensation across affected chromosomes. Using high-sensitivity allele-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing of monoclonal cell expansions spanning diverse ploidies and degrees of aneuploidy, we uncover consistent transcriptional compensation of both chromosomal gains and losses. This response operates in a region-specific manner across both complete and segmental aneuploidies, revealing an unexpected flexibility in dosage regulation. We show that chromosome losses are compensated through increased transcriptional burst frequency from the remaining allele. Complementary proteomics analyses demonstrate additional buffering at the protein level, resulting in a substantial, though still incomplete, restoration of stoichiometric balance across autosomal aneuploid chromosomes for both copy number gains and losses. Analyses of cancer transcriptomes confirm that compensatory mechanisms are active in human tumours. Together, our findings establish dosage compensation as a genome-wide and dynamic response to gene dose imbalance. This mechanism extends beyond sex chromosomes, supports transcriptional homeostasis, and represents a fundamental and evolutionarily conserved mode of gene regulation active across species and in aneuploid cancer cells. Aneuploidy alters chromosome copy number and is often associated with impaired cellular function. Here, the authors show that cells compensate for autosomal chromosome gains and losses through genome‑wide transcriptional and protein‑level buffering mechanisms, helping to maintain gene dosage balance in normal and cancer cells.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] Hypoxia-responsive IER3 promotes histone lactylation by sustaining MEK-ERK-c-Myc activation in non-small cell lung cancer
item.description:
Hypoxia, a hallmark of the solid tumor microenvironment in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), drives tumor progression. This study measured the expression of immediate early response 3 (IER3) in NSCLC under hypoxia and investigated its role in regulating glycolysis and histone lactylation. Single-cell RNA sequencing was conducted using count data from the GSE131907 dataset to analyze the expression of IER3 in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). The prognostic value of IER3 and its downstream signaling pathway was explored using data from the TCGA database. By silencing IER3 in vitro, the effects of IER3 on the proliferation, invasion, glycolysis, and histone lactylation of NSCLC cells were evaluated. In vivo, the effects of IER3 were detected through mouse xenograft tumor models. In LUAD, elevated IER3 expression was significantly associated with poorer overall survival. IER3 expression in NSCLC was found to be hypoxia-responsive. Silencing IER3 significantly suppressed the proliferation, invasion, and glycolysis of A549 and H1299 cells in vitro and inhibited the growth of xenograft tumors in vivo. In addition, by sustaining MEK-ERK-c-Myc activation, IER3 was shown to promote glycolysis in NSCLC cells. Furthermore, the results revealed that IER3 promoted histone lactylation (esp. H3K18la), thereby inducing ERO1A transcription. Hypoxia-responsive IER3 promoted glycolysis in NSCLC by sustaining MEK-ERK-c-Myc activation. Subsequently, glycolysis triggered histone lactylation (esp. H3K18la), thereby inducing ERO1A transcription and contributing to tumor growth and invasion.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.4] DDX5-mediated ferroptosis defence as a targetable vulnerability unique to glioma stem cells
item.description:
Glioma stem cells (GSCs), cancer stem cells in glioblastoma, are a major contributor to the intractable nature of this disease because they are more resistant to conventional cancer therapies than their non-stem counterparts. However, emerging evidence suggests vulnerabilities unique to GSCs, such as dependence on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). We herein demonstrate that the DEAD-box helicase 5 (DDX5) - glutathione peroxidase 4 axis is selectively activated in GSCs to prevent electron leaks associated with OXPHOS from inducing lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. FL118, a pharmacological inhibitor of DDX5, induces cell death via ferroptosis in GSCs, but not in their non-stem counterparts in vitro. In vivo, FL118 reduces the tumour-initiating population in established tumours and extends the survival of mice implanted orthotopically with GSCs. Collectively, these results suggest the potential of targeting the ferroptosis defence mechanism mediated by DDX5 as a treatment for glioblastoma and, based on the relationship between increased OXPHOS and tumour malignancy, for other malignant tumours with increased OXPHOS.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] Multimodal AI-enabled repurposing and prioritization of ferroptosis-targeting drug combinations in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
item.description:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) lacks scalable and mechanism-informed computational strategies for prioritizing repurposable drug combinations. Here, we developed FeNetDP, a multimodal AI-guided framework that integrates transcriptomic, proteomic, single-cell, spatial, and clinical survival data to enable biologically grounded drug repurposing and combination prioritization in PDAC. FeNetDP combines gene-level network proximity analysis with a biologically constrained neural ranking model to identify candidate compounds and drug pairs linked to a disease-relevant ferroptosis suppressor program. Using this framework, we defined an eight-gene ferroptosis suppressor module enriched in ductal cells and associated with poor prognosis, and prioritized candidate repurposable compounds and combinations targeting this network state. Prospective experimental validation identified panobinostat plus sorafenib as a synergistic combination that suppresses tumor growth and promotes ferroptosis in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, the combination impaired ferroptosis resistance through coordinated disruption of glutathione-dependent antioxidant defense and AIFM2 (FSP1)-associated glutathione-independent protection. Together, these findings establish FeNetDP as a multimodal and experimentally grounded framework for computational repurposing and mechanism-informed therapeutic prioritization in cancer.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.7] A hidden mitotic vulnerability emerges from BCAT1 redox-motif disruption in Ewing sarcoma
item.description:
Cancer cells must keep oxidative stress and chromosome-segregation errors within tolerable limits to sustain rapid proliferation. Because redox homeostasis supports faithful chromosome segregation, disrupting redox-dependent mitotic safeguards could drive chromosomal instability (CIN) beyond cell tolerance and suppress tumor growth. Here, we investigated whether selectively disrupting redox-dependent safeguards could uncouple oxidative-stress adaptation from faithful chromosome segregation, exposing a therapeutic vulnerability at the interface of metabolic regulation and genome maintenance. We used Ewing sarcoma (EwS) as a model because it combines low genomic complexity with elevated oxidative stress and limited redox-buffering capacity. A survival analysis of cell-cycle-associated genes prioritized branched-chain amino acid transaminase 1 (BCAT1), whose high expression was associated with adverse outcomes in both primary and relapsed EwS. Functional genomics analyses revealed that BCAT1 is transcriptionally regulated by the EwS-specific EWSR1::FLI1 fusion oncoprotein through a distal enhancer-like GGAA microsatellite. Using prime-edited endogenous alleles and isogenic cell models, we found that disrupting BCAT1 redox-active CXXC motif increased sensitivity to oxidative stress and impaired recovery from it. Motif disruption also caused chromosome-segregation defects and DNA damage, reduced three-dimensional growth, and suppressed tumor formation and metastasis in vivo. By contrast, catalytic inactivation had limited effects. Although acute BCAT1 protein depletion reduced proliferation and tumor formation, constitutive BCAT1 knockout cells remained viable in culture and reduced tumor formation less than motif disruption. Mechanistically, CXXC motif disruption reduced casein kinase 2 (CK2) activity and increased Aurora kinase B (AURKB) activity, whereas BCAT1 degradation left CK2 activity unchanged and reduced AURKB activity. The enhanced sensitivity of CXXC-mutant cells to AURKB inhibition suggests a therapeutic vulnerability that could be exploited in BCAT1-wild-type EwS cells through combined CK2 and AURKB inhibition with silmitasertib and barasertib, increasing maximal growth inhibition and lowering the barasertib concentration required to suppress proliferation. Collectively, these findings reveal a mitotic vulnerability associated with BCAT1 redox-motif disruption that is not fully reproduced by protein loss and can be therapeutically exploited using clinically evaluated CK2 and AURKB inhibitors.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.9] Pharmacodynamic encoding of tumor exposure identifies a mesenchymal state associated with antitumor sensitivity
item.description:
Predictive biomarker discovery in oncology relies on response phenotypes that do not account for tumor-site drug exposure. Here we developed PHENIX, a model informed framework that uses tumor exposure driven pharmacodynamic parameters as quantitative phenotypes for molecular-state discovery. Using PM534, a colchicine site tubulin inhibitor, we integrated measured drug concentrations with physiologically based pharmacokinetic and longitudinal pharmacokinetic pharmacodynamic modeling. This yielded K2, quantifying the efficiency with which intratumoral exposure is converted into tumor damage across cell-derived xenograft models. Higher K2 was associated with a mesenchymal state enriched for epithelial to mesenchymal transition, focal adhesion and extracellular matrix programs. An interpretable pathway based model retained epithelial to mesenchymal transition and focal adhesion as candidate features and showed preliminary cross dataset transferability. Proteomic analyses supported this molecular axis, whereas projection across CCLE and TCGA mapped its occurrence in cancer contexts. Patient derived orthotopic xenograft profiling provided orthogonal in vivo support. PHENIX demonstrates the feasibility of using model derived pharmacodynamic parameters as molecular phenotypes for tumor state discovery.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.1] The PD-L1 metabolic interactome in glioma is bounded by IDH1 genotype
item.description:
Immune checkpoint blockade has failed in glioblastoma, and part of the reason may lie in the tumour cell itself: if the checkpoint and the metabolism that sustains the cell hold each other up, then lowering one arm hands the tumour the other, and a single agent cannot win. We tested that possibility in GL261 glioma cells of IDH1-wildtype and IDH1-mutant genotype, silencing Chka or Cd274, blocking PD-L1 with an antibody, and reading the consequences by RT-qPCR, RNA sequencing, flow cytometry of surface PD-L1 and high-resolution 1H NMR of dual-phase cell extracts. The two genes proved reciprocal in both genotypes: silencing either transcript raised the other, and silencing choline kinase roughly doubled PD-L1 at the cell surface. Antibody blockade did something the silencing did not. In IDH1-wildtype cells it lowered soluble phosphocholine, the only one of twenty-two aqueous signals to survive correction for multiple testing, and raised total lipid per cell without changing lipid composition, whereas silencing PD-L1 raised phosphocholine instead; in IDH1-mutant cells neither change occurred. The transcriptome drew the same boundary, engaging a sterol programme and lowering glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation in wild-type cells only. The interferon response did not respect that boundary and rose under every perturbation in both genotypes. Removing PD-L1 from inside the cell and blocking it from outside are therefore not the same intervention, and the metabolic half of the response stops at the IDH1 genotype.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.0] Single-agent PD-L1 blockade and tumour volume in orthotopic GL261 glioma, with an exploratory lipid analysis of the treated tumours
item.description:
Immune checkpoint blockade has not yet changed outcomes in glioblastoma (GBM), and in immunocompetent mouse glioma the effect of a single blocking antibody is usually reported as survival rather than as tumour volume with its own confidence interval. We treated mice bearing orthotopic GL261 gliomas with anti-PD-L1 as a single agent in an IDH1-wild-type and in an IDH1-mutant line, and followed tumour volume by MRI. At day 14, tumours of treated animals were 0.33 times the volume of control tumours in the IDH1-wild-type line (95 % CI 0.21 to 0.53; p < 0.001; 16 anti-PD-L1 and 20 control animals) and 0.42 times in the IDH1-mutant line (0.22 to 0.78; p = 0.006; 10 and 10 animals), from a linear mixed model of log tumour volume over days 8 to 16. Diffusion imaging of the same tumours gave a higher apparent diffusion coefficient in the treated IDH1-wild-type tumours, by 23 % over the whole tumour (p = 0.027), and lower fractional anisotropy in the treated IDH1-mutant tumours, by 25 % over the whole tumour (p = 0.023), and in the periphery of the IDH1-wild-type ones, by 24 % (p = 0.005). We also imaged the lipid composition of treated and control IDH1-wild-type tumours ex vivo by mass spectrometry imaging: relative to the healthy brain of the same section, sphingomyelin was higher in the treated tumours and phosphatidylcholine species shifted towards shorter chains (p = 0.016 for both). In orthotopic GL261 glioma, anti-PD-L1 as a single agent reduces tumour volume in the IDH1-wild-type and in the IDH1-mutant line.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] FN1 is produced by cancer-associated fibroblasts and carries no immune-exclusion signal beyond the collagen program: a two-cohort single-cell re-examination in non-small cell lung cancer
item.description:
Fibronectin 1 (FN1) has been proposed as a macrophage-derived driver of T-cell exclusion and AP-1-mediated resistance to checkpoint blockade in lung cancer. The human evidence was never tested against the two confounders most likely to generate them: collagen/extracellular-matrix (ECM) abundance and dissociation-induced immediate-early gene (IEG) expression. We reanalyzed two public non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cohorts, GSE148071 (42 treatment-naive tumors) and GSE207422 (15 specimens; 92,330 cells), with 24 pre-treatment bulk transcriptomes. Malignant epithelium was called by compartment-level inferCNV; FN1 source was attributed within macrophage and fibroblast compartments and by ligand-receptor scoring; exclusion associations were tested by partial Spearman correlation with permutation testing, controlling for a 22-gene collagen/ECM signature; AP-1 regulon activity was quantified before and after masking the 27-gene IEG panel, benchmarked against a dissociation-stress score. FN1 was produced predominantly by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs): the FN1-positive fraction was higher in CAFs than macrophages in both cohorts (paired Wilcoxon P = 1.6 x 10?? and P = 0.002), and CAF-to-epithelium communication exceeded macrophage-to-epithelium by about six-fold (median 0.32 vs 0.05, P = 1.5 x 10??). An independent lung-adenocarcinoma cohort (GSE131907) replicated this cell of origin (FN1-positive fraction 0.88 in CAFs versus 0.44 in TAMs; 11 paired samples, P = 0.001). The bulk FN1-cytotoxic association ({rho} = -0.53, P = 0.008) disappeared after collagen adjustment across three independent FN1 scoring schemes (partial {rho} = +0.21 to -0.16, all P > 0.33) and was not reproduced at single-cell level. Sample-level AP-1 activity tracked dissociation stress ({rho} = 0.88, P = 2.3 x 10??); IEG masking shrank histology-associated effect sizes by 40-64%, yet masked activity remained stress-coupled ({rho} = 0.82). FN1 is therefore a CAF product whose apparent link to immune exclusion is absorbed by the collagen program, and AP-1 readouts from dissociated tissue are stress-dominated; stress scores should accompany AP-1-based resistance claims.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.8] Monitoring cancer evolution under iatrogenic selection pressure by cellular liquid biopsy.
item.description:
Cell-free liquid biopsy (LB) provides information about real-time tumor burden in cancer patients. In contrast, cellular LB can resolve the co-occurrence of actionable mutations within individual CTCs and their clonal architecture, revealing emerging treatment opportunities, information increasingly needed as the number of available drugs grows. Here, we describe a case with repeated blood sampling and CTC analysis using a single-cell-adapted IMPACT assay (scIMPACT). We observed therapeutically relevant alterations and clonal shifts arising in response to selected therapies. Applied systematically, such analyses have the power to uncover cellular adaptations to therapy-induced selection pressures and enable flexible treatment adjustments to evolving disease.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.7] Opportunities and challenges for cancer therapy with menin inhibitors
item.description:
Menin, encoded by MEN1, is a crucial scaffolding component of the histone-lysine N-methyltransferase 2A (KMT2A; also known as MLL1) complex, which is involved in histone methylation and epigenetic regulation of gene expression. The potential importance of menin in leukaemias harbouring KMT2A rearrangements was first recognized two decades ago. KMT2A fusion proteins generated by KMT2A rearrangements interact with menin and drive aberrant expression of HOXA cluster genes and MEIS1, which maintains leukaemic cells that harbour these rearrangements in an immature and highly proliferative state. Wild-type KMT2A in complex with menin also sustains this gene expression programme across genetically distinct subtypes of leukaemia, including nucleophosmin 1-mutant (NPM1c) and nucleoporin 98 (NUP98)-rearranged acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). Together, these subtypes comprise more than 40% of all AML cases. Small-molecule menin inhibitors disrupt the crucial menin–KMT2A interaction, thus reversing leukaemogenic transcriptional programmes and inducing leukaemia cell differentiation. Early-phase clinical trials have demonstrated clinically meaningful remission rates with menin-inhibitor monotherapy in participants with relapsed and/or refractory KMT2A-rearranged or NPM1c acute leukaemias, leading to regulatory approvals of two such agents: revumenib and ziftomenib. However, responses are often incomplete and/or transient, and acquired MEN1 mutations have emerged as a recurrent mechanism of resistance. Combination strategies with chemotherapy, venetoclax-based regimens and other targeted agents are now advancing rapidly through clinical development. In this Review, we discuss the biology of the menin–KMT2A complex, the preclinical and clinical development of menin inhibitors, emerging mechanisms of resistance, strategies to improve response durability and the expanding therapeutic potential of menin inhibition beyond acute leukaemias. Dysregulated transcriptional programmes mediated by the menin–histone-lysine N-methyltransferase 2A (KMT2A) complex are key drivers of acute leukaemias harbouring various genetic alterations, including KMT2A or nucleoporin 98 gene rearrangements and nucleophosmin 1 mutations. This Review outlines the biology of the menin–KMT2A complex, the preclinical discovery and clinical development of menin inhibitors that disrupt it, mechanisms of resistance to such agents and strategies to improve their efficacy, as well as the potential to expand menin inhibition beyond acute leukaemias to certain solid tumour types.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.1] Exon-skipping antisense oligonucleotides targeting SUMO1 and SUMO2 demonstrate chemosensitizing effects in NSCLC cells in vitro
item.description:
Lung cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related death, highlighting the urgent need for new treatment strategies. SUMOylation, a post-translational modification that regulates DNA repair, replication, and cell cycle progression, is often increased in cancers and is a promising therapeutic target. Previously, we identified alternative splicing events affecting the SUMO transcripts, resulting in variant mRNAs coding for both non-conjugatable (SUMO1α and SUMO2α) and conjugatable (SUMO3α) isoforms—potentially helping to regulate overall cellular SUMOylation. In this study, we investigated whether increasing the levels of the transcripts coding for the non-conjugatable isoforms could decrease SUMOylation and improve chemotherapy efficacy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). To test this, we designed two sets of exon-skipping morpholinos called SUM2IN and SUMO1IN, targeting the pre-mRNAs of SUMO2 and SUMO1, respectively, and tested them in A549 and HCC827 cell lines. While treatment with SUM2IN significantly increased SUMO2α mRNA and reduced overall SUMO1 and SUMO2 conjugation in all tested cell lines, SUM1IN affected the proportion of SUMO1 mRNA variants and overall SUMO conjugation in a cell-type-specific manner. Still, both SUM2IN and SUM1IN altered cell cycle progression, decreased cell growth, and enhanced the cytotoxic effects of cisplatin and etoposide in A549 and HCC827 cells, while having a notably smaller impact on these parameters in the non-malignant lung fibroblast cell line HEL-299. Therefore, SUM2IN and SUM1IN display chemosensitizing activity against NSCLC and provide a strong foundation for developing SUMO-targeted chemosensitizers for NSCLC and other aggressive human cancers.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.0] Caspase-7 cleavage repurposes AAK1 to suppress mRNA decay and promote tolerance to anti-tubulin agents
item.description:
Prolonged mitotic arrest imposed by anti-tubulin chemotherapy suppresses transcription, making mRNA preservation critical for tumor-cell survival. Here, we identify an unexpected kinase-repurposing mechanism that sustains this adaptation. A kinome-wide screen revealed clathrin-adaptor kinase AAK1 as a determinant of taxane tolerance. During mitotic arrest, CDK1 phosphorylates AAK1 at T389 to enhance catalytic activity, while caspase-7 cleaves AAK1 at D767, removing a clathrin-binding domain. These modifications produce a cleaved fragment with reduced clathrin association and increased association with CCR4-NOT, suppressing mRNA decay and maintaining glycolytic gene expression. Mutant-rescues establish that both phosphorylation and cleavage contribute to cancer-cell survival during paclitaxel-induced arrest. A clinical-stage AAK1 inhibitor developed for neuropathic pain sensitized cancer cells to paclitaxel. Together, these findings reveal how coordinated phosphorylation and proteolysis repurpose a trafficking kinase to maintain mRNA stability, uncovering an unexpected tolerance-promoting function of caspase cleavage and a therapeutically actionable vulnerability of chemotherapy-arrested cancer cells.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] A KRASG12D-based organoid model for early oncogenic transformation of the mammary epithelium
item.description:
Modeling cancer initiation, progression, and metastasis has greatly impacted our understanding of fundamental cell and molecular mechanisms driving disease and has led to breakthrough treatments that greatly improve patient outcomes. Understanding the earliest stages of tumor formation is particularly important for uncovering the root causes of oncogenic transformation and tumor evolution. It has been historically difficult to model the cellular dynamics that drive the earliest stages of tumor evolution, largely due to difficulties in culturing and manipulating normal primary cells in 3-dimensional environments, triggering oncogenesis, and observing the resulting effects. Recent advances in 3D organoid culture provide a promising avenue to address these challenges. In this study, we have developed a Kras based organoid model of early tumorigenesis. In our model, oncogenic transformation was triggered by Cre-mediated expression of oncogenic KRASG12D in otherwise healthy murine-derived mammary epithelial organoids. While normal organoids displayed controlled organoid growth and morphogenesis, induction of KRASG12D caused neoplastic organoid growth that occurred with the absence of lumen formation. Gene expression analysis revealed up regulation of several KRAS effectors, and a broad repertoire of genes associated with tumor development and human breast cancer. Induction of oncogenic Kras in our model resulted in heterotypic organoids that possessed KRASG12D + cells growing alongside KRASG12D- cells. In this context, amplification of KRASG12D + cells occurred at the expense of KRASG12D- cells. Finally we observed that neoplastic growth of KRASG12D expressing organoids was associated with a suppression of apoptosis. We believe that our organoid model provides a platform that is suitable to examine the earliest stages of tumor development and can be expanded to study several questions related to cancer biology, prevention studies, therapeutic development, and beyond.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.0] A novel of synthetic iridoid glycoside, Picroside II inhibits temozolomide resistance proliferation by upregulating DHRS2 in glioblastoma
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor, characterized by pronounced cellular heterogeneity that contributes to chemoresistance and frequent recurrence. Resistance to temozolomide (TMZ) remains a major therapeutic challenge, highlighting the urgent need for alternative treatment strategies. Picroside II (PII), a natural iridoid glycoside, has demonstrated anticancer activity; however, its effects on TMZ-resistant GBM and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unexplored. TMZ-resistant GBM cell lines were established by intermittently exposing parental GBM cells to gradually increasing concentrations of TMZ over a six-month period. The antitumor effects of PII were evaluated in vitro using assays for cell proliferation, migration, invasion, colony formation, cell cycle distribution, and apoptosis. Expression levels of apoptosis- and cell cycle–related proteins were analyzed by Western blotting. Transcriptomic alterations induced by PII were identified using next-generation sequencing (NGS). The therapeutic efficacy of PII alone or combined with TMZ was further examined in vivo using a xenograft mouse model. PII significantly inhibited cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and clonogenic capacity in TMZ-resistant GBM cells. PII treatment induced dose-dependent cell cycle arrest, characterized by an accumulation of cells in the G1 phase and a corresponding reduction in the G2/M phase population. Moreover, PII triggered intrinsic mitochondrial apoptosis, accompanied by dose-dependent modulation of key apoptosis- and cell cycle–regulatory proteins. NGS analysis revealed a marked upregulation of dehydrogenase/reductase 2 (DHRS2) following PII treatment. Consistent with in vitro findings, PII effectively suppressed tumor growth and enhanced DHRS2 expression in xenograft tumor tissues. PII exerts potent antitumor effects against TMZ-resistant GBM by inducing cell cycle arrest and mitochondrial apoptosis, potentially through the upregulation of DHRS2. These findings support PII as a, promising therapeutic candidate for overcoming TMZ resistance in GBM.
