item.title: [1.6] GATA6 modulates cellular metabolism to influence chemotherapy sensitivity in non-small cell lung cancer
item.description:
As a key transcription factor, GATA binding protein 6 (GATA6) has recently emerged as a critical regulator in tumorigenesis and cancer progression. However, its functional role in chemotherapy resistance, particularly in Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), remains poorly understood. This study aimed to elucidate the mechanistic link between GATA6 expression and chemosensitivity in NSCLC cells. The chemoresistant phenotype was modeled using chemoresistant NSCLC cell lines. GATA6 expression was genetically modulated to assess its impact on chemosensitivity via cell viability assays and in vivo xenograft experiments. Cellular metabolic phenotypes were profiled using cellular energy metabolism analyzers, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) detection assays were used by fluorescent probes. Mechanistic investigations included qPCR and western blotting to dissect the GATA6/c-Myc regulatory axis. GATA6 expression was found to be lower in chemoresistant lung cancer cells compared to their parental counterparts, and overexpression of GATA6 was able to partially reverse chemotherapy resistance. We observed that GATA6 regulates the metabolic phenotype of lung cancer cells, particularly affecting oxidative phosphorylation in chemoresistant lung cancer cells. This regulation of metabolism was associated with GATA6-mediated suppression of c-MYC mRNA expression. Furthermore, through reactive oxygen species (ROS) detection assays, we identified that GATA6 predominantly influences ROS production, ultimately affecting the chemosensitivity of lung cancer cells. In summary, this study demonstrates that GATA6 expression is associated with chemotherapy sensitivity in NSCLC cells, potentially through the modulation of metabolic phenotypes and steady‑state ROS levels. Our data suggest that GATA6 may regulate c‑Myc expression, which in turn influences mitochondrial respiration and ROS homeostasis, ultimately affecting cellular responses to cisplatin.

item.title: [2.8] TEAD Palmitoylation Inhibitors are Brain Penetrant and Enhance Survival in Preclinical Models of Recurrent Glioblastoma in Combination with Standard-of-Care Therapy
item.description:
Abstract Purpose: Oncogenic addiction to YAP-TEAD signaling drives adaptive plasticity, therapeutic resistance, invasion and tumor progression in many cancers, including in glioblastoma (GBM), and represents an actionable vulnerability to explore as adjuvant therapy during tumor recurrence. This study evaluated the translational potential of orally bioavailable Vivace Therapeutics (VT) TEAD palmitoylation inhibitors in preclinical GBM models. Experimental Design: The effects of VT103 and VT104 on GBM proliferation, migration, and TEAD activity were first assessed across patient-derived GBM cell lines with diverse genomic drivers. The drugs pharmacokinetics (PK) and biodistribution were measured using mass spectrometry in mice bearing patient-derived orthotopic xenograft (PDX) GBM. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in two genetically distinct PDX models of recurrent GBM, administering VT104 as monotherapy or in combination with standard-of-care radiotherapy plus temozolomide (RT+TMZ). Results: VT104/VT103 treatment significantly impaired GBM proliferation and migration in-vitro, with concomitant downregulation of TEAD-target expression. PK studies confirmed sustained VT104 plasma levels and robust brain biodistribution in PDX mice, with brain:plasma ratio >150% at therapeutic dosing without systemic toxicity. While VT104 monotherapy showed modest anti-tumor effects, combination therapy (VT104+RT+TMZ) significantly extended overall survival in both recurrent GBM PDX models. The survival benefit was most prominent in EGFR-mutant GBM and corresponded to significant decrease in overall and infiltrative tumor burden. Mechanistically, VT104 potentiated TMZ-dependent {gamma}-H2AX genotoxic stress and RT+TMZ synergized with VT104 to abolish TEAD activity. Conclusion: Integrating YAP-TEAD inhibition with standard therapy introduces a clinically-relevant paradigm for synergistic treatment in recurrent GBM that both inhibits tumor infiltration and reduces therapeutic resistance to chemoradiation.

item.title: [1.9] The tumor suppressor role of the KRAS proto-oncogene in metastatic pancreatic cancer.
item.description:
KRAS is the most frequently mutated proto-oncogene in human cancers. Progression to advanced disease is frequently associated with allelic imbalance of the KRAS locus with gain of the mutant allele and loss of the wild-type allele through clonal and sub-clonal loss of heterozygosity (LOH). While a large body of literature has focused on the effects of allelic imbalance on oncogene addiction through gain of the mutant allele, the role of the wild-type KRAS proto-oncogene in malignant progression has not been fully elucidated. To capture this phenomenon, we developed a first-in-class somatic mosaic and lineage tracing genetically engineered mouse model (smGMLT) of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma allowing for real time in vivo tracing of Kras-LOH. Longitudinal characterization of the smGMLT demonstrated the presence of a strong evolutionary bottleneck towards the selective loss of the wild-type allele at metastatic sites. Cross species analysis leveraging research autopsies and surgical specimens revealed that KRAS-LOH is associated with metastatic dissemination and shorter overall survival. Transcriptomic analysis through single-cell RNA sequencing uncovered a conserved phenomenon whereby KRAS-LOH is paralleled by an immune evasive phenotype through loss of the tumor-cell interferon response and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. In line with this evidence, orthotopic transplants of isogenic tumor populations differing for the Kras allelic status demonstrated that only cancer cells with Kras-LOH are are able to form tumors in immune competent animals. Restoration of the wild-type allele abrogates tumorigenesis in KrasLOH transplants in immunocompetent through activation of the TBK1-IRF axis. Altogether, these studies demonstrate that the KRAS proto-oncogene is a functional tumor suppressor in pancreatic cancer exerting its function through interferon-mediated, cell-extrinsic modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.5] A parallel preclinical trial of pembrolizumab, binimetinib, and anti VEGFR2 therapy in humanized patient derived xenografts of MSS metastatic colorectal cancer
item.description:
Microsatellite-stable (MSS) metastatic colorectal cancer (CRC) is largely refractory to immune checkpoint inhibitors, highlighting the need for immunomodulatory-combination strategies. Preclinical and clinical evidence suggest that inhibition of the MEK and VEGF pathways may sensitize MSS tumors to PD-1 blockade by reshaping the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). Here, we evaluated the antitumor and immunologic effects of combined MEK, PD-1, and VEGFR2 inhibition using matched human-immune system patient-derived xenograft models generated from patients enrolled in a parallel phase II clinical trial. Six distinct MSS CRC PDX models were implanted into humanized BALB/c‑Rag2−/−Il2rγ−/−SIRPαNOD mice and treated with vehicle, binimetinib alone, binimetinib plus pembrolizumab, or the triple combination of binimetinib, pembrolizumab and the VEGFR2 inhibitor DC101. Triple therapy reduced tumor growth relative to control and monotherapy, though the responses were heterogeneous across PDXs. Treatment was associated with increased intratumoral human T-cell infiltration, enrichment of effector memory and multifunctional cytotoxic CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells, and reduced regulatory T-cell frequency in responding tumors. Immune correlates observed in HIS-PDX models, including increased effector memory CD8+ T cells and reduced TIGIT-expressing CD8+ T-cells, parallel biomarkers associated with disease control in the matched clinical trial. In contrast, MEK inhibitor monotherapy had fewer cytotoxic CD8 T-cells. These findings demonstrate that combined MEK, PD-1, and VEGF pathway inhibition can reprogram the TIME and elicit antitumor immunity in a subset of MSS CRCs, supporting rational combination immunotherapy approaches and biomarker-driven patient selection. Furthermore, testing in the HIS-mouse model shows tumor heterogeneous responses and can recapitulate immune tumor responses observed in the clinic. The data generated in this study are available upon request from the corresponding author and on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03475004), as a community-recognized, structured repository does not exist.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.6] Efficacy of nano-formulated Nitazoxanide compared with tablet-derived free Nitazoxanide against human oral squamous cell carcinoma cells
item.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains a therapeutic challenge. This study compared the in-vitro anticancer activity of tablet-derived free Nitazoxanide (NTZ) and Nitazoxanide-nanostructured suspension (NTZ-NS) against SCC-9 cells, using HaCaT keratinocytes as non-malignant controls and Cisplatin as a reference chemotherapeutic drug. Cytotoxicity was assessed by MTT assay, apoptosis and cell-cycle distribution by flow cytometry, and BCL2 and VEGF levels by ELISA. Both formulations of NTZ reduced SCC-9 viability in a dose-dependent manner, with NTZ-NS showing greater potency (IC₅₀ 2.628 µM versus 5.934 µM). HaCaT keratinocytes exhibited lower sensitivity to all treatments, maintaining higher viability than SCC-9 cells across tested concentrations, demonstrating a broader in-vitro selectivity margin rather than complete absence of toxicity at elevated concentrations. NTZ increased late apoptosis to 28.3 ± 0.3% and sub-G1 to 15.00 ± 0.30%; NTZ-NS further increased late apoptosis to 35.6 ± 0.3% and sub-G1 to 19.00 ± 0.30%, while altering S- and G2/M-phase distributions (n = 3, P < 0.05). Both treatments lowered BCL2 and VEGF, with stronger effects after NTZ-NS. Nano-formulation enhanced the in-vitro activity of NTZ against SCC-9 cells. These findings support further preclinical evaluation; therapeutic applicability cannot be inferred from the present cell-culture data alone.

item.title: [1.6] SIRT6 coordinates copper homeostasis to modulate cuproplasia and cuproptosis in colorectal cancer
item.description:
Imbalance in copper ion homeostasis is closely associated with the development and progression of various cancers, yet its dynamic regulatory mechanisms and targeting value in colorectal cancer remain unclear. This study reveals the relationship between endogenous metabolites and copper-dependent proliferation in CRC, identifying the histone deacetylase SIRT6 as a critical hub regulating copper homeostasis and determining cell fate. SIRT6 knockout promotes copper-dependent proliferation but simultaneously sensitizes CRC cells to cuproptosis. Mechanistically, SIRT6 epigenetically suppresses the transcription of SLC31A1 by deacetylating H3K9/K56, thereby limiting intracellular copper accumulation and inhibiting cuproplasia. On the other hand, SIRT6 directly binds to and deacetylates the transcription factor MTF1, inhibiting its ubiquitination-mediated degradation and enhancing its transcriptional activity, consequently promoting the expression of metallothioneins. MT1A/MT2A remodel subcellular copper distribution through copper chelation, reducing mitochondrial copper load and conferring resistance to cuproptosis. Importantly, the combined application of the SIRT6 inhibitor OSS_128167 and the copper ionophore Elesclomol demonstrated significant synergistic anti-tumor efficacy in patient-derived xenograft models. This study discovers and elucidates the novel function of SIRT6 as a master regulator of copper metabolism, redefines the high-copper tumor microenvironment as a targetable metabolic vulnerability, and provides a new theoretical foundation and a highly promising combination therapy strategy for the precision treatment of colorectal cancer. Colorectal cancer tissues contain high levels of copper. Copper can both promote tumor growth and trigger cell death. This study identifies a protein called SIRT6 that acts as a “regulatory switch” inside cancer cells: it limits copper entry into cells and also increases copper‑binding storage proteins that mop up excess copper, thereby protecting tumor cells from copper‑induced death. When we used a drug to inhibit SIRT6 together with another drug that shuttles copper into cells, we observed strong synergistic anti‑tumor effects in animal models, without obvious side effects. This work reveals how tumors cleverly manage copper and provides a new combination therapy strategy for precision treatment of colorectal cancer, potentially offering more effective options for patients.

item.title: [2.0] TERRA engages MDA5 to shape the immune landscape in ALT brain tumors
item.description:
In cancer, telomere maintenance is mediated by telomerase reactivation or by the alternative lengthening of telomere (ALT) pathway. Both mechanisms contribute to cancer cell replicative immortality, but ALT, generates telomere instability and promotes inflammation, thus contributing to cancer progression also through non-cell autonomous mechanisms. How ALT telomeres modulate inflammatory signals in cancer is not fully understood, mostly because of the lack of organismal models of ALT+ cancers. Here we used a zebrafish model of ALT+ brain tumor to demonstrate that ALT telomeres promote inflammation through increased transcription of TERRA, which engages RNA-sensing pathways through MDA5. Analysis of ALT+ brain tumors shows that MDA5-MAVS signaling results in the production of interferon responsive genes and cytokines that induce a pro-tumoral immune microenvironment, which can be prevented by abrogating TERRA signaling through in vivo antisense technology, or by CRISPR/Cas9 mediated knock-out of MDA5 or MAVS. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals that abrogating TERRA signaling using ASOs affects both cancer cells and immune cell compartments in a long-lasting manner. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized role of TERRA in modulating immune responses in ALT+ brain tumors and highlight the potential of TERRA-targeting ASOs as a novel therapeutic strategy for ALT tumors.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] Computational workflows for neoantigen identification in non-small cell lung cancer: a scoping review and meta-analysis of neoantigen vaccine trials
item.description:
Computational identification of tumor-specific neoantigens is central to personalized vaccine development for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, variation in sequencing, HLA typing, epitope prediction, candidate prioritization, and reporting may limit reproducibility and clinical translation. A scoping review with an embedded random-effects meta-analysis of vaccine-induced T-cell responses was conducted to evaluate computational workflows for neoantigen identification in NSCLC and examined progression towards functional validation and vaccine development for studies between 2005 and 2025. Computational workflow methods and reporting completeness were assessed across eight workflow computational domains. Clinical studies were quantitatively pooled only when explicit patient-level post-vaccination responder numerators and immune-evaluable denominators were available. The primary meta-analysis used a random-effects binomial-logit generalized linear mixed model (GLMM). Twenty-five unique studies published between 2005 and 2025 were identified, and their contributions included: 22 to the computational workflow synthesis, 5 to human clinical vaccine synthesis; 1 study contributed to translational evidence. Whole-exome and RNA sequencing were used in 86.4% and 63.6% of computational studies, respectively. All studies performed MHC class I prediction, whereas only 22.7% incorporated MHC class II prediction, and 31.8% reported clonality assessment. Reporting completeness was 85.8%, with the greatest variability occurring in downstream neoantigen candidate prioritization and validation. Four clinical studies provided extractable patient-level immunogenicity data, with 35 of 46 immune-evaluable patients demonstrating a vaccine-induced T-cell response. The primary GLMM yielded a pooled response estimate of 92.53% (95% CI 42.71–99.52%), although alternative random-effects models yielded estimates of approximately 81–82%, indicating substantial uncertainty in the magnitude of the pooled response. Alternative random-effects sensitivity analyses yielded estimates of approximately 81–82%. All five human clinical vaccine studies were judged to have an overall serious risk of bias. Vaccination was generally well tolerated, although clinical efficacy remains uncertain because of small early-phase cohorts, concomitant therapies, and heterogeneous outcome assessment. The study incompleteness and variability in neoantigen downstream analysis call for standardization of computational workflows, and larger cohort studies may give better insights into long-term vaccine-specific T-cell responses compared to small cohort clinical trials.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.6] Targeting SMYD3 in cancer-associated fibroblasts relieves immune suppression and improves anti-PD-L1 response in HPV-negative HNSCC
item.description:
Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), as crucial stromal components in the tumor microenvironment, promote tumor progression and impair responses to immunotherapy. However, targeted therapies against CAFs remain limited in HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HPV- HNSCC). Here, integrated analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), bulk RNA sequencing, ChIP sequencing, and spatial transcriptomic data identified a candidate epigenetic fibroblast target. We revealed that SET and MYND domain-containing 3 (SMYD3) played a critical role in the transformation of fibroblasts into myofibroblasts. It promoted collagen production to impair infiltration of CD8+ T cells and upregulated THBS2 in CAFs to induce M2‑like macrophage polarization. Functional studies confirmed that targeting SMYD3 not only improved the immune environment but also enhanced the efficacy of anti‑PD‑L1 therapy in vivo. Our findings established SMYD3 as a central mediator of CAF-dependent immune suppression and nominated its inhibition as a promising strategy to improve immunotherapy outcomes in HPV- HNSCC.

item.title: [1.6] FKBP10 dictates RAD51 stability to drive resistance of DNA-damaging therapies in breast cancer
item.description:
Despite substantial advances in targeted therapeutic regimens for breast cancer (BC), clinical management remains challenging for refractory and therapy-resistant cases, especially for molecular subtypes lacking validated actionable targets. Here, we identified that FK506-binding protein 10 (FKBP10), a peptidyl-proline isomerases, was strikingly elevated in BC tissues and potentiated the malignant behaviors of BC cells in vitro and in vivo. Besides, we discovered that FKBP10 was positively correlated with enhanced homologous recombination (HR)-mediated DNA repair and drove broad resistance to multiple DNA-damaging therapies, including cisplatin, ionizing radiation (IR) and PARP inhibitor. Mechanistically, FKBP10 physically interacted with the core HR repair protein RAD51 via a proline 22-containing motif. This interaction competitively disrupted the recognition of RAD51 by heat shock cognate 70 (HSC70), thereby protecting RAD51 from chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA)-dependent degradation. Furthermore, FKBP10 attenuated excessive CMA flux to further stabilize RAD51 in the manner of ATF6-mediated endoplasmic reticulum stress (ERS). Importantly, we characterized a clinically actionable repurposing strategy using selumetinib, which transcriptionally repressed FKBP10 by blocking the MEK/ERK/ELK1 signaling cascade. This pharmacological intervention robustly sensitized multiple preclinical BC models to chemoradiotherapy and PARP inhibition. Collectively, our findings uncover a previously unappreciated function of FKBP10 in driving BC progression and resistance to DNA-damaging therapies, underscoring its strong potential as a tractable therapeutic target for treatment-refractory BC subsets.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.2] Combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition produces synergistic anti-tumour activity across preclinical glioblastoma models
item.description:
Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains difficult to treat because of tumour heterogeneity and the limited activity of single-target therapies. Our previous phenotypic drug screen identified JAK2/STAT3 signalling and HSP90-dependent protein homeostasis as pharmacological vulnerabilities. We investigated whether combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition could produce broader anti-tumour activity across GBM models. Methods: Multiple JAK2 and HSP90 inhibitors were tested alone and in combination across 2- and 3-dimensional patient-derived GBM stem cell models. Drug interactions were quantified using the zero-interaction potency (ZIP) synergy model. Mechanistic studies included RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, western blotting, immunofluorescence and FUCCI live-cell imaging. Activity was also assessed in cerebral organoid GBM co-cultures, non-malignant human neural and glial cells and orthotopic GBM xenografts. Results: Combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition produced synergistic interactions in 12 of the 13 GBM cell lines tested, using multiple structurally distinct inhibitor pairs. Gandotinib and NMS-E973 were selected for further mechanistic studies, where the combination reduced spheroid growth and increased caspase-3 activation and PARP cleavage. Combination treatment was associated with G2/M accumulation, altered mitotic regulation, abnormal chromosome and spindle organisation, and increased gamma-H2AX signalling. Anti-tumour combination activity was maintained in cerebral organoid co-cultures, where tumour burden was reduced as assessed by imaging, histological and luciferase-based measurements, while the drug combination had relatively limited effects on non-malignant human neural and glial cell types tested over the same concentration range. In vivo, combined Pacritinib and NMS-E973 treatment significantly reduced tumour burden in orthotopic G7 xenografts compared with vehicle or either single agent. Conclusions: JAK2/HSP90 co-inhibition produces reproducible anti-tumour activity across heterogeneous GBM models and disrupts cell-cycle and mitotic progression. These findings support further evaluation of this combination strategy in GBM.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.5] Saruparib recapitulates PARP-BRCA synthetic lethality with PARP1-trapping properties limiting its cytotoxicity
item.description:
The original concept of PARP synthetic lethality proposes that loss of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) activity selectively kills homologous recombination (HR)-deficient cells. However, clinically approved PARP1/2 inhibitors (PARPis) are used at exposures exceeding those required for catalytic inhibition. At these doses, PARP trapping is cytotoxic to HR-proficient cells and limits the therapeutic window in HR-deficient cancers. Saruparib has been developed as a PARP1-selective inhibitor to reduce PARP2-associated toxicity; yet its PARP1-trapping properties remain incompletely characterized. Here, we show that saruparib exhibits trapping properties distinct from those of conventional PARPis. It causes minimal cytotoxicity in HR-proficient cells and remains minimally toxic in XRCC1-deficient cells, which are highly sensitive to trapping-associated cytotoxicity induced by conventional PARPis. Although methyl methanesulfonate, which induces extensive base damage, increases saruparib-induced PARP1 trapping and cytotoxicity, the overall trapping-associated cytotoxic response is weaker than that induced by olaparib and shows little further dose-dependent increase once catalytic PARP1 inhibition is achieved. Biochemical measurements demonstrated that PARP1-DNA complexes formed in the presence of saruparib are less stable than those in the presence of olaparib or talazoparib. Notably, saruparib potently kills BRCA1-, BRCA2-, and PALB2-deficient cells at concentrations sufficient for near-maximal catalytic inhibition, without a corresponding increase in cytotoxicity in HR-proficient cells. Thus, saruparib combines potent HR-deficient-selective cytotoxicity with limited PARP1 trapping and associated toxicity. Consequently, saruparib closely recapitulates the PARP-BRCA synthetic lethality while sparing HR-proficient cells, providing a mechanistic framework for its rational clinical use.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.0] SHMT1 and SHMT2 inhibition disrupts metabolic adaptation in glioblastoma
item.description:
Glioblastoma cells adapt to hypoxia and nutrient restriction through metabolic reprogramming. Serine hydroxymethyltransferases 1 and 2 (SHMT1, SHMT2) channel serine-derived one carbon units into folate metabolism, linking biosynthesis, respiration and redox defence. Its contribution to tumour metabolic homeostasis and adaptation to hypoxia and nutrient restriction remains unclear. We combined dual pharmacological SHMT inhibition using (+)-SHIN1 in glioblastoma cell lines, including patient-derived glioma stem-like models, with stable SHMT2 knockdown in LNT-229 cells. Functional analyses assessed clonogenic survival, invasion, migration and susceptibility to metabolic stress. Bioenergetics were measured by extracellular flux analysis and oxygen depletion, redox state by NADPH/NADP; assay, and molecular responses by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry-based metabolomics and 13C6-glucose tracing and tandem mass tag proteomics. Formate supplementation tested the contribution of limited one-carbon availability, three-dimensional co-cultures with human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived embryoid bodies assessed tumour expansion, and in silico analyses of public glioblastoma datasets examined SHMT expression, regional distribution and associations with hypoxia-related genes. SHMT2 was enriched in hypoxic and perinecrotic tumour regions and correlated with hypoxia-inducible factor-1 target genes. SHMT inhibition impaired clonogenic growth, reduced invasion and migration, limited tumour expansion in co-culture, and sensitised cells to death under combined hypoxia and glucose restriction. Under normoxia, it increased respiration and estimates of glycolytic and oxidative ATP production. In G55T2 cells, SHMT inhibition lowered intracellular and extracellular lactate and altered tricarboxylic acid cycle metabolite levels and 13C isotopologue signals. SHMT inhibition increased oxidative stress, reduced the NADPH/NADP; ratio in a cell line- and condition-dependent manner, and reduced extracellular formate accumulation. In G55T2 cells, SHMT inhibition led to a depletion of glutathione. Formate supplementation most prominently restored invasion and partially reversed other antitumour effects of SHMT inhibition, with the extent of rescue varying between cell lines. Under combined stress, SHMT inhibition attenuated hypoxia-inducible factor-1-alpha; accumulation, an effect counteracted by formate supplementation. These findings link SHMT-dependent one-carbon metabolism to redox homeostasis, invasive behaviour and survival under metabolic stress in glioblastoma. SHMT inhibition increases respiratory activity under normoxia while compromising tolerance to combined oxygen and glucose restriction, identifying metabolic adaptation as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in glioblastoma.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.9] Cerulean Protein Tagging Enhances Immunogenicity and Osimertinib Response of Transplantable Murine EGFR Mutant Lung Cancer Cell Lines
item.description:
Lung cancers bearing mutations in epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFR) exhibit marked, but incomplete responses to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) like osimertinib. We previously developed genetically-engineered mouse models (GEMMs) for EGFR exon 19 deletion (del19) and L860R (mouse equivalent of L858R). Sequences encoding mC3 cerulean fluorescent protein were included to mark emergent tumor cells. Orthotopic implantation of mEGFRdel19 cell lines into syngeneic C57BL/6J mice yielded tumors that were eliminated upon osimertinib therapy which is not typically observed in patients while mEGFR-L860R cell lines failed to establish tumors. Herein, mEGFRdel19 and mEGFR-L860R cell lines formed tumors in non-induced mEGFRdel19 and mEGFR-L860R GEMMs and green fluorescent protein-transgenic mice, supporting mC3-derived epitopes as mediators of immunoelimination. CRISPR-Cas9 mediated disruption of the mC3 cerulean sequence in established mEGFR cell lines yielded two independent mC3-deleted cell lines that formed orthotopic tumors and exhibited partial osimertinib responses. These studies provide a cautionary tale regarding use of fluorescent proteins in murine cancer models and reinforce host immunity as a participant in anti-tumor TKI responses initiated. These mC3-deleted cell lines serve as improved models to explore mechanisms of incomplete TKI response, acquired resistance and cancer cell interaction with the host immune microenvironment.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.5] The KMT2A-MENIN complex is a therapeutic vulnerability in SETBP1-mutant leukemia
item.description:
SET binding protein 1 (SETBP1) is recurrently mutated in high-risk myeloid malignancies, including myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative overlap disorders (MDS/MPNs) and is associated with poor clinical outcomes. Although SETBP1 mutations promote self-renewal and HOX-driven transcription in murine and cell line models, the epigenetic dependencies sustaining these programs in human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) remain poorly defined. Here, we identify the KMT2A-MENIN complex as a targetable dependency in SETBP1-mutant leukemia. Expression of SETBP1D886N enhanced growth and serial replating of human HSPCs and established a transcriptionally permissive chromatin state, with increased H3K4me3, H3K27ac and KMT2A occupancy at SETBP1-regulated loci. Integrated transcriptional and chromatin profiling defined a 94-gene SETBP1 regulome containing HOXA9, MEIS1, MECOM, and MYBand was enriched for transcriptional programs associated with KMT2A-rearranged, NUP98-HOXA9, and NPM1-mutant leukemias. CRISPR-Cas9 disruption revealed a functional requirement for KMT2A, but not for KMT2B or DOT1L in SETBP1D886N HSPCs. Strikingly, deletion of the KMT2A cofactor MEN1 phenocopied KMT2A loss. Disruption of either KMT2A or MEN1 suppressed SETBP1-driven proliferation and leukemogenic transcriptional programs, including leukemia stem cell-associated signatures. We next exploited this dependency pharmacologically. A KMT2A-MENIN inhibitor suppressed canonical SETBP1 target genes and abolished mutant SETBP1-driven serial replating while promoting hematopoietic differentiation and reducing H3K4me3 at leukemogenic loci, despite modest effects on short-term proliferation. Most importantly, three clinically relevant KMT2A-MENIN interaction inhibitors impaired clonogenic growth across primary SETBP1-mutant leukemia patient samples, while inducing myeloid differentiation and suppressing SETBP1 target gene expression. Together, these findings identify the KMT2A-MENIN complex as a key therapeutic vulnerability in SETBP1-mutant leukemia. The consistent activity of multiple MENIN inhibitors across a variety of SETBP1-mutant patient samples and cell models validates the KMT2A-MENIN interaction as an actionable vulnerability and provides a strong rationale for expanding MENIN-directed therapies to SETBP1-mutant myeloid malignancies.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] Connexin43 drives mitochondrial biogenesis and organelle stress in BRAF-mutant melanoma cells
item.description:
Metabolic flexibility helps cancer cells survive targeted therapy, and BRAF-mutant melanoma rewires mitochondrial metabolism in response to BRAF/MEK inhibitors (BRAF/MEKi). We previously showed that connexin43 (Cx43) acts as a tumour suppressor in BRAF-mutant melanoma and enhances the response to BRAF/MEKi. Here, we investigated whether mitochondrial remodelling contributes to these effects. Cx43 upregulation promoted mitochondrial biogenesis including selective increase of CI and CV, enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, alongside DRP1-associated mitochondrial fragmentation. Despite enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and OXPHOS, Cx43 upregulation was associated with respiratory chain remodelling, characterised by loss of complex IV, increased ER and mitochondrial stress, and enhanced mTORC1-associated signalling. These changes were accompanied by an adaptive unfolded protein response that did not engage the pro-apoptotic ATF4-CHOP axis. Notably, BRAF/MEK inhibition largely attenuated the mitochondrial biogenesis phenotype and most of the stress markers associated with Cx43 upregulation, while promoting mitochondrial network elongation and markedly increasing mitochondrial ROS. Despite this impact, Cx43-expressing tumour cells retained higher membrane potential, ROS levels and survival under glucose-limiting conditions. Collectively, these findings reveal a dissociation between the mitochondrial effects of Cx43 and its enhancement of the response to BRAF/MEKi, highlighting the complexity of Cx43-mediated metabolic regulation in BRAF-mutant melanoma. By distinguishing mitochondrial remodelling from therapeutic sensitisation, this study provides new insights into the response to BRAF/MEK inhibition and highlights mTORC1-associated signalling and mitochondrial oxidative stress as potential therapeutic vulnerabilities for further investigation.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.0] Glioblastoma exhibits bidirectional adaptation to treatment through JARID2-associated developmental plasticity
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits bidirectional transcriptional reprogramming following standard-of-care (SoC) treatment, yet the direction cannot be predicted from primary tumours. Using independent longitudinal bulk and single-cell datasets, we show that this response is captured by a framework, the JARID2 Binding Site (JBS) axis. Tumours and cells can be positioned along this axis according to expression of JBS genes, with responder subtypes defined by movement along the axis from primary to recurrent states. The JBS axis aligns with established GBM ecosystems and their constituent cell populations, and recurrent tumours polarise towards opposite ends. Changes in tumour microenvironment composition strongly influence this polarisation and drive adaptive transcriptional responses more profoundly than chemoradiation alone. Mechanistically, JBS genes are enriched for promoters marked by persistent bivalent chromatin and neurodevelopmental regulatory programmes. These findings suggest that JARID2-associated Polycomb regulation maintains a reservoir of developmental plasticity that enables treatment-driven ecosystem adaptation and represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.5] Alterations in homologous recombination repair genes and impact on survival among Chinese pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma patients detected using next-generation sequencing
item.description:
Detection of homologous recombination repair (HRR) deficiency in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is advancing, yet germline HRR mutation landscapes and survival impact remain poorly characterized in Chinese patients. In this study, we undertook next-generation sequencing among 126 Chinese PDAC patients using a 32-gene panel. Pathogenic and likely pathogenic (P/LP) germline mutations were diagnosed according to the ACMG variant classification categories. Mutation frequencies of HRR-related genes were analyzed statistically, and hotspot genes with high mutation prevalence were identified. Simultaneously, we compared the differences in demographic information, tumor characteristics, and clinical outcomes between P/LP mutation carriers and non-carriers. Germline P/LP variants were identified in 11.1% of the 126 patients, most frequently involving ATM and BRCA2. VUS were detected in 31.7% of patients, with ATM, BRCA2, and BRIP1 being the most commonly involved genes. Survival analysis of 103 patients showed longer overall survival in carriers of germline P/LP variants than in non-carriers (P = 0.032). In the platinum-treated subgroup (n = 20), overall survival was numerically longer in P/LP variant carriers than in non-carriers, but the difference was not statistically significant. SMAD4 loss was associated with shorter survival in the 39 patients with complete pathological data. These findings characterize the distribution of germline HRR variants in this cohort and suggest an association between P/LP variants and overall survival that warrants confirmation in larger prospective studies.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.8] Chromosomally unstable cancer cells exhibit heightened dependence on the mitotic SKA complex
item.description:
Aneuploidy and chromosomal instability are common characteristics of cancer but remain underexploited therapeutically. Chromosomally unstable cells are often selectively vulnerable to inhibition of the kinesin KIF18A, and this dependence is related to altered mitotic control. Here, we identify the spindle and kinetochore-associated (SKA) complex as a mitotic regulator that establishes a similar dependency. SKA complex loss is tolerated in cells with a defective mitotic checkpoint, but when mitosis is prolonged, it leads to mitotic errors and loss of viability. Genetic analysis reveals that the SKA complex  and KIF18A are epistatic, although they function through mechanistically distinct mitotic pathways. SKA complex depletion selectively impacts chromosomally unstable cancer cells and mirrors the effects of KIF18A inhibition. We thus identify a cellular vulnerability associated with prolonged mitosis in chromosomally unstable cancers. Targeting chromosome segregation in chromosomally unstable cancer cells holds promise for anti-cancer therapy. Here, Schoot Uiterkamp et al. identify the mitotic SKA complex as a potential target to combat chromosomally aberrant cancer.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] B7-H3 Orchestrates Fibro-Immune Spatial Organisation in Pancreatic Cancer
item.description:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal cancers in the western world and is largely resistant to treatment. A major barrier to effective treatment is the highly desmoplastic and immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment, where the organisation of tumour, stromal and resident immune cells limit immune infiltration. B7-H3 (CD276) is an emerging immune checkpoint marker investigated in phase I and Ib/2 clinical trials in PDAC, yet its biological role within the tumour environment remains poorly understood. We performed an integrated multiscale spatial profiling study to map B7-H3 expression across regional and single-cell spatial contexts in treatment-naive resected human PDAC. Furthermore, we explored the B7-H3 landscape in the neoadjuvant setting. Our results demonstrate that B7-H3 is not simply overexpressed in cancer but may act as a spatial organiser of the PDAC microenvironment, associated with a transition from epithelial-intrinsic tumour architecture to fibro-inflammatory immune states that underpin immune suppression, aggressive disease and poor prognosis. This fibro-inflammatory state appears conserved within the neoadjuvant landscape.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.0] CD3⁺CD4-CD8- (Double-Negative) T-cells Provide Inflammatory Signals That Influence Myeloid Cells and Enhance Survival in Glioblastoma
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) remains resistant to immunotherapy, in part because of a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. While investigating the consequences of conventional T-cell depletion in a murine glioma model, we unexpectedly identified a population of double-negative T-cells (DNTs; CD3CD4-CD8-) that persisted following combined depletion of CD4 and CD8 T-cells. DNT enrichment was associated with significantly prolonged survival and revealed a distinct inflammatory transcriptional program characterized by activation-associated gene expression. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses demonstrated extensive remodeling of the glioma myeloid compartment, including enrichment of inflammatory signaling pathways and reduced expression of immunosuppressive markers. In complementary human studies, unmodified healthy donor-derived DNTs suppressed glioma stem cell viability, enhanced macrophage phagocytic activity, and reduced expression of the inhibitory myeloid receptor LAIR1. Intracranial administration of these unmodified DNTs significantly prolonged survival compared with PanT cells in an orthotopic glioblastoma xenograft model.. Collectively, these findings identify DNTs as previously underappreciated regulators of glioblastoma immunity that exert antitumor effects through both direct tumor suppression and inflammatory remodeling of the glioma myeloid compartment. These results support further investigation of DNT-based cellular therapies for the treatment of glioblastoma.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.7] Multiomic analysis of a pleural mesothelioma organoid biobank defines gene dependencies and therapeutic vulnerabilities
item.description:
Pleural mesothelioma (PM) remains an incurable cancer with few effective therapeutic options and limited understanding of its targetable dependencies, owing in part to a scarcity of clinically relevant, scalable models. Here, we describe establishment of an annotated biobank of 26 patient-derived PM organoids that faithfully recapitulate the clinical, genomic and histopathological landscapes of their parent tumours, including driver mutations, copy-number alterations and mutational signatures. By integrating these organoid models with a complementary collection of low-passage primary PM cell lines, we generate a functional precision oncology platform for PM. Genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 screening across 23 patient-derived PM models uncovered 1,150 core fitness genes, including 638 not shared with pan-cancer core essentials, highlighting critical requirements for proteostasis, DNA repair, RNA processing and cell-cycle control. Parallel profiling of 106 compounds across 36 PM models revealed broad therapeutic vulnerabilities in proteostasis, growth signalling and epigenetic regulation. Beyond these shared vulnerabilities, both screens uncovered genotype-specific dependencies and drug responses linked to recurrent PM alterations. This functional map of shared and genotype-specific dependencies establishes patient-derived organoids as a scalable platform for precision therapeutic discovery in pleural mesothelioma
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] A phenotypic-transport model of selection and therapy-associated phenotypic redistribution in the VC-Resist glioblastoma state
item.description:
Glioblastoma recurrence is sustained by tumour cells that survive chemoradiation and infiltrate the peritumoural brain. We previously identified VC-Resist, a Nestin-high, vessel-co-opting and therapy-resistant state induced by DNA-damaging therapy and vascular cues. Whether its short-term enrichment reflects selection of pre-existing cells, phenotypic redistribution, or both remains unclear because death, proliferation and state transitions co-occur. We formulate a phenotypic-transport model for glioblastoma-cell density along a continuous Nestin-reporter axis. The model separates phenotype-dependent net growth from conservative transport and is calibrated to seven-day flow-cytometric Nestin distributions after irradiation of MGG4 cells, with Sytox measurements informing treatment-associated death. It reproduces dose-dependent Nestin-high enrichment and is consistent with a graded association between higher Nestin expression, reduced proliferation and greater radiation resistance. Under the specified uncertainty ranges, transport parameters are among the strongest determinants of the modelled day-7 mean Nestin coordinate. Because the velocity field is inferred from the distributions being fitted, independent longitudinal data and transition-specific perturbations are needed to establish whether the redistribution depends causally on therapy-induced reprogramming. Counterfactual simulations compare attenuation of phenotypic transport with reduction of Nestin-associated protection. Our framework provides an interpretable, data-constrained basis for designing experiments that directly test therapy-induced plasticity in glioblastoma.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] Rac1-Abi-1 Signaling Links DNA Repair to Tumorigenesis
item.description:
The DNA damage response governs genomic integrity, and abnormal DNA repair can drive tumorigenesis. We previously identified a Rac1-Abi-1 signaling pathway in which Rac1 activates protein phosphatase 5, leading to Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation and enhanced non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Given the error-prone nature of NHEJ and its potential to promote genomic instability, we sought to determine whether Rac1-Abi-1-mediated regulation of NHEJ contributes to tumorigenesis. Here, we demonstrate the tumorigenic role of Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation in nonmalignant cell models and multiple tumorigenesis models established using a newly generated genetically engineered Abi-1 mouse model. We first found that the dephospho-mimetic Abi-1-S323A mutant promoted transformation-associated phenotypes in nonmalignant human cells and enhanced orthotopic glioblastoma growth under unperturbed conditions. To further investigate its tumorigenic potential in vivo, we generated CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Abi-1-S296A knock-in mice, in which S296 corresponds to human S323. Abi-1-S296A mouse embryonic fibroblasts exhibited increased proliferation, while mutant mice developed spontaneous tumors involving lymphoid tissues and organs under unperturbed conditions. Furthermore, Abi-1-S296A increased susceptibility to tumorigenesis following DNA damage. In a low-dose whole-body irradiation model, Abi-1-S296A mice showed a trend toward shortened survival and increased tumor development, with lesions including Harderian gland papillary cystadenomas, round-cell neoplasms, and anaplastic sarcomas. In addition, in an azoxymethane/dextran sulfate sodium (AOM/DSS)-induced colorectal tumor model, Abi-1-S296A mice developed significantly more tumors and had a greater tumor burden. These findings identify Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation as a previously unrecognized regulator of tumorigenesis and establish a new mouse model for investigating the physiological and pathological consequences of constitutive activation of upstream NHEJ-regulatory signaling.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] Targeting AURKA by CRISPR/SaCas9 Alters Cell Cycle Progression and Enhances Lenvatinib-Associated Reduction in Cell Viability in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: An Integrated In Silico and HepG2 in Vitro Study
item.description:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) presents substantial clinical concerns as a result of its high treatment resistance, frequent recurrence, and strong correlation with chronic liver diseases. Aurora kinase A (AURKA) is overexpressed in HCC correlating with poor prognosis and treatment resistance. Our bioinformatics analyses revealed that AURKA overexpression in HCC is associated with mitotic proteins and oncogenes, emphasizing its role in cancer progression. CRISPR/SaCas9-mediated AURKA knockdown markedly reduced AURKA expression levels through inducing several indels in the AURKA gene sequence, resulting in functional consequences including upregulation of p21, p53, and caspase-8, as well as downregulation of CDK1, CDK2, PI3K (alpha subunit), P38, and BCL-2 genes. Flow cytometry verified that these alterations were compatible with G2-phase cell cycle arrest and slight activation of apoptosis. Also, scratch and colony formation assays indicated a significant reduction in metastatic and proliferative potential. Furthermore, AURKA knockdown combined with Lenvatinib significantly reduce HepG2 cell viability compared with either treatment alone. Mechanistically, this study indicated that AURKA suppression reduced cell viability/proliferation by the modulation of oncogenic PI3K/AKT and p38/MAPK pathways. These in-silico and in-vitro findings highlight the critical role of AURKA in HCC pathogenesis. Here, the CRISPR/SaCas9-mediated genetic disruption of AURKA reveals its mechanistic role in regulating cell cycle, apoptosis, and tumor-suppressor signalling. Our study demonstrates AURKA as a potential molecular target to suppress HCC, while providing genetic evidence that its downregulation enhances Lenvatinib effect.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.2] NXP800 suppresses HSF1 through coordinated stress signaling and GCN2-dependent translational repression in glioblastoma
item.description:
Under states of proteotoxic stress, Heat Shock Factor 1 (HSF1) serves as the primary transcription factor responsible for restoring protein homeostasis. General Control Nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) similarly alleviates cellular stress. Activated by a shortage in amino acids, GCN2 triggers the phosphorylation of eIF2 to downregulate global protein synthesis while selectively translating survival-promoting proteins like Activating Transcription Factor 4 (ATF4). Cancer cells often exploit these pathways to mitigate damage from rapid proliferation and metabolic demands. In Glioblastoma (GBM), HSF1 promotes tumor growth and apoptosis evasion, while GCN2 maintains cancer cell homeostasis and survival. NXP800 has recently emerged as both an HSF1 inhibitor and GCN2 agonist with potent antitumor activity, yet the mechanism by which these pathways integrate to modulate GBM fate remains unclear. Herein, we show NXP800 induces an initial, GCN2-independent downregulation of HSF1 transcriptional activity, followed by a delayed, GCN2-p-eIF2-dependent decrease in HSF1 translation. This temporal regulation is accompanied by altered phosphorylation of the HSF1-activating kinase AKT1. Furthermore, we show NXP800 directly engages the HSF1 protein and that HSF1 suppression is important for the NXP800 anti-proliferative effects. Analysis of cell line and patient data further establishes a negative correlation between GCN2 and HSF1 signaling across multiple cancer types, including GBM. Collectively, our data provide a molecular framework for the dual inhibitory action of NXP800 and offers a comprehensive understanding of how this compound impairs cancer progression.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] Deubiquitination of C/EBPβ by FAM63A mediates resistance to glutaminolysis inhibition in MYC-amplified hepatocellular carcinoma
item.description:
Oncogenic MYC amplification drives glutamine addiction in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), rendering glutaminase (GLS) a promising therapeutic target. However, MYC-amplified HCC frequently exhibits intrinsic resistance to the GLS inhibitor CB-839, with the underlying adaptive survival mechanisms remaining elusive. Here, we demonstrate that MYC-high HCC cells critically depend on mitofusin 1 (MFN1)-mediated mitochondrial fusion to maintain survival under glutaminolysis inhibition. Furthermore, we show that glutaminolysis inhibition enhances the stability of CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein β (C/EBPβ), which directly activates MFN1 transcription. Mechanistically, MYC-dependent transactivation of FAM63A mediates the deubiquitination of C/EBPβ, specifically suppressing its K48-linked polyubiquitination to enhance C/EBPβ protein stability under glutamine deprivation. Importantly, inhibition of C/EBPβ abrogates MFN1-mediated mitochondrial fusion and triggers autophagic cell death, thereby sensitizing MYC-high HCC cells to GLS inhibition. Our findings identify a novel MYC-FAM63A-C/EBPβ-MFN1 signaling axis that confers adaptive resistance to GLS inhibitors in MYC-high HCC by sustaining mitochondrial fusion. Thus, targeting C/EBPβ represents a promising combinatorial therapeutic strategy to overcome CB-839 resistance in this clinically challenging HCC subtype.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] A scFv-based immunotoxin for selective targeting and cytotoxicity against c-Met-overexpressing cancer cells: an integrated in silico and in vitro study
item.description:
C-Met receptor is frequently overexpressed in multiple cancers, driving tumor invasiveness, metastasis, and therapy resistance. Although amivantamab has received clinical approval as a c-Met inhibitor, its large molecular size and lack of intrinsic cytolytic activity limit its broader therapeutic application, underscoring the need for next-generation dual-mechanism agents. To address this, we designed, produced, and characterized a novel immunotoxin, SM1, comprising an anti-c-Met scFv derived from amivantamab fused to the cytolytic peptide melittin via flexible (G4S)3 linkers. Among four computationally designed models, SM1 exhibited the most favorable binding free energy toward c-Met and was selected for experimental validation. SM1 was successfully expressed in Escherichia coli C41 (DE3) as a SUMO fusion protein, while the scFv without melittin (S1) was expressed in BL21 (DE3). Both proteins were overexpressed as inclusion bodies, solubilized using sarcosyl, and purified for functional characterization. Cell-ELISA showed stronger apparent cellular binding of both constructs to c-Met-overexpressing MKN-45 cells than to HT-29 cells, consistent with c-Met expression levels, while indicating that melittin fusion did not substantially affect scFv binding. To assess whether the melittin domain retained its lytic activity after fusion, the antibacterial activity of SM1 was evaluated against E. coli JM109, and the observed growth inhibition confirmed the retention of melittin-associated lytic activity in the fusion construct. In cytotoxicity assays, SM1 exhibited greater activity than S1 against both MKN-45 and HT-29 cells, with the strongest response observed in MKN-45 cells, while HEK-293 viability remained above 80% under the tested conditions. This selective cytotoxicity was accompanied by limited hemolytic activity, with both constructs showing less than 10% hemolysis at the highest concentration tested of 200 µM. Flow cytometry analysis further revealed potent apoptosis induction (97.03%) and extensive Sub-G1 accumulation in MKN-45 cells, with markedly lower effects in HEK-293 cells (9.22%), confirming target-dependent cytotoxicity. These findings demonstrate the preferential cytotoxicity of SM1 toward c-Met-expressing cancer cells and support its potential as a dual-mechanism immunotoxin for targeted therapy of c-Met-driven malignancies.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.5] Targeting Telomere Integrity Enhances Radiosensitivity and Reveals Adaptive DNA Damage Response Vulnerabilities in Diffuse Midline Glioma
item.description:
Diffuse midline glioma (DMG), including diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG), remains one of the most lethal pediatric malignancies, with limited durable benefit from radiotherapy (RT) due in part to adaptive DNA damage response (DDR) mechanisms. Here, we investigated whether targeting telomere integrity with the telomerase substrate analogue 6-thio-2'-deoxyguanosine (6-thio-dG; THIO) could induce therapeutically exploitable DNA damage in patient-derived DIPG models. THIO selectively suppressed DIPG cell proliferation while sparing telomerase-negative normal diploid fibroblasts and induced telomere dysfunction, as evidenced by increased telomere dysfunction-induced foci (TIFs), {gamma}H2AX accumulation, G2/M checkpoint arrest, and apoptosis. In orthotopic DIPG xenografts, THIO increased intratumoral TIF formation, suppressed tumor growth, and prolonged survival. Transcriptomic profiling further revealed activation of cellular stress-response pathways and downregulation of E2F genes, mitotic, and metabolism-associated gene programs. Mechanistically, THIO-induced progressive genomic and telomeric damage was associated with sequential activation of ATM and ATR signaling, consistent with engagement of adaptive DDR pathways. Combining THIO with ionizing radiation (IR) produced synergistic antitumor effects across three independent DIPG models representing distinct H3 mutation subtypes, with increased G2/M accumulation, genomic and telomeric DNA damage, and apoptotic cell death. In vivo, THIO combined with IR significantly improved therapeutic efficacy and prolonged median survival compared with monotherapy, including RT alone. Notably, pharmacologic inhibition of ATM or ATR attenuated THIO-induced checkpoint arrest and increased apoptosis, implicating DDR checkpoint signaling as an adaptive survival dependency following telomere damage. Collectively, these findings identify telomere-directed DNA damage as a promising therapeutic approach for DMG and provide a mechanistic rationale for combining THIO with RT and DDR checkpoint inhibition.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.2] TR-107 and Capivasertib Synergistically Inhibit Pancreatic Cancer Organoid Growth In Vitro
item.description:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in the United States, highlighting the need for effective therapeutic strategies. Oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) has emerged as a promising therapeutic target due to metabolic reprogramming and the pro-survival role of mitochondria in PDAC. The mitochondrial ClpXP complex, composed of the AAA+ ATPase ClpX and the peptidase ClpP, regulates mitochondrial homeostasis through protein degradation. Madera Therapeutics has developed novel ClpP activators, including TR-107. Here, we demonstrate that TR-107 reduces viability in four PDAC organoids and four cell lines at low-nanomolar concentrations while decreasing ClpX expression in a dose-dependent manner. Transcriptomic analysis revealed alterations in ferroptosis, amino acid metabolism, and HIF-1 signaling pathways. Notably, TR-107 retained its efficacy and mechanism of action under hypoxic conditions. Furthermore, TR-107 synergized with the AKT inhibitor capivasertib to suppress cell viability and modulate downstream signaling pathways. Collectively, these findings identify TR-107 as a promising therapeutic candidate that targets the mitochondrial ClpXP complex, disrupts mitochondrial function, and induces cellular stress and metabolic dysregulation. These effects may provide opportunities for combination therapies to improve treatment outcomes in PDAC.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.7] Author Correction: The pro-oncogenic noncanonical activity of a RAS•GTP:RanGAP1 complex facilitates nuclear protein export
