item.title: [1.5] Epigenomic circuits shaping cellular heterogeneity in pleural mesothelioma
item.description:
Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is an aggressive and lethal malignancy with current treatments offering limited clinical benefit. In this study, we utilized single-cell chromatin accessibility and transcriptomic profiling of patient-matched samples to infer the epigenomic regulation underlying cellular heterogeneity in PM. High-resolution epigenomic profiling suggested transcriptional regulators with putative pro-tumoral roles in mesothelioma, whose function was experimentally tested using genetic perturbations across four PM cell lines. Furthermore, we observed several putative associations between epigenomic circuits and macrophage ontogeny, a sarcomatoid-like neoplastic state, and a fetal-like endothelial cell state. Our analysis also showed similarities between the chromatin accessibility landscapes of exhausted CD8 T and KLRC1 natural killer cells and identified NR4A2 as a potential shared regulator of dysfunction in both lymphocyte subsets. We further identified a state-specific distal enhancer near NR4A2 and experimentally validated its regulation of NR4A2 expression in Jurkat cells. Together, we provide an epigenomic map of PM and nominate candidate transcription factors and regulatory elements for future functional investigation, including their potential relevance to epigenetic editing strategies to limit tumor growth and enhance anti-tumor immunity.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.1] mRNA-LNP vaccination induces microenvironment remodeling and generation of tissue-resident memory T cells in glioblastoma
item.description:
Glioblastoma remains highly refractory to immunotherapy, in part because of a profoundly immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment that limits effective T-cell responses. Although mRNA vaccines can induce anti-tumour immunity, how they reshape the glioblastoma immune ecosystem to support durable tumour control is not well understood. Here we use an immunocompetent EGFRvIII-driven syngeneic glioblastoma model and antigen-specific mRNA lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccination to define the cellular and spatial mechanisms underlying therapeutic response. In our model, vaccination induced durable EGFRvIII-specific humoral and cellular immunity, resulting in complete tumour eradication and long-term protection against intracranial rechallenge. Integrative analyses incorporating flow cytometry, tumour interstitial fluid profiling, multiplex immunostaining, spatial transcriptomics and ligand-receptor modelling demonstrated extensive remodelling of the tumour microenvironment following vaccination. Early tumour control was associated with expansion of pro-inflammatory and antigen-presenting myeloid populations, increased cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltration and activation, enhanced interferon-responsive signalling, and the formation of immune-supportive spatial niches enriched for antigen presentation and chemokine-mediated cellular communication. Vaccination promoted inflammatory chemokine relay networks centred on the CXCL16-CXCR6 axis, a pathway linked to tissue residency programming in the central nervous system. Functional depletion studies identified CD4 and CD8 T cells as essential mediators of therapeutic efficacy, while durable protection was maintained by tumour-specific brain-resident memory CD8 T cells that persisted despite peripheral lymphocyte depletion. Together, these findings identify T-cell-driven microenvironmental remodelling as a critical mechanism linking mRNA vaccination to the establishment of long-term brain-resident anti-tumour immunity in glioblastoma.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] Intrinsic and acquired transcriptional programs shape heterogeneous tumor cell responses to PARP, Akt, and CDK4/6 inhibitors
item.description:
Targeted therapies are increasingly utilized across cancer types, yet their efficacy in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains limited due to the disease’s high heterogeneity and aggressive nature. In a heterogeneous tumor, treatment failure can occur due to the presence of therapy-tolerant cells, which may either be innately resistant or readily adaptive to therapy. To investigate how transcriptomic heterogeneity influences response and adaptation to targeted therapy in TNBC, this study leverages the ClonMapper cell barcoding system with single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to track differential responses of DNA barcoded clonal subpopulations during treatment with PARP-, Akt-, and CDK4/6-targeting therapy. Survival during drug exposure is then modeled as a combination of (1) each subpopulation’s transcriptomic state prior to treatment and (2) persistent gene expression changes occurring during treatment, providing an approach for distinguishing between intrinsic and acquired transcriptional programs associated with heterogeneous response to targeted therapy. This work demonstrates that non-genetic heterogeneity is an important contributor to response and resistance to a set of targeted molecular therapies, highlighting the importance of considering population heterogeneity when studying therapeutic response in TNBC.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.3] ISG15 promotes PARP inhibitor resistance in BRCA1-deficient cells by facilitating DNA replication and repair
item.description:
The use of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) has proven largely successful in targeting BRCA1/2-mutated tumours. However, the emergence of PARPi-resistant disease can reduce the efficacy of this treatment, posing significant challenges in the clinic. Here, we use multiple models of BRCA1-/- cells and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) that have been treated with PARPi until they no longer responded to the drug, to characterise genomic and transcriptomic alterations specific to PARPi resistance. We find that abrogation of TP53BP1 expression occurs spontaneously during prolonged PARPi treatment, alongside TP53BP1 genomic deletions and promoter methylation. Additionally, innate immune response genes, including ISG15 and factors of the ISGylation machinery are upregulated in PARPi-resistant cells and tumours. We demonstrate that ISG15 inhibition re-sensitises PARPi-resistant cells to the drug and, conversely, that ISG15 overexpression in BRCA1-/- cells promotes PARPi resistance. Mechanistically, BRCA1-/- PARPi-resistant cells rely on ISG15 for replication fork progression and restart of stalled forks and for DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair via homologous recombination (HR). Our results indicate that complex ISG15 interactions with DNA replication/repair factors can drive PARPi resistance in BRCA1-deficient cancer cells and that targeting ISG15 has the potential to overcome PARPi resistance. Despite promising initial responses, BRCA1/2-mutated cancers treated with PARP inhibitors (PARPi) often develop resistance. Here, the authors show that PARPi-resistant BRCA1-deficient models lose TP53BP1 expression and upregulate factors of the ISGylation machinery, including ISG15, which supports replication fork progression/restart and facilitates homologous recombination-mediated DNA repair, driving PARPi resistance.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] Comparative network meta-analysis of immunotherapy and targeted agents for glioblastoma survival and response
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) remains a lethal malignancy. While immunotherapy has revolutionized oncology, its success in GBM has been inconsistent. We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) to quantify the comparative efficacy of immunotherapeutic and targeted agents against the Standard of Care (SoC). Following PRISMA-NMA guidelines, we searched PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov for randomized controlled trials. A Bayesian random-effects NMA was conducted using gemtc in R interfaced with JAGS. Heterogeneity was summarized using tau-squared, I-squared and Cochran's Q. Node-splitting was planned but was not estimable because the network geometry lacked comparisons informed by both direct and indirect evidence. Twenty-six randomized contrasts from 23 trials contributed to the overall survival (OS) network and 28 randomized contrasts from 24 trials to the progression-free survival (PFS) network, across 24 unique trials; because trials could contribute to more than one outcome network, these overlapping counts are not additive. Objective response rate (ORR) was too sparse for treatment ranking and was reported descriptively for two trials contributing five arms and three treatment–control contrasts. No investigational regimen showed a pooled OS or PFS advantage over harmonized control regimens, as all pooled relative-effect 95% credible intervals included 1.0, and rankings were sensitive to sparse network structure.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.6] A novel interaction between MNT and CCDC6: structural insights and distinct roles in cell migration and the DNA damage response
item.description:
MNT is a transcription factor of the MYC-MAX-MXD network whose biological functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify CCDC6, a tumor suppressor involved in the DNA damage response (DDR), as a novel MNT-interacting protein. Co-immunoprecipitation and interaction mapping analyses identified a part of the CCDC6 coiled-coil domain and the MNT bHLH-LZ region as major determinants of binding. Structural modelling further identified MNT residues predicted to mediate CCDC6 binding that are also critical for MNT-MAX dimerization. Transcriptomic analyses revealed substantial overlap between the gene expression programs regulated by MNT and CCDC6. Loss of either protein promoted cell migration, whereas MNT and CCDC6 cooperated in the regulation of {gamma}H2AX signalling, cisplatin responses and CCDC6 localization during the DDR. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized connection between CCDC6 and the MYC-MAX-MXD network through its interaction with MNT, revealing an additional layer of regulation within this transcriptional network.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.3] Overcoming resistance to KRAS inhibition in KRAS/PIK3CA co-mutated colorectal cancer
item.description:
Oncogenic alleles of KRAS drive colorectal cancers (CRC) growth and are associated with worse disease outcomes. Despite potent allele-specific and pan-RAS inhibitors targeting now in clinical test, CRC patients are not experiencing the same therapeutic benefit as patients with other cancers. PI3-Kinase (PI3K) is a direct RAS effector and is co-mutated in about 45% of CRC cases, raising the possibility that frequent oncogenic PI3K mutations contribute to the limited benefit of KRAS inhibition in CRC. Using isogenic colorectal cancer cells engineered to harbor either of the two most common activating PIK3CA mutations, we show that oncogenic PI3K promotes resistance to the pan-RAS inhibitor daraxonrasib (RMC-6236). Global phosphoproteomic profiling revealed that PIK3CA-mutant cells undergo a distinct adaptive response to RAS inhibition, characterized by sustained PI3K-AKT signaling and extensive remodeling of pathways controlling cell-cell adhesion and junction signaling, alongside suppression of apoptotic signaling. Combined RAS and PI3K inhibition overcame this resistance, suppressed signaling through both pathways and induced apoptosis in PIK3CA-mutant cells. Together, these findings identify oncogenic PIK3CA as a determinant of resistance to RAS inhibition in KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer and provide a mechanistic rationale for combined KRAS and PI3K inhibition in KRAS/PIK3CA co-mutant tumors.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.2] Loss of CDKN2A remodels Golgi morphology to create a lipid peroxidation vulnerability
item.description:
Loss of the tumor suppressor CDKN2A/p16 occurs in ~50% of human cancers, yet no therapies specifically target tumors with complete loss or reduced CDKN2A/p16 expression (hereafter CDKN2A/p16-Low). Identifying selective vulnerabilities in CDKN2A/p16-Low tumors therefore represents a critical unmet need. Here, we identify altered Golgi morphology as a vulnerability in CDKN2A/p16-Low melanoma. A CRISPR knockout screen revealed that genes associated with Golgi membranes are essential for CDKN2A/p16-Low cell survival. CDKN2A/p16 knockdown in human and murine cancer cells was associated with striking Golgi compaction. CDKN2A/p16 knockdown sensitized cells to pharmacologic Golgi disruption via lipid peroxidation both in vitro and in vivo. Notably, reduced Retinoblastoma-associated protein (RB1) expression did not recapitulate the increased sensitivity to Golgi disruption, supporting a role for non-canonical p16 functions in this vulnerability. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized link between CDKN2A/p16-Low status and Golgi remodeling, revealing a Golgi-associated metabolic vulnerability in CDKN2A/p16-Low melanomas.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.5] The SOX9 C-terminus encodes a transferable cBAF-recruitment module for enhancer remodeling and cell-state control
item.description:
Transcription factors select genomic targets, but how they recruit chromatin remodelers to convert DNA occupancy into cell-state-specific accessibility remains unclear. Here, we identify an intrinsically disordered SOX9 C-terminal module that recruits SMARCB1-containing canonical BAF (cBAF) to stem-like enhancers that open during APC-mutant adenoma formation. Acute, reversible SOX9 degradation displaces cBAF from ~80% of co-bound enhancers, exceeding effects on pBAF and ncBAF, and collapses accessibility and stem-like identity; SOX9 re-expression restores these features. C-terminal truncation preserves DNA binding but disrupts cBAF engagement and chromatin opening. Enforced SMARCB1 docking to truncated SOX9 partially restores cBAF recruitment, accessibility, stem-like transcription, and organoid self-renewal, identifying remodeler recruitment as a limiting effector function. The isolated C-terminus supports higher-order cBAF assembly and, when fused to dCas9 as COMET, redirects endogenous cBAF to targeted loci to open chromatin. Disordered TF regions can therefore encode transferable instructions that deploy specific remodeling complexes to control cell state.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.4] Methylene blue modulates G3BP1-associated condensation and attenuates Kras-driven pancreatic preneoplastic lesions
item.description:
Abstract Stress granules (SGs) are dynamic biomolecular condensates implicated in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), with G3BP1/2 serving as key regulators of their assembly. We combined structure-based screening of FDA-approved drugs with cellular and biochemical assays and identified methylene blue (MB) as a modulator of SG assembly. MB suppressed SG accumulation across multiple PDAC cell lines under arsenite (AS)-induced stress, nutrient deprivation, and heat shock without reducing the abundance of major SG-associated proteins. In reconstituted systems, MB inhibited G3BP1 condensation with or without added RNA and showed a nonsignificant trend toward lower G3BP1-Caprin1 co-immunoprecipitation in cells. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations predicted a potential MB interaction site within the G3BP1 NTF2-like (NTF2L) domain. The G3BP1 V11A/F15A/F33A/F124A mutant retained basal condensate-forming capacity but showed reduced responsiveness to MB compared with wild-type G3BP1, implicating this region in MB-mediated regulation. In Kras-driven KC mice, chronic oral MB administration was associated with reduced pancreatic G3BP1-positive puncta, increased acinar preservation, and decreased preneoplastic lesion burden, epithelial proliferation, and stromal remodeling, without overt abnormalities in the evaluated endpoints. Together, these findings identify MB as a small-molecule probe that modulates G3BP1 condensation dynamics and demonstrate that chronic MB treatment is associated with the attenuation of early Kras driven pancreatic preneoplastic lesion progression in vivo.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.4] S100A4 Is a Targetable Regulator of Immune Suppression in Glioblastoma
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor that remains largely refractory to immunotherapy owing to a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Here, we use mouse models of GBM to identify S100A4 as an actionable regulator of immune suppression and demonstrate that its inhibition converts GBM into an immunotherapy-responsive state. Genetic knockdown of S100a4 in glioma cells reprogrammed the GBM TME, enhancing CD8 T cell infiltration and effector function while promoting maturation of antigen-presenting cells. These changes translated into significant survival benefits across diverse molecular subtypes of GBM. Therapeutically, a novel S100A4/Transferrin Receptor (TfR) bispecific antibody phenocopied S100a4-KD and showed significant therapeutic efficacy, particularly in combination with PD-1 blockade. Notably, BsA+anti-PD1 combination treatment generated tertiary lymphoid-like structures in GBM. Together, these findings establish S100A4 as a targetable driver of immune evasion in GBM and provide a translational strategy for overcoming resistance to immunotherapy in this lethal disease.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] Transactivation of EGFR by LCK underlies an activity-defined dependency that predicts response to EGFR inhibition in cholangiocarcinoma
item.description:
Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is an aggressive biliary tract malignancy with limited molecularly guided treatment options. The Src-family kinase LCK is a therapeutic vulnerability in CCA, yet its canonical T-cell substrates are minimally expressed in CCA cells, leaving its downstream effectors undefined. Unbiased proximity labeling in HuCCT1 cells identified EGFR within the LCK signaling neighborhood. LCK depletion or inhibition reduced EGFR phosphorylation, whereas recombinant LCK increased EGFR phosphorylation in a cell-free assay, supporting a noncanonical role for LCK upstream of EGFR. Given the failure of EGFR-directed therapies in unselected CCA populations, we hypothesized that EGFR activity, rather than abundance or mutation status, identifies EGFR-dependent tumors. Among 28 patient-derived xenografts ranked by pretreatment substrate-inferred EGFR activity, the activity score correctly classified afatinib response in all six models tested. An analogous EGFR activity score stratified primary tumors in two human CCA cohorts. Together, these findings identify a therapeutically actionable LCK-EGFR signaling axis and nominate EGFR activity as a functional biomarker to guide tumor selection for EGFR-directed therapy in CCA, warranting prospective clinical validation.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.6] A Three-Axis Framework for Therapy Prioritization in MBD4-Deficient Tumors: De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Modeling, Replication-Stress Pharmacology, and PARP1 Trapping Decoupling
item.description:
Background: Loss-of-function mutations in MBD4 (methyl-CpG-binding domain protein 4) cause a specialized base excision repair (BER) deficiency characterized by hypermutated CpG>TpG signatures and sensitivity to immune checkpoint blockade. However, post-immunotherapy treatment prioritization remains empirically unmapped. In clinical oncology, DNA damage response (DDR) defects are frequently extrapolated to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) sensitivity by analogy to homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), without testing whether upstream glycosylase loss generates the nicked single-strand break (SSB) intermediates required for toxic PARP1-DNA trapping. Methods: We developed a three-axis framework integrating mechanistic curation, large-scale pharmacogenomics (DepMap 24Q2 CRISPR/RNA-seq, n=1,517; GDSC2 dose-response profiling, n=928; PRISM Repurposing), and a 5-Layer De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Machine Learning (SL-ML) Engine (SL-XGBRanker). To prevent functional dilution from variants of uncertain significance, MBD4 loss-of-function (MBD4-LOF) was strictly restricted to truncating and canonical splice-site alleles (21 of 36 mutated lines), independently validated by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD; two-sided p2s = 0.0367), while excluding 15 lines harboring 19 non-truncating variants (18 missense, 1 inframe deletion). All primary pharmacogenomic comparisons were evaluated using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (p2s), bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs), Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) multiplicity correction across six pre-specified candidate axes, and Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) for expression equivalence. Results: Our analysis delineates three distinct therapeutic axes in MBD4-LOF tumors: (1) Cytidine Analog Vulnerability (Axis 1): Mechanistic structural evidence demonstrates that MBD4 loss impairs excision of 5-substituted pyrimidine analogs and deaminated bases, creating a direct biochemical bottleneck to gemcitabine and 5-fluorouracil incorporation. (2) ATR-Check1 Replication-Stress Vulnerability (Axis 2): In GDSC2 profiling, MBD4-LOF cell lines exhibit significant sensitivity to the ATR inhibitor ceralasertib (AZD6738). In the clinically relevant TP53-mutant background-which disables the G1/S checkpoint and forces reliance on ATR-mediated S/G2 arrest-MBD4-LOF lines (n=11 vs n=619 WT) demonstrate pronounced ceralasertib hypersensitivity (Delta LN_IC50 = -1.07, 95% CI [-1.62, -0.41], Cohen's d = -0.74, p2s = 0.0060, BH-FDR q = 0.036; Delta AUC = -0.087, d = -0.89, p2s = 0.0017), with 11/11 leave-one-out (LOO) jackknife iterations retaining two-sided significance (p2s <= 0.014). This genotype-associated dependency remains robust in the unstratified pan-cancer cohort (n=14 vs n=914 WT; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.73, 95% CI [-1.31, -0.11], d = -0.50, p2s = 0.0430; Delta AUC = -0.056, d = -0.56, p2s = 0.0259) and after purging microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) lines (n=10 vs n=906 WT MSS; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.91, 95% CI [-1.50, -0.22], d = -0.62, p2s = 0.0307). By contrast, Wee1 inhibition (adavosertib; n=15 vs n=920 WT; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.35, p2s = 0.1667) does not reach statistical significance. (3) Absence of Single-Agent PARPi Sensitivity (Axis 3): While PARP1 transcript abundance strongly governs pan-cancer PARPi cytotoxicity across n=481 cell lines (rho = -0.416, p < 10^-21 across five clinical PARPi), MBD4-LOF tumors (n=19 vs n=1,498 WT) show zero compensatory PARP1 upregulation (median 6.77 vs 6.66 log2[TPM+1], Delta median = +0.11, 95% CI [-0.39, +0.71], p2s = 0.605; TOST equivalence p_TOST = 0.0199 within +/- 0.50 log2[TPM+1]). Direct GDSC2 evaluation of MBD4-LOF (n=8) versus WT (n=478) confirms complete absence of single-agent PARPi sensitization across talazoparib (p2s = 0.973), olaparib (p2s = 0.522), niraparib (p2s = 0.877), rucaparib (p2s = 0.804), veliparib (p2s = 0.538), and the composite 5-drug mean PARPi Z-score (Delta median Z = -0.024, 95% CI [-0.84, +0.60], p2s = 0.841). Under Leave-One-Anchor-Out cross-validation across 12 canonical DDR genes (370 gene-drug pairs), our 5-Layer De-confounded SL-ML Engine achieves an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.9716, AUPRC of 0.8007, and Top-1 accuracy of 82.86%, zero-shot ranking gemcitabine (#1) and ceralasertib (#2) as the top therapeutic dependencies for held-out MBD4 while rejecting all PARP inhibitors (ranks #13, #27, #28, #31). Conclusion: MBD4-LOF tumors exhibit a selective, TP53-potentiated pharmacological dependency on ATR kinase inhibition alongside mechanistic vulnerability to cytidine analogs, but lack both the nicked BER repair intermediates and the PARP1 target expression required for single-agent PARP inhibitor efficacy.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.8] Transcriptional upregulation of NDUFA10 by ATF3 sustains mitochondrial bioenergetics and malignant phenotypes in NSCLC
item.description:
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of global cancer mortality, necessitating the identification of novel therapeutic vulnerabilities. This study identifies NDUFA10, a key mitochondrial Complex I subunit, as a critical driver of NSCLC pathogenesis. Multi-cohort analysis of TCGA and clinical datasets revealed significant NDUFA10 upregulation in neoplastic tissues, which correlated with advanced pathological stage, metastasis, smoking history, and poor overall survival. Single-cell RNA sequencing further localized NDUFA10 enrichment to proliferating malignant epithelial subpopulations, where its expression positively associated with oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and ATP synthesis across primary and metastatic sites. Functionally, NDUFA10 ablation (shRNA or CRISPR/Cas9) in primary NSCLC and A549 cells disrupted mitochondrial homeostasis—evidenced by impaired respiration, attenuated Complex I activity, and augmented ROS production—while inhibiting cell viability, migration, and invasion. Mechanistically, NDUFA10 modulates the Akt-mTOR signaling axis; constitutively active Akt1 partially rescued the proliferative and survival deficits induced by NDUFA10 silencing. Furthermore, intersectional bioinformatics and ChIP-qPCR identified ATF3 as the direct transcriptional activator driving NDUFA10 overexpression. In vivo, NDUFA10-silenced xenografts exhibited significantly attenuated growth, characterized by compromised mitochondrial function and inhibited Akt-mTOR activation. In summary, our findings characterize NDUFA10 as a critical metabolic checkpoint in NSCLC, where its ATF3-driven its overexpression coordinates mitochondrial bioenergetics and Akt-mTOR signaling to sustain malignant progression.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.7] HSPB8 regulates CTP synthase filaments to couple nucleotide metabolism and autophagy in tumors
item.description:
Metabolic adaptation and proteostasis are essential for tumor survival under nutrient stress, yet how these processes are mechanistically integrated remains unclear. Here, we identify CTP synthase (CTPS) filament dynamics as a regulatory nexus linking nucleotide metabolism to autophagic flux. Under glutamine deprivation—a hallmark of poorly vascularized solid tumors—CTPS undergoes polymerization into filamentous assemblies that exhibit reduced enzymatic activity. We demonstrate that filament formation is driven by intracellular asparagine availability and regulated by the accumulation of misfolded proteins. Using APEX2-based proximity labeling and proteomics, we identify the small heat shock protein HSPB8 as a filament-associated regulator. HSPB8, acting within the chaperone-assisted selective autophagy (CASA) pathway, antagonizes CTPS polymerization by promoting clearance of misfolded proteins, thereby restoring soluble, catalytically active CTPS. Filament disassembly increases CTP production and enhances synthesis of autophagy-related phospholipids, including phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylethanolamine, resulting in accelerated autophagic flux. Cells expressing filament-deficient CTPS mutants display elevated autophagosome formation and increased LC3-II accumulation upon lysosomal blockade, confirming enhanced flux. In vivo, disruption of CTPS filament assembly impairs xenograft tumor growth and is associated with excessive autophagy. Analysis of TCGA datasets further reveals that high CTPS and low HSPB8 expression correlate with poor patient survival across multiple cancers. Collectively, our findings establish CTPS filament dynamics as a proteostasis-sensitive metabolic switch that coordinates nucleotide biosynthesis with autophagy, revealing a previously unrecognized vulnerability in tumors adapting to nutrient limitation.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.7] Normalized membrane ratio of TROP2 as a predictor of clinical outcomes with datopotamab deruxtecan in non-small-cell lung cancer
item.description:
Datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd)—a trophoblast cell surface antigen 2 (TROP2)-directed antibody–drug conjugate—has demonstrated efficacy in patients with advanced nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ± actionable genomic alterations. However, TROP2 expression by pathologist assessment using conventional immunohistochemistry with visual scoring does not predict response to TROP2-directed antibody–drug conjugates in NSCLC. We developed TROP2 quantitative continuous scoring (QCS)—a fully supervised computational pathology approach that quantifies TROP2 expression in individual NSCLC cells and subcellular components from immunohistochemistry-stained slides. Using QCS to determine TROP2 expression at the tumor cell membrane and cytoplasm, normalized membrane ratio (NMR) was developed (ratio of membrane relative to membrane + cytoplasmic TROP2) in the biomarker-evaluable population of patients with advanced NSCLC in the TROPION-PanTumor01 study (n = 115). The TROP2 NMR cut-point was optimized and validated in patients with nonsquamous NSCLC without actionable genomic alterations (primary intended-use population, n = 221) in the biomarker-evaluable population (n = 352) of the TROPION-Lung01 trial. Association with clinical outcomes was assessed. Progression-free survival was longer in Dato-DXd-treated (median 7.2 versus 4.0 months; hazard ratio 0.40, 95% confidence interval 0.25–0.64) but not docetaxel-treated (median 4.1 versus 4.4 months; hazard ratio 0.94, 95% confidence interval 0.59–1.49) patients with TROP2 NMR-positive versus TROP2 NMR-negative samples (treatment by biomarker status interaction P = 0.0098), indicating that TROP2 NMR may be a predictive biomarker for Dato-DXd. This work developed and validated a computational pathology biomarker—the TROP2 normalized membrane ratio—that quantifies subcellular TROP2 localization and predicts improved progression-free and overall survival with datopotamab deruxtecan in patients with nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer lacking actionable genomic alterations.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.0] Lysine 69 deacetylation of NFIC drives autophagy-induced epithelial–mesenchymal transition and chemoresistance in glioblastoma
item.description:
Acquired temozolomide (TMZ) resistance is a major obstacle in improving glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) treatment. Accumulating evidence has indicated that autophagy has dual effects on the regulation of chemoresistance. In our previous study, we reported that autophagic inducers can upregulate the E3 ligase HERC3 and then mediate TMZ resistance by activating the HERC3/SMAD7/TGF-β pathway. However, the underlying mechanism within the increasing expression of HERC3 induced by autophagy is still unknown. Herein, we show that autophagy promotes the deacetylation of nuclear factor I C (NFIC) at lysine 69, which induces the transcriptional activation of forkhead box protein K1 (FOXK1) and thus promotes HERC3 dependent epithelial‒mesenchymal transition (EMT). The dynamic equilibrium of NFIC K69Ac is controlled by the acetyltransferase P300 and the deacetylase HDAC6. Pe-k69, a cell-penetrating peptide, can specifically block NFIC K69 deacetylation and sensitise GBM cells to TMZ. Our study reveals an acetylation-dependent regulatory mechanism, which may provide mechanistic clues for targeting NFIC to overcome GBM chemoresistance. Autophagy-induced the deacetylation of NFIC at Lysine 69 site accelerates tumorigenesis by activating FOXK1/HERC3 axis, revealing an acetylation-dependent mechanism that can be targeted by peptide Pe-k69 to overcome TMZ resistance in glioblastoma.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.0] Synergistic effect of XYL-1 and Olaparib in BRCA-proficient TNBC cells is associated with RAD51 and BRCA1 downregulation
item.description:
Poly-ADP-ribose polymerase1/2 (PARP1/2) inhibitors are approved for HER2-negative breast cancer harboring germline BRCA1/2 mutations, including TNBC. However, the majority of patients with BRCA-proficient derive limited benefit from these agents. In this study, we demonstrate that the efficacy of the PARP1/2 inhibitor Olaparib in BRCA-proficient TNBC cell lines can be markedly enhanced by co-treatment with the PARP7 inhibitor XYL-1. Our results demonstrated that the combination of Olaparib and XYL-1 significantly inhibited the proliferation of BRCA-proficient MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells compared with either monotherapy, with the strongest synergistic effect observed at a 1:1 molar ratio in MDA-MB-231 cells. Furthermore, the combination of Olaparib and XYL-1 significantly increased cellular ROS levels, induced DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), and ultimately promoted apoptosis. In vivo, the combined treatment significantly suppressed MDA-MB-231 tumor growth compared with either monotherapy, while exhibiting a favorable safety profile. Mechanistically, co-treatment with XYL-1 and Olaparib significantly downregulated RAD51 and BRCA1 expression, which may be associated with impaired homologous recombination (HR)-mediated DNA repair. Collectively, these findings suggest that dual targeting of PARP7 and PARP1/2 represents a promising combination strategy for the treatment of BRCA-proficient TNBC.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.6] Mitochondrial protein import defects enhance tumour immunogenicity
item.description:
Tumour cells evade detection and elimination by the immune system through a suite of adaptations1, including the repression of antigen presentation, which is required for the recognition of tumour cells by CD8+ T cells. Mitochondria have emerged as targets for enhancing antitumour immunity; however, the extensive mitochondrial proteome has remained largely unstudied for its ability to modulate immune responses. Here we show that defects in the mitochondrial protein import machinery promote tumour immunogenicity and synergize with immune checkpoint blockade treatment in melanoma models. Mitochondrial protein import perturbation, specifically through depletion of the TIM23 import complex subunit TIMM50, enhances tumour immunogenicity through a pathway involving mitochondrial DNA escape, cGAS–STING pathway activation and interferon-β (IFNβ) secretion. Secreted IFNβ signals through the type I IFN receptor to activate the JAK–STAT pathway, resulting in increased antigen presentation on MHC class I complexes. Mitochondrial DNA escape in Timm50-depleted cells is linked to the formation of mitochondrial-derived vesicles. Depletion of SNX9 and RAB9, involved in mitochondrial-derived vesicle formation2, suppresses mitochondrial DNA-dependent type I IFN production and signalling. By disrupting mitochondrial proteostasis and membrane architecture, defective protein import in Timm50-depleted cells drives the immune phenotype. This study shows that mitochondrial protein import inhibition causes tumour immunogenicity, including sensitization to immune checkpoint blockade, by promoting mitochondrial DNA escape and IFNβ-driven MHC class I antigen presentation. Inhibition of mitochondrial protein import can enhance tumour immunogenicity by promoting mitochondrial DNA release.

item.title: [1.6] Serum extracellular vesicle proteomics reveals treatment-associated biomarkers in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
item.description:
Background Longitudinal biomarkers of treatment response in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are needed. Extracellular vesicle (EV)-enriched serum proteomics may provide a minimally invasive approach for monitoring systemic and tumor-associated responses to therapy. Methods Paired pre-treatment and post-treatment serum samples were analyzed from 51 patients with pancreatic cancer, including 25 treated with FOLFIRINOX and 20 treated with gemcitabine-based therapy. EVs were enriched using the Mag-Net method and profiled by data independent acquisition mass spectrometry. After batch correction and filtering, 941 proteins were retained for differential and pathway analyses. Paired linear models and gene set enrichment analyses were used to assess treatment-associated changes. Baseline protein abundance and longitudinal changes were evaluated in relation to overall survival (OS) using Cox models. Results A total of 2,089 EV-associated proteins were identified, with an average of 1,186 proteins quantified per sample. Across the cohort, 26 proteins differed between post- and pretreatment samples. Proteins that increased after treatment were primarily related to extracellular matrix organization and cell adhesion, whereas proteins that decreased after treatment were associated with actin cytoskeletal organization, coagulation, and hemostasis. Treatment-associated changes were more pronounced in the FOLFIRINOX group, in which 32 proteins were differentially expressed. FOLFIRINOX was characterized by coordinated reductions in platelet- and coagulation-associated proteins, including PF4, PF4V1, PPBP, GP5, ITGA2B, and ITGB3, accompanied by enrichment of platelet activation, coagulation, and hemostasis pathways among down-regulated processes. No individual proteins met the same significance threshold in the gemcitabine group. A composite seven-protein platelet score decreased significantly after FOLFIRINOX but not for gemcitabine, and the between-regimen difference in score change was significant. Higher pretreatment ITGB1 abundance was associated with longer OS after multiple-testing correction (HR, 0.112; BH-FDR = 0.0063). In multivariable analysis, greater treatment-associated platelet-score depletion was independently associated with shorter OS (HR per unit increase in {Delta}score, 0.56; P = 0.030). Conclusions Longitudinal serum EV-enriched proteomics identified treatment-associated biological changes in PDAC, including a coordinated platelet-related response predominantly observed after FOLFIRINOX. Baseline ITGB1 abundance and longitudinal platelet-score changes represent potentially complementary prognostic and pharmacodynamic markers. These findings are exploratory and require validation in larger, independent cohorts incorporating platelet counts, coagulation measurements, and targeted proteomic assays.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] Genotype-Informed Drosophila Kinome Screening Prioritizes PRKX as a Candidate Vulnerability in Bladder Cancer
item.description:
Muscle-invasive bladder cancer is molecularly heterogeneous, and the basal/squamous subtype frequently exhibits elevated EGFR expression and TP53 and RB1 alterations. Functional vulnerabilities associated with these alterations remain incompletely defined, while large-scale in vivo screening in mammalian models is experimentally demanding. Therefore, we developed a genotype-defined Drosophila melanogaster model combining Egfr overexpression, mutant p53, and Rbf suppression in Malpighian tubules. The resulting 3-hit model showed increased Malpighian tubule volume and reduced adult eclosion rate. A dominant modifier screen targeting 216 kinase genes identified 72 genes whose perturbation significantly increased the eclosion rate, and a complementary RNA interference screen identified eight kinases whose knockdown increased the eclosion rate. Among these hits, Pka-C3, which is a Drosophila ortholog of human PRKX, emerged as one of the strongest suppressors of the 3-hit phenotype. PRKX was prioritized for further study because public transcriptomic datasets showed higher PRKX expression in bladder tumors than in normal bladder tissue. PRKX knockdown reduced spheroid volume in four human bladder cancer cell lines with distinct EGFR, TP53, and RB1 profiles. Both small interfering RNAs produced significant reductions in two cell lines, whereas only one siRNA reached significance in the other two. These findings nominate PRKX as a candidate vulnerability in bladder cancer and highlight a cross-species approach that combines genotype-informed Drosophila screening with functional testing in human cancer cells to prioritize targets for further investigation.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.8] The Phospholipase A2 Activity of Peroxiredoxin 6 Protects Hepatocarcinoma Cells Against Ferroptosis and Mitophagy Impairment
item.description:
Peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6) is a moonlighting protein that plays a key role in regulating redox homeostasis and lipid metabolism through its unique dual peroxidase and calcium-independent phospholipase A2 (iPLA2) activities. Here, we generated a stable HepG2 cell line harboring a D140A mutation to selectively ablate iPLA2 activity, and we compared its phenotype with that of wild-type (WT) and PRDX6-knockout (KO) cells. D140A exhibited low ROS leves, similar to WT cells, confirming that oxidative stress is due to peroxidase deficiency. In contrast, D140A cells displayed higher lipid peroxidation than WT cells, though significantly lower than that of KO cells. Furthermore, the D140A mutant mirrored the KO phenotype regarding intracellular ferrous iron accumulation, impaired lipid droplet biogenesis, and the downregulation of the key ferroptosis regulator GPX4. Mechanistically, integrated proteomic, lipidomic, and enzymatic analyses revealed that a deficiency in iPLA2 activity of PRDX6 disrupted the release of key lipid species necessary for cell structure and signaling. Consequently, organelles involved in lipid synthesis and trafficking, such as peroxisomes, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and lipid droplet, were affected. Specifically, we found that mitochondria exhibited a reduction in cristae and a diminished capacity for mitophagy and autophagy, which ultimately makes cells much more susceptible to erastin-induced ferroptotic cell death. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that PRDX6 iPLA2 activity uniquely coordinates organelle lipid homeostasis and mitophagy to protect cancer cells from ferroptotic cell death. Consequently, the use of iPLA2 inhibitors such as MJ33, which decreased PRDX6 iPLA2 activity to a level comparable to the mutant D140A, could represent a promising therapeutic strategy for inducing ferroptotic cell death in hepatocellular carcinoma.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.7] Integrated multi-omics prioritizes small-molecule candidates for the N-cadherin HAV site and reveals endpoint-level toxicity trade-offs
item.description:
N-cadherin (CDH2) is a central effector of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) that contributes to invasion, metastasis and therapy resistance. Although peptide and antibody approaches validate N-cadherin as a therapeutic target, small-molecule modulators of its adhesive interface remain limited. We aimed to prioritize candidate compounds that suppress EMT-associated transcriptional programs, show plausible binding at the N-cadherin HAV (His79-Ala80-Val81) hotspot, preserve the biomass objective in context-specific metabolic models, and minimize predicted endpoint-level toxicity liabilities. LINCS L1000 level-5 profiles were screened for concordant down-regulation of CDH2, SNAI1 and SNAI2, yielding 20 compounds across cell lines, doses and exposure times. Compounds were docked to the N-cadherin EC1 HAV pocket and compared with a spatially separated non-HAV EC1 control surface. Toxicity was evaluated using a multi-task DeepChem Graph Convolutional Network trained on Tox21 with a scaffold-based split. Predicted toxicity risk was summarized using max-risk, defined as the highest predicted positive-class probability across 12 endpoints. Context-specific metabolic effects were modeled with Human1 using E-Flux, pFBA and FVA, and summarized using Objective Preservation Ratio (OPR), Metabolic Impact Score (MIS), Targeted Pathway Selectivity (TPS), and Homeostasis Disruption Score (HDS). Evidence pillars were winsorized, normalized and integrated using a transparent weighted composite score. Docking energies ranged from − 8.1 to − 5.9 kcal mol–1, and 19 of 20 compounds showed more favorable predicted binding at the HAV pocket than at the non-HAV control surface. The toxicity model achieved a micro-averaged ROC-AUC of 0.775 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.756–0.794) and PR-AUC of 0.335 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.298–0.374). Across modeled conditions, median OPR was 1.12, median TPS was 0.165, median MIS was 0.79, and HDS was uniformly low. Under the conservative max-risk-based integration, BRD.K09587429 ranked first (composite score 0.656). It showed concordant suppression of CDH2, SNAI1 and SNAI2, a HAV-site docking score of − 6.7 kcal mol–1, OPR of 1.081, TPS of 0.184, and max-risk of 0.554 at SR-ARE. BRD.K04021425 ranked second and was retained as the alternative candidate, with the strongest docking score and the lowest endpoint-level max-risk. A 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation showed persistent computational occupancy of the HAV-site region, with His79 and Ala80 remaining within 0.4 nm of the ligand in 96.9% and 99.1% of frames, respectively, over the 20–100 ns interval. MM-PBSA analysis of 81 snapshots yielded a favorable end-state binding-energy estimate of − 24.58 ± 6.90 kcal mol–1, which remained consistent when analysis was restricted to the final 50 ns (– 27.22 ± 5.68 kcal mol–1). This multi-omics framework prioritizes candidate N-cadherin/EMT modulators by jointly considering transcriptomic directionality, HAV-site docking, endpoint-resolved toxicity, and metabolic selectivity. BRD.K09587429 emerged as the highest-ranked discovery-stage candidate, with molecular dynamics showing persistent computational occupancy of the HAV-site region and MM-PBSA indicating a favorable model-dependent end-state energetic profile; however, direct binding, functional N-cadherin antagonism, molecular mechanism, and the predicted SR-ARE-associated liability require experimental validation. The framework distinguishes structural plausibility from safety and can be adapted to other protein-protein interfaces relevant to metastatic cancer biology.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] Cancer drug resistance as a temporal process: cell plasticity, adaptive buffering, signaling pathways and therapeutic interception
item.description:
Cancer drug resistance remains a principal barrier to durable cancer control, yet it is still often interpreted through endpoint-centred models that emphasise pre-existing resistant clones, incomplete drug exposure or late-acquired mechanisms. These explanations are essential but incomplete. The question is not only why resistant cells exist, but also how residual cells remain alive long enough to become resistant. Across tumour types and therapeutic modalities, treatment reshapes residual populations while it is acting, driving transitions through non-genetic heterogeneity, stochastic cell-fate variability, reversible tolerance, stress adaptation, microenvironmental support and eventually stable resistance. This Review develops a temporal framework in which resistance is resolved into a phase-structured trajectory organised around two mechanistic transitions: entry into adaptive buffering and later stabilisation into resistance hardening. Adaptive buffering is defined operationally as a transient, support-dependent survival state in which residual tumour cells preserve viability by recruiting physiological support systems while molecular and phenotypic reorganisation proceeds. It is not a single pathway or a synonym for drug tolerance, but a functional demand-capacity state whose dependencies change over time. We distinguish adaptive buffering from drug tolerance, persister states, dormancy, minimal residual disease and established resistance and discuss how buffering can be evaluated experimentally using perturbational, single-cell, spatial, computational and functional readouts. The framework suggests that informative biomarkers should assign residual populations to adaptive phases, so that therapy can intercept transient dependencies before adaptive states become hardened and clinically entrenched.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.6] Microbiota-based modulation of intratumoral cholesterol metabolism for colorectal cancer treatment
item.description:
Excess cholesterol accumulates in colorectal cancer (CRC) and promotes its progression, yet systemic cholesterol-lowering has limited benefits and safety concerns. Here we show that redirecting intestinal cholesterol metabolism through the gut microbiota generates a metabolite, 4-cholesten-3-one (4-C-3), which suppresses CRC growth. A screen of microbial cholesterol metabolites showed that 4-C-3 is depleted in faecal and tumour samples from patients with CRC. 4-C-3 suppresses tumour growth in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids and xenografts. Mechanistically, 4-C-3 suppresses two major oncogenic drivers of CRC by inhibiting epidermal growth-factor receptor activation and stabilizing mutant oncogenic KRAS in an inactive state, thereby overcoming KRAS-driven resistance to anti-epidermal growth-factor receptor therapy. As proof of concept, restoring 4-C-3 using either Oscillibacter ruminantium, a natural 4-C-3 producer reduced in CRC, or a non-pathogenic Escherichia coli engineered to convert intestinal cholesterol into 4-C-3, lowered intratumoral cholesterol and induced tumour regression in preclinical models without overt toxicity. These findings uncover a microbiota–cholesterol metabolic pathway that can be harnessed through microbiome engineering to selectively target CRC and overcome therapy resistance. Modulation of intratumoral cholesterol metabolism through delivery of a microbiota-derived metabolite is shown to induce colorectal cancer regression in mice.

item.title: [1.9] RSK2 and β-Trcp-mediated ubiquitination of FOXN3 impairs DNA damage and confers radioresistance in lung cancer
item.description:
Aberrant DNA damage responses can result in genomic instability, thereby affecting the efficacy of radiotherapy. The transcription factor FOXN3 plays critical roles in cellular growth and proliferation, inflammation, and the response to injury; however, its involvement in lung cancer radioresistance remains unclear. Here, we revealed that reduced expression of FOXN3 was correlated with poor prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma patients and that FOXN3 depletion impaired the DNA damage response, thereby conferring radioresistance in lung cancer. Mechanistically, FOXN3 promoted BRCA1 transcription by binding to the BRCA1 promoter region, thereby increasing DNA damage. Furthermore, the protein kinase RSK2 and E3 ubiquitin ligase β-Trcp collaboratively interacted with FOXN3, facilitating its ubiquitination-mediated degradation via a conserved DSGYAS motif. Importantly, this cooperative degradation of FOXN3 attenuated DNA damage and promoted radioresistance in lung cancer cells. Our study provides a mechanistic foundation for targeting FOXN3-related pathways as a potential strategy to overcome radioresistance in lung cancer.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] Na+/Ca2+ exchanger 1 (NCX1) drives migration and vasculogenic mimicry in mesenchymal glioblastoma
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor characterized by diffuse invasion, marked cellular plasticity, and poor prognosis, particularly in the mesenchymal subtype. The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger 1 (NCX1) has been implicated in glioblastoma motility, but its role in patient-derived mesenchymal GBM and vasculogenic mimicry (VM) remains unclear. Here, we investigated NCX1 function in GBM19, a primary mesenchymal glioblastoma stem cell-enriched culture. GBM19 cells displayed coordinated migration and formed Vascular Endothelial (VE)-cadherin-positive loop-like structures consistent with VM, whereas leading-edge cells showed a more migratory phenotype. NCX1 was enriched at the migratory front and was functionally active in both leading-edge and loop cells, as demonstrated by patch-clamp recordings and pharmacological inhibition with bepridil. NCX1 blockade impaired wound closure, disrupted actin organization, altered cell polarity and directional migration, reduced spheroid invasion, and prevented proper loop formation and closure. In vivo, VM-like tumor structures were positive for NCX1 and VE-cadherin. Transcriptomic analysis further showed a positive correlation between NCX1 and the VM-related regulator E74-like factor 2 (ELF2) specifically in mesenchymal GBM, where high ELF2 expression was associated with worse survival. These findings identify NCX1 as a regulator of migration and vasculogenic mimicry in mesenchymal glioblastoma and support its potential as a therapeutic target in aggressive GBM.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.7] B3GNT9-mediated O-glycosylation reprograms fatty acid metabolism in peroxisomes to promote invasion progression of peritumoral glioma cells
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor characterized by rapid recurrence and invasion, particularly in the peritumoral brain zone (PBZ), a critical site for tumor spread. Through RNA-seq of tumor core and PBZ tissues from GBM patients, we identified B3GNT9 as significantly upregulated in tumor cells within the PBZ. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that elevated B3GNT9 expression is associated with poor prognosis. Functional studies in glioblastoma cell lines, patient-derived cells, and animal models showed that B3GNT9 overexpression promotes cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Mechanistically, RNA-seq and in vitro experiments demonstrated that B3GNT9 enhances glioma invasiveness by regulating the fatty acid metabolism gene ACOX1. Quantitative proteomics further identified PPARD as a key transcription factor mediating the B3GNT9-ACOX1 signaling axis. B3GNT9 increases mucin-type O-glycosylation in glioblastoma cells, facilitating O-GalNAc glycosylation of PPARD, which enhances its transcriptional activity and drives ACOX1 expression. High-throughput metabolomics and cellular, organoid, and animal studies revealed that activation of the B3GNT9–PPARD–ACOX1 axis reduces intracellular eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) levels, promoting GBM invasiveness. These findings highlight the critical role of B3GNT9 and O-glycosylation in GBM progression, suggesting that targeting the B3GNT9–PPARD–ACOX1 axis could offer a promising therapeutic strategy to suppress GBM invasion and recurrence.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.7] EWSR1::ATF1 hyperactivation via TRIM11 depletion triggers lethal metabolic rewiring in clear cell sarcoma
item.description:
Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is an ultra-rare and aggressive soft tissue sarcoma driven by the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion oncoprotein. Currently, no effective and well-tolerated treatment options are available to CCS patients. Direct inhibition of fusion transcription factors is precluded by the absence of defined ligand-binding pockets, whereas their abundance is under the control of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), offering an alternative avenue for biology-guided treatment. Here we show the abundance of EWSR1::ATF1 is tightly regulated by the UPS, and that release of this constraint is lethal to CCS cells. A reporter-based CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen of UPS components identified TRIM11 as an E3 ligase that regulates turnover of EWSR1::ATF1, which it recognises as a neosubstrate without altering wild-type EWSR1 or ATF1. Depletion of TRIM11 increased nuclear fusion protein abundance, amplified the fusion-driven transcriptional programs and reduced viability. Proteomic analysis identified the cataplerotic enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1), a direct EWSR1::ATF1 target, as the key mediator of lethal effects of fusion hyperactivation. Extracellular flux analysis, isotope tracing and quantitative metabolomics revealed excessive cataplerotic carbon withdrawal and impaired oxidative phosphorylation as the underlying mechanism. In patient tumors, high PCK1 expression associated with metastatic transcriptome programs and disease presentation, as well as shorter survival. Taken together, we report that hyperactivation of EWSR1::ATF1 opens a metabolic vulnerability, establishing TRIM11 as an actionable dependency and PCK1 as a candidate prognostic biomarker in CCS.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.0] Ultra-low-dose same-target combinations control drug resistance across stages
item.description:
The emergence of drug resistance continues to limit the long term effectiveness of cancer therapies [1], as tumour cells adapt to therapeutic selective pressure through diverse genetic and non-genetic routes [2,3]. Despite advances in more potent and next generation inhibitors and mechanism based combination therapies [4,5], durable disease control remains difficult to achieve. Here we tested an alternative strategy: combining multiple inhibitors directed against the same oncogenic driver, each at ultra low doses with minimal individual activity, to delay resistance emergence. In epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) driven cancer models, such ultra low dose same target combinations (ULDCs) distributed individually weak perturbations across multiple inhibitors directed against the same target and achieved substantial growth inhibition in vitro and antitumour activity in vivo despite weak effects of the corresponding single agents. Under similar levels of growth inhibition (~50%), single-agent EGFR inhibitors generated resistant outgrowth, whereas a five drug ULDC delayed resistance emergence. Increasing the number of inhibitors further delayed resistance emergence, with no detectable resistant outgrowth observed for combinations containing 8 to 14 inhibitors within the experimental timeframe. The five drug ULDC also retained measurable growth inhibitory activity against gefitinib resistant PC-9/GR cells, and resistant cells arising under five drug ULDC treatment exhibited markedly greater reversibility following drug withdrawal than those arising under single agent treatment. Although pharmacological additivity or synergy may contribute to the collective growth inhibitory effects of ULDCs, the divergent long term resistance outcomes observed under similar levels of growth inhibition indicate that resistance behaviour is not determined by inhibitory strength alone. Instead, our findings support a model in which increasing same target inhibitor diversity progressively constrains the adaptive trajectories available during resistance evolution, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states that emerge. More broadly, these findings support the concept of same target collective suppression, in which multiple individually weak perturbations directed against the same target can collectively produce substantial antitumour activity and constrain resistance evolution across multiple stages. We propose that increasing same target inhibitor diversity may restrict accessible adaptive trajectories, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.4] Developing a Multimodal miR-15a Mimic to Overcome Gemcitabine and RAS(ON) Inhibitor Daraxonrasib Resistance in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
item.description:
Gemcitabine remains a mainstay of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) treatment, while the RAS(ON) inhibitor daraxonrasib has recently demonstrated improved survival in previously treated metastatic disease. However, acquired resistance to both therapies remains a major clinical challenge. Here, we developed MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a, a multimodal microRNA (miRNA)-based therapeutic, by chemically modifying tumor-suppressive miR-15a with methotrexate (MTX), 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), and gemcitabine (Gem) to combine sequence-specific gene regulation with disruption of nucleotide metabolism. MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a exhibited low-nanomolar potency across five PDAC cell lines and retained activity in gemcitabine- and daraxonrasib-resistant models under vehicle-free conditions, substantially exceeding that of stoichiometrically matched free antimetabolites. Treatment induced S-phase accumulation, increased DNA damage and apoptosis, and suppressed checkpoint and survival-associated proteins, including WEE1, CHK1, YAP1, and BCL-2. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed increased DNA replication, replication-stress, and repair-associated programs, together with reduced oncogenic signaling. In gemcitabine-resistant cells, treatment restored the gemcitabine-activating enzyme dCK, reduced ABCC1 and ABCC3 expression, and suppressed resistance-associated signaling programs, indicating partial remodeling of resistance-associated pathways. MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a also synergized with daraxonrasib (mean Bliss synergy score, 22.52) and activated tumor-cell-intrinsic STING-TBK1 signaling, accompanied by increased interferon stimulated gene expression and IFN-{beta} and CXCL10 secretion. Finally, MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a retained low-nanomolar potency in three patient-derived PDAC organoids and significantly suppressed metastatic tumor growth in vivo at 4 mg/kg. Together, these findings support a multimodal miRNA therapeutic strategy that combines replication-associated DNA damage, checkpoint protein suppression, and innate immune activation-associated responses to target therapeutic resistance in PDAC.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.0] Miniaturized Traceless Staudinger Ligation Enables Direct-to-Biology Screening of Potent BRD4 PROTACs
item.description:
Direct-to-biology (D2B) approaches accelerate PROTAC discovery by enabling biological screening of crude reaction mixtures without intermediate purification. However, the range of chemical transformations compatible with these workflows remains limited. Herein, we establish a miniaturized, base-free traceless Staudinger ligation platform diversifying linker chemistry for a preexisting library of E3-ligand-linker adducts bearing azide moieties. As a proof-of-concept target, BRD4 was chosen, yielding amide-linked BRD4-targeting PROTACs. By combining phosphine-functionalized JQ1 derivatives with 72 selected azide building blocks, reactions were performed on a 5 L scale in 384-well plates, achieving a mean LC-MS conversion of approximately 65%. Spiking experiments confirmed that the phosphine starting materials had no significant impact on BRD4 degradation, supporting the direct biological evaluation of crude reaction mixtures in the presence of residual starting material. Cellular screening identified 23 hits at 250 nM screening concentration, reducing BRD4 levels below 40%. Two resynthesized and purified PROTACs were subsequently validated, displaying pDC50 values of 8.2 and 7.0 and a Dmax of 90% and 96%, respectively. This work establishes traceless Staudinger ligation as a complementary D2B strategy for the rapid discovery of amide-linked PROTACs.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [2.2] ZNF598 promotes glioblastoma progression and temozolomide resistance by facilitating MFN1-mediated mitochondrial quality control
item.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor and frequently develops intrinsic or acquired resistance to temozolomide (TMZ). Mitochondrial quality control (MQC) is essential for tumor cell survival and therapeutic adaptation, yet its upstream regulatory mechanisms in GBM remain poorly defined. Here, we identify zinc finger protein 598 (ZNF598), an E3 ubiquitin ligase with RNA-binding capacity, as a critical regulator of MQC and TMZ resistance in GBM. Analysis of public datasets revealed that ZNF598 expression is significantly elevated in TMZ-resistant GBM cells and human glioma tissues, correlating with adverse patient prognosis. Functionally, ZNF598 knockdown suppressed GBM cell proliferation, induced apoptosis, and disrupted mitochondrial homeostasis, as reflected by reduced ATP production and mtDNA copy numbers, elevated reactive oxygen species, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitochondrial fragmentation. ZNF598 silencing suppressed tumor growth in subcutaneous and intracranial orthotopic xenograft models and markedly enhanced TMZ sensitivity in vitro and in subcutaneous xenografts. Mechanistically, ZNF598 associated with mitofusin 1 (MFN1) mRNA and maintained its stability, thereby sustaining MFN1 expression and MFN1-mediated mitochondrial fusion. Notably, this regulation was independent of the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of ZNF598, as the catalytically inactive ZNF598C29A mutant restored MFN1 mRNA stability, MFN1 protein abundance, and mitochondrial function in ZNF598-depleted cells. Restoration of MFN1 partially rescued mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis induced by ZNF598 knockdown. Furthermore, screening of the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer dataset identified the BET inhibitor RVX208, which rapidly reduced ZNF598 mRNA and protein levels, phenocopied the mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis caused by ZNF598 suppression, and increased TMZ responsiveness at least partly through ZNF598 downregulation. These findings establish ZNF598 as a pivotal upstream regulator of MFN1-mediated MQC and a key determinant of TMZ response in GBM, highlighting the ZNF598–MFN1 axis as a promising therapeutic target for overcoming TMZ resistance.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.5] Conditional biologics in cancer immunotherapy: mechanisms, applications and clinical progress
item.description:
Immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment, enabling durable responses and long-term survival in many patients. However, widespread use remains limited by refractory indications, immune-related toxicities and acquired resistance. Complications such as cytokine release syndrome, immune-related adverse events, infusion-related reactions and on-target, off-tumour toxicities have emerged as specific safety concerns. Approaches that can direct immunotherapy to the tumour microenvironment (TME), such as intratumoural administration, have only partially mitigated these risks and present additional logistical and technical barriers. Conditional biologics, in which proteins are engineered to become active in response to tumour-associated signals or in the TME, enable the uncoupling of efficacy from toxicity. By enhancing tumour accumulation, targeting activity to a particular cell type and minimizing off-target effects, conditional activation offers a potential strategy to expand the therapeutic window of cancer therapeutics. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms, applications, challenges and future directions of this approach, while assessing completed and ongoing clinical trials. Conditional biologics (CBs) — protein therapeutics engineered to selectively activate within the tumour microenvironment — have the potential to increase the potency and limit the off-target adverse effects of cancer immunotherapies. This Review describes the design principles and activation mechanisms of CBs, assesses those being investigated in the clinic, and addresses ongoing challenges and future directions for the field.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] Mechanosensitive YAP–RUNX1 signaling drives TH1 cell dysfunction and tumor immunosuppression
item.description:
Tissue stiffening is a predominant malignant physical alteration in cancer progression, yet its effect on specific immune subsets within the tumor microenvironment is not well defined. Here we show that elevated tissue stiffness subverts tumor-infiltrating type 1 helper T (TH1) cells to drive immunosuppression in pancreatic cancer. Mechanistically, stiffness triggers integrin-mediated mechanotransduction to activate YAP, which translocates to the nucleus and cooperates with RUNX1 to transcriptionally upregulate a set of dysfunction-associated genes. These reprogrammed TH1 cells acquire a distinct dysfunction-associated secretory phenotype, which in turn drives M2-like polarization of macrophages and amplifies local immunosuppression. Notably, inhibiting YAP expression or disrupting YAP–RUNX1 interaction reverses the dysfunctional state of TH1 cells and restores antitumor immunity. These findings delineate a mechano–immunological mechanism by which tumor stiffness subverts TH1 cell functions, indicating a possible therapeutic avenue to alleviate immunosuppression and potentiate immunotherapy efficacy in stiff tumors. Solid tumor stiffness can limit the ability of immune cells to enter and kill tumor cells. Here the authors show that this stiffness activates YAP signaling in type 1 helper T cells, making them dysfunctional and thereby leading to a more immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.0] E2F1 signatures stratify immunotherapy response and reveal YWHAQ vulnerability in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
item.description:
To improve biological interpretation of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) response in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), we developed an E2F1 transcriptional regulation-related framework integrating spatial multi-omics and experimental validation. Single-cell and post-treatment spatial analyses localized E2F1-associated activity predominantly to malignant epithelial states. In ten ESCC Xenium specimens, paired patient-level analyses linked E2F1-high epithelial neighborhoods to lower CD8 effector T-cell and B-cell densities, a lower immune-active niche score, and higher epithelial CD274-positive fractions. In harmonized public ICI cohorts, E2F1.Sig functioned as an exploratory response-stratification signature, achieving the highest mean area under the curve (AUC) among evaluated immune signatures across validation and external testing cohorts. Separately, TCGA analyses supported prognostic associations of a 20-gene Hub-E2F1.Sig risk score. In ESCC, Hub-E2F1.Sig-based subtyping defined three immune microenvironmental states with distinct survival patterns. Cluster1 showed a more favorable immune contexture and better prognosis, suggesting its association with immune responsiveness. YWHAQ, a key Hub-E2F1.Sig gene, was associated with poor prognosis, and YWHAQ depletion reduced malignant phenotypes, increased cisplatin-associated apoptosis, and attenuated PD-1/PD-L1-associated immunosuppressive features in vitro and in vivo. Virtual screening identified 6’-Sialyllactose as an in silico candidate YWHAQ-binding compound. These findings support an exploratory E2F1-centered framework and nominate YWHAQ as an ESCC-focused therapeutic hypothesis.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.5] Redox, lipid, and metabolic changes associated with early tolerance to combination chemotherapy in two pancreatic cancer cell models
item.description:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) shows limited responsiveness to chemotherapy and rapidly develops resistance, which can be facilitated by early adaptive tolerance to sub-lethal drug exposure. Here, we investigated changes associated with the development of early tolerance to a chemotherapy combination analogous in composition to FOLFIRINOX in MIA PaCa-2 and PANC-1 cells using a stepwise adaptation approach. Comparison of metabolic similarities and divergences between the two cell lines by dose-response analysis revealed limited, yet progressive and cell-specific, shiftsin drug sensitivity. At the consolidated stage, Nile Red imaging and targeted lipidomics revealed cell line-specific lipid remodeling, including elongation of membrane phospholipid acyl chains in both lines. PANC-1 cells show increased saturation of phosphatidylcholine and triacylglycerols and reduced polyunsaturation of phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine. Antioxidant profiling also shows model-dependent patterns: MIA PaCa-2 cells exhibit increased total catalase, total glutathione S-transferase, and glutathione reductase activities, whereas PANC-1 cells show reduced catalase activity together with increased total glutathione S-transferase activity. These changes are accompanied by increased cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidation-dependent fluorescence in MIA PaCa-2 cells and reduced mitochondrial oxidation-dependent fluorescence in PANC-1 cells. MIA PaCa-2 cells also showed reduced extracellular lactate production, while cellular energy charge remained unchanged in both models. Whether these adaptations can be exploited therapeutically remains to be tested; they nevertheless identify redox- and lipid-related pathways as candidates for functional studies aimed at preventing the transition from tolerance to stable resistance.

item.title: [1.8] Development of quinoline derivatives as dual EGFR/HDAC-2 inhibitors: design, synthesis, anticancer evaluation, and molecular dynamics simulations
item.description:
The quinoline scaffold is widely exploited in the design of new anticancer candidates. As a continuation of our previous work in the search for promising anticancer candidates, we designed novel quinoline-based compounds linked to a range of heterocyclic rings by applying a molecular hybridization strategy. In this work, the resulting quinoline derivatives were synthesized and evaluated for their anti-proliferative activity against three cancer cell lines, namely PC-3, HCT-116, and MDA-MB-231, in addition to one normal cell line, WI-38. Among these compounds, two derivatives (4) and (11) showed potent anti-proliferative activity against MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells with IC₅₀ values of 4.91 and 8.25 µM, respectively. The same two derivatives also showed significant activity against the HCT-116 colon cancer cell line with IC₅₀ values of 6.38 and 9.44 µM, respectively. Mechanistic studies further showed that compound (4) potently inhibited EGFRWT (IC₅₀ = 0.084 µM) and mutant EGFR forms, as well as HDAC-2 with IC50 = 0.123 µM. All biological assays were performed in three independent experiments (n = 3), and all reported differences versus the untreated control were significant at a two-sided adjusted P < 0.05. Additionally, western blot analysis of compound (4) revealed downregulation of pEGFR, pERK, and pAKT, while RT-qPCR analysis showed upregulation of BAX and caspase-3, -7, and − 9 and downregulation of BCL-2 at the mRNA level. Cell-cycle analysis showed that derivative (4) induced arrest at the G1/S boundary. Taken together, all these results, along with molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations, supported the stable binding within the ATP-binding site of EGFR and the zinc-binding pocket of HDAC-2.

item.title: [1.7] Histone lysine demethylases in the third decade: biology and therapeutic prospects
item.description:
Histone post-translational modifications, such as methylation, acetylation, phosphorylation and ubiquitination, have fundamental roles in regulating chromatin structure and gene expression. Histone methylation was once considered a static modification until the discovery of the histone lysine demethylase LSD1 (KDM1A), more than two decades ago. Since then, numerous KDMs in two main enzyme classes have been identified. Their diverse roles in regulating gene expression, metabolism, immune responses and disease pathogenesis have been extensively studied and small-molecule inhibitors have been developed. KDMs exert context-dependent functions as either oncogenes or tumour suppressors, which complicates their therapeutic targeting. As we enter the third decade of investigations into histone demethylation, unlocking the full therapeutic potential of inhibiting KDMs will require a deeper understanding of their biology, substrate specificity, interaction networks and regulatory crosstalk. In this Review, we discuss the functions of KDMs in metabolic and immune regulation and their roles in cancer and other diseases. We describe the landscape of KDM inhibitors, especially LSD1 inhibitors, which are the most advanced demethylase inhibitors in clinical trials. We highlight the need for more potent and selective KDM inhibitors, biomarkers of therapeutic response, novel combinatorial treatments and innovative drug discovery strategies. Histone lysine demethylases regulate gene expression and chromatin structure and help to integrate epigenetics with metabolic and immune responses. This Review discusses the diverse contributions of these demethylases to disease pathogenesis, particularly cancer, and the efforts underway to target them with small molecules.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.7] EGF and EREG regulate early oncoprotein-mediated tissue transformation in intestinal organoids.
item.description:
Somatic mutations, coupled with abnormal extracellular signaling cues, promote tumor development. The abundance and affinity of EGF-family ligands for EGFR influence tissue development and play a central role in organoid culture by differentially regulating the balance between crypt proliferation and villus differentiation in mouse small intestinal organoids (mSIOs). To test how medium ligand composition affects early oncogenic transformation, we generated a Ptprg KO organoid line by CRISPR/Cas9 and two previously described organoid lines harboring synthetic bio-orthogonal expression systems for KRASG12V and {beta}-Ctn4A, activated by the membrane-diffusible ligands TMP or TMP-Cl. Measurements of crypt and villus region area showed that acute oncogenic activity did not alter organoid growth in media containing 50 ng/mL EGF; however, organoids grown without EGF consistently showed differential growth of the crypt region. Furthermore, EREG and sub-saturating EGF (0.5-5 ng/mL) treatments differentially affected crypt/villus development in each organoid line. Finally, we measured organoid morphology and found that crypt domain spatial distribution is independent of crypt area and requires EGF or EREG, highlighting the role of both proliferation and crypt organization in oncogenic tissue transformation.
