item.title: [2.5] Targeting mutant p53 aggregates in pancreatic cancer using an autophagy-targeting chimera
item.description:
Protein aggregation is increasingly recognized as a fundamental feature of cancer biology, particularly in tumors experiencing chronic proteotoxic stress. TP53 is one of the most frequently mutated genes in human cancers, and many cancer-associated missense mutations promote p53 misfolding and amyloid-like aggregation. These aggregates impair wild-type tumor-suppressive functions while conferring oncogenic gain-of-function (GOF) activities that promote tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. Despite decades of effort, direct pharmacological targeting of mutant p53 has remained challenging because of its structural properties, including the lack of a readily druggable pocket, as well as its extensive mutational heterogeneity. Here, we employed the AUTOTAC platform to target mutant p53 aggregates by exploiting aggregation-associated conformational features characteristic of β-sheet-rich oligomers and protofibrillar aggregates. ATC-37 was designed by linking a methylene blue-derived amyloid-binding ligand, which preferentially recognizes β-sheet-rich protein aggregates, to an autophagy-targeting ligand (ATL) that allosterically activates the autophagy receptor p62/SQSTM1. This design enables engagement of amyloid-like mutant p53 aggregates and promotes their recruitment to autophagosomes. ATC-37 exhibits a dual, concentration-dependent mechanism of action. At low concentrations, it promotes autophagic degradation of mutant p53 aggregates and suppresses downstream GOF signaling. At higher concentrations, it induces p62-dependent sequestration of mutant p53 aggregates that exceeds autophagic capacity, leading to proteotoxic cell death. In a PANC-1 pancreatic cancer xenograft model, ATC-37 significantly inhibited tumor growth, reduced amyloid-like mutant p53 aggregates, and attenuated mutant p53-associated GOF programs. Importantly, ATC-37 also enhanced the response of mutant p53 pancreatic cancer cells to radiation, suggesting potential utility in combination with radiotherapy. These findings establish aggregation-state-directed AUTOTAC therapy as a conceptually innovative, mutation-agnostic strategy for targeting aggregation-prone mutant p53 and potentially other aggregation-prone oncoproteins.

item.title: [1.5] CD3ε F(ab’)₂ PET imaging captures systemic and intratumoral T-cell response to immune checkpoint blockade
item.description:
Immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment, yet only a subset of patients achieve durable responses. Because the spatial distribution of T cells within tumors and lymphoid tissues shapes therapeutic outcomes, noninvasive methods capable of monitoring these populations could improve the evaluation of antitumor immune responses. Here, we report the validation of a CD3ε-targeted F(ab’)2 positron emission tomography (PET) probe for noninvasive mapping of T-lymphocytes across tumors and lymphoid tissues and characterize its effects on endogenous T-cell biology. Relative to the full-length IgG construct, the F(ab’)2 format demonstrated more rapid blood clearance, enabled high-contrast imaging within 24 h, produced limited changes in endogenous T-cell populations, and did not measurably impair T-cell activation at imaging-relevant concentrations. CD3ε F(ab’)2 PET detected tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and lymphocytes within the tumor-draining lymph nodes (TDLN) across multiple syngeneic tumor models and in a genetically engineered mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma. In a combination immunotherapy study, tumor uptake distinguished responding from non-responding lesions and detected treatment-associated changes across peripheral lymphoid tissues. These results support CD3ε F(ab’)2 PET as a noninvasive imaging approach that enables assessment of T-cell distribution during tumor growth and therapy, with potential applications in mechanistic studies, biomarker development, and preclinical evaluation of immunomodulatory therapies.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.1] Phosphorylation-driven targeted protein degradation of oncogenic β-catenin
item.description:
Therapeutic strategies to inhibit the Wnt signaling pathway for cancer treatment have, so far, failed to advance to the clinic. Induced-proximity drugs are revolutionizing our ability to tackle targets previously considered undruggable. Here, we use an unbiased genome-scale approach to identify induced-proximity protein candidates that inhibit the central Wnt signaling effector β-catenin in colorectal cancer cells. While the identification of several E3 ubiquitin ligases validates our approach, we uncover that inducing proximity to members of the Casein kinase I (CSNK1) family leads to β-catenin degradation and inhibits the growth of colorectal cancer cells harboring Wnt pathway mutations. We show that β-catenin degradation induced by CSNK1 proximity is kinase activity- and proteasome-dependent. We propose that the formation of a neo-degron, through kinase recruitment, can expand induced-proximity drug targeting strategies. Wolf et al. used proteome-scale induced-proximity screens for inhibitors of the oncogene β-catenin in colorectal cancer and discovered induced kinase-dependent degradation as an expansion of the Targeted Protein Degradation concept.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.1] The methionine cycle sustains the mesenchymal phenotype of tumor cells and drives PDA progression
item.description:
Mesenchymal traits are associated with poor prognosis in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDA), but direct targeting of mesenchymal tumor cells remains a challenge. Metabolic profiling of tumor cells isolated from murine PDA and liver metastases (LM) revealed that LM rely more on the methionine cycle than does primary PDA. This metabolic shift was specifically associated with increased activation of the methionine cycle in mesenchymal tumor cells compared to differentiated tumor cells. We show that the targeting of the key enzyme of the methionine cycle S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase (SAHH) in mesenchymal cells lowers the levels of homocysteine (Hcy) and glutathione, resulting in reduced antioxidant capacity, deregulated intracellular calcium homeostasis, and ultimately loss of mesenchymal markers. Together, these events decrease cell proliferation and invasion, blunting the tumorigenic and metastatic potential of SAHH-deficient cells, eventually impeding tumor growth and progression of the metastatic disease. Clinically, the high expression of SAHH in patients with mesenchymal PDA is correlated with poor survival, positioning SAHH as a potential therapeutic target to impede the pro-metastatic, mesenchymal phenotype of PDA.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.5] Computational discovery of lead natural compounds targeting the HPV16 E6–E6AP–p53 interaction
item.description:
Human papillomavirus type 16 (HPV16) contributes to malignant progression by recruiting host E6-associated protein (E6AP), which facilitates ubiquitin-mediated degradation of the tumor suppressor protein p53.This study employed an integrated computational strategy to screen natural compounds for their potential to bind HPV16 E6 binding pocket and disrupt​ its interaction with the E6AP, thereby potentially preserving p53 function. The HPV16 E6–E6AP–p53 complex (PDB ID: 4XR8) was retrieved, assessed for structural quality, and analyzed for binding pocket identification. GO and KEGG were performed to explore associated biological functions and pathways. Pharmacophore-based virtual screening and molecular docking were conducted to screen high-affinity compounds, followed by ADMET, toxicity prediction, density functional theory (DFT) analysis, and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation. Finally, protein–ligand interactions were analyzed to characterize key binding residues. Functional enrichment analysis indicated that the E6–E6AP–p53 gene set is associated with apoptosis, DNA damage response, and viral carcinogenesis pathways. Structural validation showed acceptable stereochemical and structural quality metrics. Pharmacophore-based screening of ​511 natural compounds followed by molecular docking identified several molecules with favorable binding affinities (−​11.0 to −​11.7 kcal/mol). The six top-ranked compounds were then filtered by ADME and toxicity predictions, and C-12 and C-17 were prioritized because they combined high docking affinity (−​11.4 kcal/mol) with acceptable pharmacokinetic properties and safety profiles. Interaction analysis confirmed stable binding within the E6–E6AP–p53 pocket. DFT calculations revealed that C-17 exhibited the smallest HOMO–LUMO energy gap compared with the luteolin and C-12, indicating a distinct electronic profile. Molecular dynamics and MM-GBSA analyses indicated greater stability and a more favorable binding free energy for C-17, followed by C-12, over the reference inhibitor, luteolin. Overall, C-12 and C-17 emerged as promising candidates for inhibiting the E6–E6AP–p53 interaction, which may help restore p53 function in HPV-driven tumor biology, and warrant further experimental validation.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] In situ CAR engineering and nanoparticle-mediated TREM2 degradation for macrophage reprogramming in malignant ascites
item.description:
Peritoneal metastasis (PM) and the resulting malignant tumour ascites characterize advanced gastrointestinal cancers, often leading to poor prognosis and limited response to current therapies. Single-cell analysis of patient-derived PM and malignant tumour ascites reveals an approximately 90% enrichment of TREM2+-tumour-associated macrophages, which drive CD8+ T cell dysfunction and tumour growth. Here we develop lipid nanoparticles encapsulating mRNA to reprogram these tumour-associated macrophages into chimeric antigen receptor macrophages targeting Claudin18.2-positive tumour ascites. The lipid nanoparticles incorporate a TREM2+ ligand to enhance the targeting of TREM2 macrophages. The piperazine-containing phosphoramide ionizable lipid synergizes with the TREM2 ligand to inhibit ligand dissociation, promoting TREM2 internalization and degradation via lysosomal and autophagosomal pathways. This inhibits AKT signalling and reprograms tumour-associated macrophages towards an antitumour phenotype, enhancing progenitor exhausted and effector memory CD8+ T cell responses, altering the PM transcriptome, and reducing immunosuppression in both malignant tumour ascites and tumours. Combined with PD-1 blockade, this therapy suppresses tumour growth and extends survival in mice, and with matching immunological effects in clinical samples, demonstrates its translational potential for PM immunotherapy. Targeted lipid nanoparticles reprogram TREM2+-tumour-associated macrophages in ascitic fluid into chimeric antigen receptor macrophage cells, providing an in situ cell engineering strategy that alters the tumour microenvironment and promotes tumour cell elimination in rodent models.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] Targeting REV1 Exposes Context-Dependent Therapeutic Responses in Colorectal Cancer
item.description:
Translesion synthesis (TLS) promotes DNA damage tolerance and contributes to chemotherapy resistance by enabling replication across damaged DNA templates. REV1, a central TLS regulator, is a potential therapeutic target to enhance the efficacy of genotoxic chemotherapy. Here, we investigated the therapeutic consequences of pharmacologic and genetic REV1 targeting in colorectal cancer (CRC) and evaluated the sensitivity of patient-derived CRC organoids to the REV1 inhibitor JH-RE-06. JH-RE-06 enhanced oxaliplatin sensitivity in HCT116 cells and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) sensitivity in HT-29 cells, whereas reciprocal combinations produced limited sensitization, indicating treatment- and cellular context-dependent responses. siRNA-mediated REV1 depletion similarly enhanced chemotherapy sensitivity, supporting REV1 involvement in these responses. MNNG sensitivity assays and MLH1 expression analyses did not reveal consistent treatment-associated changes in mismatch repair function, while targeted HPRT1 sequencing identified no detectable sequence alterations in the region examined. Chemosensitization was not accompanied by consistent increases in caspase-3/7 activation under the conditions tested. REV1 inhibition also caused LC3-II accumulation and, after prolonged inhibitor exposure, reduced beta-tubulin abundance, indicating additional autophagy-associated and cytoskeletal responses. In two patient-derived CRC organoid models, JH-RE-06 exhibited single-agent growth-inhibitory activity, with mean IC50 values of 2.01 micromolar and 1.4 micromolar, respectively. Together, these findings demonstrate context-dependent chemosensitization and organoid growth inhibition following REV1 targeting, suggesting that its therapeutic consequences may extend beyond canonical TLS-mediated DNA damage tolerance.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] Arrest-associated transcriptional programmes outweigh apoptosis-associated programmes in treatment-naive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
item.description:
Background: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is driven by mutant KRAS, and RAS inhibitors now extend survival in previously treated metastatic disease. Whether treatment shrinks a tumour or only halts its growth depends partly on whether cancer cells die or stop dividing, yet how untreated PDAC cells are balanced between these programmes is unknown. Aims: We aimed to characterise the balance between apoptosis-associated and arrest-associated transcriptional programmes in treatment-naive PDAC and to examine their relationships with tumour subtype, TGM2 expression, tissue organisation, survival and drug sensitivity. Methods and results: We scored 52,999 malignant cells from 18 untreated patients in the Hwang atlas using a transcriptional contrast between genes associated with apoptosis and genes associated with resistance to apoptosis or cell-cycle arrest. In every patient the contrast was shifted toward the arrest-associated side: using equality between the two sides as the dividing threshold, 86.3% of cells with an informative score fell on that side, although the proportion depends on the threshold chosen. The shift recurred in the independent Steele atlas (median 71.6% per sample, range 37.1% to 90.8%). In the discovery cohort, tumours with higher basal-like scores had fewer arrest-side cells, and TGM2 expression was modestly higher on the arrest-associated side in both cohorts. The contrast did not track cell-line drug sensitivity or survival in bulk tumours. Conclusion: Untreated PDAC cells show a reproducible transcriptional bias toward anti-apoptotic and cell-cycle-arrest programmes. Whether this bias predicts cellular responses to treatment remains to be tested.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.6] Quantitative live imaging reveals region-dependent medulloblastoma disseminationin the zebrafish brain
item.description:
Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor, and relapse is frequently driven by dissemination within the central nervous system. Yet the early dynamics of tumor spread remain difficult to resolve in vivo. Here, we orthotopically transplanted human medulloblastoma cells into larval zebrafish and followed individual xenografts by longitudinal high-resolution confocal imaging. ONS-76 showed particularly robust dissemination, with hindbrain tumors spreading into the developing cerebellum in 81.5% of larvae, more than fourfold the frequency observed for forebrain or midbrain tumors. Disseminating cells extended along brain-surface and leptomeningeal-like regions and frequently associated with cerebral vasculature. Quantitative analysis of tumor area, perimeter, compactness, convex hull area, and fractal dimension captured changes in growth and spatial complexity over time. Dasatinib reduced tumor expansion and dissemination-related features in a concentration-dependent manner, while higher doses revealed host toxicity. These findings establish a powerful in vivo model for resolving medulloblastoma dissemination and therapeutic response.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.8] WDR54 stabilizes the fatty acid transporter SLC43A3 via the deubiquitinase OTUB1 to drive HNSCC progression
item.description:
Metabolic reprogramming drives head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identify WDR54 as a critical oncogenic driver. Clinical analyses reveal WDR54 is overexpressed in HNSCC and correlates with poor patient survival. Mechanistically, WDR54 interacts with the deubiquitinase OTUB1, enhancing its capacity to deubiquitinate and stabilize the fatty acid transporter SLC43A3. This prevents SLC43A3 proteasomal degradation, inducing lipid metabolic reprogramming essential for HNSCC proliferation and invasion. Furthermore, pharmacological intervention with dihydroergotamine effectively disrupts this WDR54-OTUB1-SLC43A3 axis, significantly suppressing HNSCC tumor growth in vivo. Collectively, our findings elucidate a previously unrecognized signaling axis integrating protein deubiquitination with lipid metabolism, highlighting dihydroergotamine as a promising targeted therapeutic strategy for HNSCC.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.5] Acquired resistance to vorinostat in cutaneous T cell lymphoma involves augmented ERK phosphorylation
item.description:
Vorinostat is the first approved histone deacetylase inhibitor used in many countries for treating advanced cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL). However, prolonged application of this drug leads to the development of resistance, presenting a significant challenge to therapy. To better understand the mechanisms through which CTCL cells gain resistance, we established a vorinostat-resistant clone of the human CTCL line HuT78 (HuT78VR). HuT78VR cells exhibited enhanced drug efflux ability with increased expression of the drug efflux pumps ABCB1 and ABCG2. Employing an integrated transcriptomics and proteomics approach, we identified molecular signatures of vorinostat resistance. Specifically, HuT78VR cells presented increased expression of metastasis-related genes (LAIR2, VIM, MMP-9, IFNG, FASLG, CCND1, and CDKN1A) with increased cellular invasiveness and defective apoptosis. Further scrutiny of differentially expressed genes and proteins revealed the involvement of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling. In line with this, HuT78VR cells gained cross-resistance to inhibitors of histone deacetylase and topoisomerase but remained sensitive to inhibitors of MAPK/ERK. Ulixertinib, an ERK inhibitor, re-sensitized HuT78VR cells to vorinostat in vitro as well as in cell-derived xenografts in mice. These findings expand the understanding of vorinostat resistance in CTCL and suggest that ERK inhibition is an effective therapeutic approach to overcome vorinostat resistance.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.7] Lactylation couples glycolysis with cell cycle progression in cancer cells
item.description:
Aurora B is essential for mitotic progression, yet whether its activity is regulated by tumour metabolism remains unclear. Here we show that Aurora B functions as a sensor of glycolytic activity and is activated through lactate-dependent signalling. Mechanistically, increased lactate production during aerobic glycolysis promotes KAT2A-mediated lactylation of phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) at K131. Lactylated PGK1 phosphorylates Aurora B at T232, leading to cell cycle progression. Disruption of this pathway, either by expressing a PGK1 K131R mutant or a PGK1 variant defective in Aurora B binding, leads to mitotic defects and cGAS–STING activation. These effects suppress tumour cell proliferation and inhibit tumour growth in mice. Furthermore, combining a peptide that disrupts the PGK1–Aurora B interaction with anti-PD-1 therapy enhances CD8+ T-cell infiltration and produces synergistic anti-tumour effects. Collectively, these findings uncover a critical role of glycolysis in governing tumour cell division. This study shows that Aurora B activation by lactylated PGK1 links glycolysis to mitotic progression and immune evasion in cancer.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.6] Evaluation of treatment response in patients with recurrent grade 4 glioma using hyperpolarized [1-13C]pyruvate MRI
item.description:
Hyperpolarized (HP) [1-13C]pyruvate MRI allows for noninvasive assessment of dynamic metabolic activity in the brain and has potential for monitoring treatment response in gliomas. This exploratory study evaluated the ability of serial HP [1-13C]pyruvate MRI to detect treatment-related metabolism and evaluate early therapeutic response. Twenty patients with recurrent grade 4 glioma undergoing cytotoxic, antiangiogenic, and targeted chemotherapies underwent serial HP [1-13C]pyruvate MRI in conjunction with routine clinical MRI. Percentage changes were calculated from the group mean at each timepoint. The lactate/pyruvate ratio in the normal-appearing white matter (NAWM) increased by 14.3% at 1-month in the bevacizumab-treated group, whereas it decreased by 13.1% at 2-month in the everolimus-treated group. Within the T2-lesion, the NAWM-normalized lactate/pyruvate ratio increased by 24.3% in the bevacizumab-treated group and decreased by 7.6% in the everolimus-treated group. Among patients with shorter 6-month progression-free survival, the NAWM-normalized lactate/pyruvate increased by 18.2% from baseline to 2-month follow-up. This exploratory proof-of-feasibility study demonstrates that serial HP [1-¹³C]pyruvate MRI can detect measurable longitudinal metabolic changes in recurrent grade 4 glioma during treatment. Larger, prospective studies with more homogeneous treatment cohorts are needed to validate these observations and determine their clinical utility as imaging biomarkers of treatment response.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.7] MR imaging and spectroscopy reveals metabolic changes in glioblastoma driven by treatment with temozolomide and lonidamine
item.description:
Resistance to temozolomide (TMZ) limits the efficacy of treatment in glioblastoma (GBM) which is fuelled by a metabolic reprogramming of the cancer cells and alterations in the tumour microenvironment. Lonidamine (LND), a glycolytic and mitochondrial inhibitor, modulates tumour metabolism and can alter tumour response to treatment. This study investigated the effects of LND in combination with TMZ and used MR imaging and spectroscopy to evaluate metabolic and microstructural changes in a syngeneic GBM model. C57BL/6 mice bearing intracranial GL261 tumours (n = 66) were treated with saline, LND, TMZ, or LND + TMZ for five consecutive days. Longitudinal imaging (days 0, 3, 6) included T2-weighted MRI, diffusion weighted imaging (DWI), and conventional and lactate-edited ¹H-MRS. Tumour volume, survival, DWI parameters, MCT4 expression, and mitotic indices were assessed. In vitro, acute and chronic bioenergetic reprogramming of GL261 cells was assessed using the Seahorse extracellular flux analysis. Lactate is a not simply an end product of high glycolytic cancer cells, but it has also emerged as a molecule capable to shaping the tumour microenvironment. A significant decrease in lactate observed in the LND and LND + TMZ groups indicated a reduction in the steady-state lactate pool suggestive of reduced lactate production, utilization or altered glycolytic flux. However, lactate remained high in the control and TMZ-only groups. This metabolic shift in the LND treatment group was consistent with a marked reduction in MCT4 protein, the lactate transporter, in LND-treated tumours. In vitro bioenergetic profiling of GL261 cells revealed an acute decrease in mitochondrial respiration in response to LND, with partial recovery at later time points. Finally, even though not significant, an enhanced survival benefit of the treatment combination was observed, with no significant differences observed between the groups for tumour volume, DWI-derived parameters, or mitotic index after 6 days. LND induces early metabolic changes detectable by MRS. Although a limited therapeutic benefit of addition LND to TMZ was observed in the early stages of tumour development, its tumour-selective activity and effect on tumour microenvironment is promising and its long-term effects on tumour development should be investigated as part of an optimized combination strategy for TMZ treatment.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.5] Positional replication fork instability drives PARP inhibitor cytotoxicity
item.description:
Although poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) show promise for treating homologous recombination-deficient cancers, the observed PARPi hypersensitivity in additional genetic contexts expands their potential use in precision oncology. Yet, the DNA lesions driving PARPi-induced cytotoxicity remain poorly defined. Here we uncover distinct replication-fork lesions in specific genomic regions as key determinants of PARPi cytotoxicity. Using CRISPR screens, we identify that loss of replication-coupled cohesin acetyltransferase ESCO2 confers PARPi hypersensitivity independently of homologous recombination deficiency. Quantitative single-molecule imaging reveals that ESCO2 loss promotes accumulation of G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures at a subset of replication-associated sites, associated with PARP1 activation and engagement of fork protection factor TIMELESS to mitigate G4-induced stress. Notably, these G4 lesions localize to fragile pericentromeric regions and engage the G4 helicase DDX11. PARP inhibition disrupts this protective G4-processing response by preventing PARP1-dependent engagement of TIMELESS and DDX11, leading to G4 accumulation, DNA damage and chromosomal instability. Together, our findings define the G4–PARP1–TIMELESS–DDX11 axis as a critical safeguard of replication fork stability at hard-to-replicate loci and reveal ESCO2 as a therapeutic target for promoting synthetic lethality in PARPi-treated cancers. Through CRISPR screens and single-molecule imaging, Gupta et al. show that loss of the cohesion acetyltransferase ESCO2 leads to increased G-quadruplex formation at specific regions and drives PARP activation and PARPi hypersensitivity.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.3] ENPP1 inhibits the cGAS–STING pathway to mediate immune evasion in EGFR-TKI–resistant non–small cell lung cancer
item.description:
Third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as osimertinib, have demonstrated promising clinical efficacy in the treatment of EGFR-mutant non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Despite substantial progress with EGFR-TKIs, the development of acquired resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Notably, the addition of immune checkpoint blockade after TKI resistance has not resulted in significant survival benefits compared to chemotherapy. In this study, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis of established osimertinib-resistant tumor models and found that the expression of the ectonucleotide phosphodiesterase ENPP1, a key regulator of extracellular cGAMP signaling, was significantly upregulated in resistant tumors compared to the parental TKI-sensitive NSCLC tumors. Mechanistically, upregulated ENPP1 in resistant cells promoted the hydrolysis of extracellular cGAMP, suppressing the cGAS–STING pathway in immune cells and subsequently impairing immune cell activation and function, thereby promoting immune suppression and tumor progression. Genetic depletion or pharmacological inhibition of ENPP1 enhanced immune cell–mediated cytotoxicity against TKI-resistant tumor cells. Furthermore, the use of ENPP1 inhibitors both in vitro and in vivo enhanced immune cell activity and antitumor efficacy in TKI-resistant lung cancers with high ENPP1 expression. Importantly, these observations were further validated by paired clinical tumor samples, which demonstrated increased ENPP1 expression following the development of acquired EGFR-TKI resistance. Collectively, our study highlights a critical role for ENPP1 in mediating immune evasion through suppression of the cGAMP–STING pathway in the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting ENPP1 as a promising therapeutic target to enhance immunotherapy efficacy in EGFR-TKI–resistant NSCLC.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] Novel formula for improving the oral bioavailability of paclitaxel using P-glycoprotein inhibitors
item.description:
Paclitaxel (PCL), a taxane derivative with potent antimitotic properties, is ubiquitously utilized as a remedy for various cancers. PCL’s therapeutic utility via the oral route is limited by poor water solubility and low permeability, resulting in inadequate bioavailability. This limitation restricts the development of effective oral formulations, particularly for conditions such as gastric cancer. The current research aimed to evaluate the effects of P-glycoprotein (P-gp) inhibitors, specifically piperine (PIP) and silibinin (SBN), on the pharmacokinetic parameters of orally administered PCL. An in-silico drug-protein docking study was performed to evaluate interactions between PCL and selected P-gp inhibitors. PCL was administered orally at a dose of 40 mg/kg, either as a single treatment or in combination with PIP or SBN at 10, 20, and 40 mg/kg. Plasma samples were obtained at predetermined sampling intervals, followed by Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis using an H-ESI source. Compared with PCL administered alone, combination treatment significantly enhanced key pharmacokinetic indices, including peak plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration–time curve (AUC). After administration of PCL with 10 mg/kg of PIP 1.67 and 1.09 fold increases in Cmax and AUC, 20 mg/kg of PIP 1.79 and 1.16 fold increases in Cmax and AUC, and 40 mg/kg of PIP 2.04 and 1.51 fold increases in Cmax and AUC. After administration of PCL with 10 mg/kg of SBN 1.36 and 1.03 fold increases in Cmax and AUC, 20 mg/kg of SBN 1.73 and 1.69 fold increases in Cmax and AUC, and 40 mg/kg of SBN 2.29 and 2.22 fold increases in Cmax and AUC. Additionally, the elimination half-life (t1/2) of PCL was extended, indicating prolonged persistence of the drug in circulation. It can thus be concluded that PCL, along with PIP or SBN, exhibits increased absorption through P-gp modulation. These findings emphasise the promising potential of incorporating such bioenhancers into the development of effective oral PCL formulations to improve cancer therapy. An AGREE score (0.69) indicates the eco-friendliness of the bioanalytical method.

item.title: [1.6] USP14-mediated deubiquitination stabilizes integrin β1 to sustain malignant progression and chemotherapy resistance in osteosarcoma
item.description:
Osteosarcoma patients with metastasis or chemotherapy resistance typically have a poor prognosis, yet the precise mechanisms underlying these adverse clinical outcomes remain elusive. In this study, we analyzed tissue proteomic data from our osteosarcoma cohort to compare protein expression profiles between metastatic and non-metastatic cases, as well as subgroups with low versus high chemotherapy-induced tumor necrosis rates. Our clinical analyses revealed that elevated ubiquitin-specific protease 14 (USP14) expression was associated with lung metastasis, a lower tumor necrosis rate, and shorter overall survival. Functional experiments in vitro and in vivo demonstrated that USP14 knockdown robustly suppressed the proliferation and metastatic potential of osteosarcoma cells. Mechanistically, USP14 interacted with and stabilized integrin β1 via deubiquitination, thereby activating the FAK/SRC axis and inducing inhibitory  phosphorylation of GSK3β. This signaling cascade blocked β-catenin ubiquitin-dependent degradation to promote β-catenin accumulation, nuclear translocation, and subsequent activation of TCF/LEF-mediated transcription of downstream oncogenes, ultimately driving osteosarcoma progression. Moreover, chemotherapy upregulated USP14 expression, thereby promoting chemoresistance. Pharmacological inhibition of USP14 with IU1 synergistically enhanced the chemosensitivity of osteosarcoma cells to doxorubicin, effectively restraining tumor growth and metastasis. Collectively, our findings delineate a core USP14-driven oncogenic cascade governing osteosarcoma progression, highlighting USP14 as a promising therapeutic target to improve chemotherapy efficacy and clinical outcomes for osteosarcoma patients.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.7] Dingxiang Guanshitong suppresses ESCC progression by modulating TAK1/NF-κB/GLUT1-associated glycolytic reprogramming
item.description:
Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is a highly aggressive tumor with poor clinical outcomes and limited treatment options. Dingxiang Guanshitong (DGST), a traditional Chinese herbal formulation, has shown potential activity in ESCC, but its molecular mechanisms require further clarification. The current study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic impact and underlying biological actions of DGST on ESCC. Network pharmacology was used to identify candidate DGST constituents and targets, followed by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis. Antitumor effects of DGST was examined in a 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide (4NQO)-induced ESCC mouse model using H&E staining, immunohistochemistry, TUNEL assay, and flow cytometry. Proteomics analysis identified differentially expressed proteins and enriched pathways. In TE-1 cells, TAK1 knockdown/overexpression stable lines were constructed by lentiviral transduction, and pathway involvement was evaluated using immunofluorescence, luciferase reporter assays, CCK-8, Transwell, scratch assays, qRT-PCR, western blotting, and metabolic indicator assays. DGST showed dose-associated suppression of ESCC tumor progression, cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, while promoting apoptosis. Proteomics suggested that DGST affected glycolysis and NF-κB-related pathways. DGST treatment was associated with reduced phosphorylation of TAK1, IκBα, and p65, lower GLUT1, HK2, PFKP, and LDHA expression, decreased ATP levels, and increased MPC1 as well as mitochondrial complex indicators. TAK1 knockdown enhanced the effects of DGST, whereas its overexpression reversed these effects. DGST may inhibit ESCC progression by modulating TAK1/NF-κB/GLUT1 axis-mediated glycolytic reprogramming. The findings elucidate the potential therapeutic value of DGST in the treatment of ESCC and provide mechanistic insights for its clinical application.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.8] MET inhibition exploits conserved regulatory dependencies in malignant rhabdoid tumors
item.description:
Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are lethal, yet genomically simple childhood cancers characterised by universal SWI/SNF dysregulation. Despite this shared molecular framework, the regulatory programs sustaining MRTs and how they wire actionable dependencies, remain poorly defined. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omic profiling and spatial transcriptomics across anatomically and molecularly diverse MRTs, generating a comprehensive multimodal MRT dataset at single-cell resolution. We leveraged this resource to identify candidate tumor-specific dependencies, which were subsequently functionally validated in vitro and in vivo in matched patient-derived models. We found that distinct malignant subpopulations are spatially patterned in complex environmentally shaped topologies, consistent with reciprocal interactions with stromal and immune compartments contributing to intratumoral transcriptional diversity. We identified recurrent transcriptional metaprograms conserved across patients and molecular subtypes, including a previously undescribed shared core rhabdoid program, as well as a metaprogram characterized by extracellular matrix interactions, and preferentially localized in tumor-stroma intermixed neighborhoods, supporting identification of niche conditioning cues. Mechanistically, we identified regulatory wiring driving these metaprograms, with the core shared rhabdoid programme coordinated by a circuit centred on TCF12, ZNF148 and CHD2. Guided by target nominations from our integrated analyses, we performed a curated drug screen using patient-derived MRT models and validated HGF/MET signaling as a selective vulnerability in extrarenal rhabdoid tumors. Pharmacologic MET inhibition was cytotoxic in sensitive models and induced a complete response in vivo using a clinically approved compound. Importantly, MET expression in primary tumors correlated with response, supporting biomarker-guided patient stratification for immediate clinical translation. Collectively, our findings define the molecular architecture of MRTs, reveal conserved regulatory programs beyond anatomical and molecular subtypes, and highlight a targetable signaling axis with immediate translational potential, establishing a framework for precision therapy in this lethal pediatric malignancy.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.9] Glioblastoma model mouse rescue from mortality by brain-targeted catalytically-enhanced angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 mutant-antibody fusion protein
item.description:
We have discovered that an engineered angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)-brain-targeted antibody fusion protein, referred to as ACE2dm-s1, improves survival of CT-2A xenograft glioblastoma (GBM) model mice when administered in combination with a small molecule STING agonist cancer therapeutic. Particularly striking about these survival results is that prior efforts that used losartan, a small molecule angiotensin receptor antagonist that acts on the same Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS) axis that is affected by the action of ACE2dm-s1, showed that this small molecule provided no survival benefit when used as an element of combination therapy in the same CT-2A GBM model used in our experiments. The improved CT-2A mouse survival, which was not observed for ACE2dm-s1 or STING agonist monotherapy, combines with our flow cytometry study results that revealed an ACE2dm-s1-mediated shift of brain immune cell populations toward an anti-tumoral composition to establish ACE2dm-s1's utility as a tumor microenvironment (TME) modulator that could serve as an adjuvant in increasing the efficacy of wide range of cancer treatment modalities including chemotherapeutic agents, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and CAR-T cells.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology

item.title: [1.9] Alpha-aminoadipate in the saccharopine pathway promotes cancer metastasis through sumoylation of transcription machinery
item.description:
Despite studies linking metabolism and cancer, our understanding of the metabolite network that drives metastasis remains incomplete. Through a metabolic RNAi-based screen for cell invasion, we identify alpha-aminoadipate (2-AAA), the intermediate metabolite of aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS) in the saccharopine pathway, as a common pivotal factor in metastasis of human cancers. Metabolite-protein connectivity mapping reveals that 2-AAA binds to SAE1, a crucial component of the SUMO-activating enzyme E1, and enhances SAE1 recruitment to UBA2, facilitating sumoylation. 2-AAA-mediated sumoylation of the RNA polymerase subunit POLR2A then partially promotes cancer cell invasion by inducing the expression of metastasis-promoting genes, including SPG11 and KCTD7. Targeting AASS with cetalkonium chloride, a newly identified small molecule inhibitor against AASS, attenuates cancer cell invasion and tumor metastasis. Our study highlights the mechanism by which metastasis is mediated by metabolite-driven sumoylation and indicates AASS as an effective therapeutic target for mitigating metastatic cancer progression. The role of metabolism in metastasis remains unclear. Here, a metabolic RNAi-based screen for cell invasion and metabolite-protein connectivity mapping reveals a mechanism by which sumoylation driven by alpha-aminoadipate, the intermediate metabolite of aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase, drives metastasis.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.6] Death pathway plasticity in therapy resistance: mechanistic switches and translational opportunities
item.description:
Regulated cell death (RCD) programs in cancer have traditionally been framed as discrete pathways defined by signature effectors, including caspases (apoptosis), RIPK1–RIPK3–MLKL (necroptosis), gasdermins (pyroptosis), lipid peroxidation control nodes (ferroptosis), PARP1–AIF/MIF (parthanatos), and FDX1-dependent lipoylation stress (cuproptosis). Here, we advance an integrated view in which these programs function as a configurable decision network rather than isolated routes. Therapeutic and microenvironmental inputs, such as death ligands, chemoradiotherapy, targeted agents, PARP inhibition, copper ionophores, nutrient/oxidative stress, extracellular matrix detachment, and cytotoxic T-cell pressure, converge on shared hub modules that act as rheostats, routing cells toward distinct execution outcomes or into drug-tolerant persister states. This circuit-level framing explains context-dependent switching and mixed phenotypes, including caspase-8/c-FLIP control of apoptosis–necroptosis, caspase–gasdermin coupling of apoptosis–pyroptosis, and metabolic–redox tuning of ferroptosis susceptibility via SLC7A11–GPX4–ACSL4–FSP1 and autophagy-linked lipid/iron handling. We outline a biomarker and functional assay framework to map tumor death wiring from biopsies and organoid challenges, enabling rational combination strategies that exploit death program plasticity while anticipating resistance and inflammatory toxicities.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] PD-L1 is associated with metabolic adaptation and mitochondrial remodeling in NSCLC cells
item.description:
Tumor metabolism is governed by a complex network of processes that can influence immune evasion. Metabolic dysregulation in tumor cells can lead to the accumulation of metabolites that may influence immune cell function. However, the relationship between PD-L1 expression and tumor cell metabolism remains incompletely understood. Here, we report that PD-L1 expression in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells is associated with increased endocytic activity and altered metabolic flux, particularly in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. PD-L1 expression is aleo associated with mitochondrial remodeling, including alterations in proteins involved in mitochondrial fusion and fission and in mitochondrial respiratory chain components. Integrated multi-omics analyses further identified differential H3K9me3 patterns associated with differences in PD-L1 expression status, including differential H3K9me3 patterns at the PTPRN2 locus. Collectively, our findings suggest that differences in PD-L1 expression status are associated with metabolic, mitochondrial, and epigenetic alterations in NSCLC cells.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [2.0] Perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy in resectable non-small cell lung cancer: a phase 2 trial
item.description:
Resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) carries a high risk of postoperative recurrence, underscoring the need for effective perioperative therapies. This nonrandomized, noncomparative phase 2 trial evaluated neoadjuvant ivonescimab monotherapy (cohort 1) or in combination with chemotherapy (cohort 2), followed by surgery and adjuvant ivonescimab. In cohort 2, the major pathological response (MPR) rate was 70.1% (47/67; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 57.7–80.7); the lower bound of the 80% two-sided CI exceeded the historical control rate of 41% and the primary endpoint was met. The MPR rate in cohort 1 was 60.0% (6/10; 95% CI = 26.2–87.8). Among patients who achieved MPR, 83.3% (5/6) in cohort 1 and 97.9% (46/47) in cohort 2 had residual viable tumor (RVT) of ≤5%, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 36.4% (4/11) patients in cohort 1 and 30.4% (24/79) of those in cohort 2, with no grade 3 or higher hemorrhage or treatment-related death. Treatment-related surgery delay occurred in one (1.3%) patient. Surgery-related AEs related to ivonescimab occurred in 10.0% (1/10) and 10.4% (7/67) patients in the two cohorts, respectively, with no grade 3 or higher events reported. These data support perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy as a promising strategy for resectable NSCLC. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05247684 . In a nonrandomized phase 2 trial, patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer received perioperative ivonescimab as monotherapy or with chemotherapy, leading to encouraging pathological response rates in both cohorts, and sustained circulating tumor DNA negativity throughout neoadjuvant therapy may be predictive of response.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.9] Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
item.description:
Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1–8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9–13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance. Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.
— Source: Cancer : nature.com subject feeds

item.title: [1.5] Early Progression Cells mark a stem-like state associated with pancreatic cancer initiation and progression
item.description:
Pancreatic cancer is deemed to progress from microscopic pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanINs). However, low grade PanINs are frequently detected in the general population without presentation or increased risk of developing cancer, suggesting that many PanINs never progress to tumours. What precisely characterises PanINs that develop into tumours is insufficiently understood. Using a mouse model where pancreatitis-induced tissue injury promotes pancreatic cancer from rare KrasG12D cells, we identify Early Progression Cells (EPCs) as a new entity, a novel population of cancer stem-like cells. Transcriptomic analyses illustrate EPCs as stress-adapted, inflammation responsive stem cells that also upregulate gene programmes indicative of microenvironment remodelling. Using identified EPC protein markers, we show that EPCs are prevalent in early metaplastic stages and in PanIN progression from low grade to high grade but are rarer in tumours. PanIN- and tumour-derived sphere and organoid assays demonstrate that EPCs possess all characteristics of stem cells in vitro and are dependent on Nupr1 stress response pathways for survival and growth. We identify APP-CD74 as a novel cell-cell interaction pathway between EPCs and neighbouring epithelial cells in PanINs and tumours. Inhibition of CD74 activity in vitro induces high-grade PanIN organoid death, suggesting EPCs are critical for high-grade PanINs. Using spatial transcriptomics of human samples, we detect gene signatures of EPCs in distinct regions of human PanIN and PDAC tissues, including APP-CD74 interactions, providing compelling evidence that EPCs are relevant to human disease. Further understanding of EPC biology will likely uncover new knowledge on why rare PanINs progress towards tumours.
— Source: bioRxiv Subject Collection: Cancer Biology
